"Not that either. That would put the court in too bad a light," replied Bilibin. "It's not treachery, not villainy, not stupidity—it's just like Ulm... it's..." He seemed to be searching for the right expression. "It's... it's a case of Mack. We've been Macked," he concluded, feeling he had produced a fresh witticism that would make the rounds. His previously furrowed brow smoothed out with pleasure, and with a slight smile he began examining his nails.
"You know, my dear fellow," said Bilibin, following him, "I've been thinking about you. Why are you going?"
"Stop joking, Bilibin," said Bolkonski.

"I'm speaking sincerely, as a friend! Think about it. Where are you going, and why, when you could stay here? You're facing one of two outcomes"—and the skin over his left temple puckered—"either you won't reach your regiment before peace is concluded, or you'll share in the defeat and disgrace of Kutuzov's entire army."
And Bilibin smoothed his temple, feeling his dilemma was unanswerable.
"My dear fellow, you are a hero!" said Bilibin.

That same night, after taking leave of the Minister of War, Bolkonski set off to rejoin the army, not knowing where he would find it and fearing he might be captured by the French on the way to Krems.

He remembered words from Bonaparte's address to his army at the beginning of the campaign: "That Russian army which English gold has transported from the ends of the earth—we shall make it share the same fate as the army at Ulm." (in French) These words awakened in him astonishment at his hero's genius, a sting of wounded pride, and a hope for glory. "And if all that's left is to die?" he thought. "Well, if it comes to that, I'll do it no worse than anyone else."
* Cette armée russe que l'or de l'Angleterre a transportée des extrémités de l'univers, nous allons lui faire éprouver le même sort—(le sort de l'armée d'Ulm).
"Here's our beloved Orthodox Russian army," thought Bolkonski, remembering Bilibin's words.
He turned around. Nesvitsky's handsome face was looking out of a small window. Nesvitsky, chewing something and moving his moist lips, was waving his arm and calling him over.
"Bolkonski! Bolkonski! Can't you hear me? Come here, quickly!" he shouted.

Going inside, Prince Andrew found Nesvitsky and another adjutant eating. They spun around to face him, asking if he had any news. On their familiar faces he read alarm and anxiety. This was especially striking on Nesvitsky's face, which was usually so cheerful.
"Where is the commander in chief?" asked Bolkonski.
"Well, is it true? Peace and surrender?" asked Nesvitsky.
"And us, my dear fellow! It's terrible! I was wrong to laugh at Mack—we're getting it even worse," said Nesvitsky. "But sit down and have something to eat."

"Well, I've managed to pack everything I need onto two horses," said Nesvitsky. "They made up excellent packs for me—good enough to cross the Bohemian mountains. Things look grim, old friend! But what's wrong with you? You must be sick—you're shivering like that," he added, noticing Prince Andrew flinch as if from an electric shock.
"I can't make it out at all," said Nesvitsky.

Passing Kutuzov's carriage and the exhausted saddle horses of his entourage, with their Cossacks talking loudly together, Prince Andrew entered the hallway. Kutuzov himself, he was told, was inside with Prince Bagration and Weyrother—the Austrian general who had replaced Schmidt. In the corridor, little Kozlovsky was squatting on his heels in front of a clerk. The clerk, with his sleeves rolled up, was scribbling furiously on an overturned tub. Kozlovsky's face looked haggard—he clearly hadn't slept all night either. He glanced at Prince Andrew without so much as a nod.
"Can't write that fast, Your Honor," said the clerk, looking up at Kozlovsky with irritation and disrespect.

Through the door came the sounds of Kutuzov's voice—agitated and unhappy—broken by another voice, one Prince Andrew didn't recognize. From the sound of these voices, from Kozlovsky's distracted expression, from the clerk's rudeness, from the fact that both Kozlovsky and the clerk were squatting on the floor by a tub so close to the commander in chief, and from the noisy laughter of the Cossacks holding the horses by the window—from all of this, Prince Andrew sensed that something critical and catastrophic was about to happen.
He turned to Kozlovsky with urgent questions.
"One moment, Prince," said Kozlovsky. "Orders for Bagration."

Prince Andrew moved toward the door where the voices were coming from. Just as he was about to open it, the voices fell silent, the door swung open, and Kutuzov appeared in the doorway with his eagle nose and puffy face. Prince Andrew stood directly in front of him, but the expression in the commander in chief's one good eye showed he was so consumed by thoughts and worries that he didn't even register who was standing there. He stared straight at his adjutant's face without recognizing him.
"Well, have you finished?" he said to Kozlovsky.
Bagration, a lean middle-aged man of medium height with a firm, impassive face of Eastern features, emerged behind the commander in chief.
"I have the honor to present myself," said Prince Andrew, louder this time, holding out an envelope to Kutuzov.
Kutuzov walked out to the porch with Bagration.
"Well, goodbye, Prince," he said to Bagration. "My blessing, and may Christ be with you in your great endeavor!"

His face suddenly softened and tears welled in his eyes. With his left hand he drew Bagration toward him, and with his right—on which he wore a ring—he made the sign of the cross over him in what was clearly a habitual gesture, offering his puffy cheek. But Bagration kissed him on the neck instead.
"Christ be with you!" Kutuzov repeated, and turned toward his carriage. "Get in with me," he said to Bolkonski.
"Your Excellency, I would like to be of use here. Allow me to stay with Prince Bagration's detachment."
"Get in," said Kutuzov, and when he noticed Bolkonski still hesitating, he added: "I need good officers myself. Need them myself!"

"There is still much, much ahead of us," he said with the penetrating insight of an old man who seemed to understand everything passing through Bolkonski's mind. "If even a tenth of his detachment comes back, I shall thank God," he added, as if speaking to himself.

Prince Andrew glanced at Kutuzov's face, only a foot away, and found his eyes drawn to the carefully washed seams of the scar near his temple where a bullet had pierced his skull at Ismail, and to the empty eye socket. "Yes, he has earned the right to speak so calmly about those men's deaths," thought Bolkonski.

Kutuzov did not answer. He seemed to have forgotten what he'd been saying and sat sunk in thought. Five minutes later, swaying gently on the soft springs of the carriage, he turned to Prince Andrew. There was not a trace of emotion on his face. With subtle irony, he began questioning Prince Andrew about the details of his interview with the Emperor, about the remarks he'd heard at court regarding the Krems affair, and about certain ladies they both knew.

On November 1st, Kutuzov had received intelligence from a spy that the army he commanded was in a nearly hopeless situation. The spy reported that the French, having crossed the bridge at Vienna, were advancing in massive force toward Kutuzov's line of communication with the reinforcements arriving from Russia. If Kutuzov chose to remain at Krems, Napoleon's army of a hundred and fifty thousand men would completely cut him off and surround his exhausted force of forty thousand—and he would find himself in the same position as Mack at Ulm. If he chose to abandon the road connecting him with the approaching Russian reinforcements, he would have to march without roads into the unknown terrain of the Bohemian mountains, fighting off a superior enemy while giving up all hope of linking up with Buxhöwden. If he chose to retreat along the road from Krems to Olmütz to join the incoming Russian troops, he risked being overtaken on that road by the French who had crossed the Vienna bridge—and burdened by his baggage and supply trains, he would have to fight on the march against an enemy three times his strength attacking from two directions.
Kutuzov chose this last option.

The French, according to the spy, had crossed the Vienna bridge and were making forced marches toward Znaim, which lay sixty-six miles along Kutuzov's line of retreat. If he reached Znaim before the French, there was real hope of saving the army. If the French got there first, the entire army faced either the kind of humiliation Mack had suffered at Ulm, or total annihilation. But it was impossible for Kutuzov to reach Znaim ahead of the French with his whole army. The French road from Vienna to Znaim was shorter and better than the Russian road from Krems to Znaim.

The night he received this intelligence, Kutuzov sent Bagration's advance guard—four thousand men—to the right, across the hills from the Krems-Znaim road to the Vienna-Znaim road. Bagration was to make this march without stopping to rest and to take up a position facing Vienna with Znaim at his back. If he managed to get there ahead of the French, he was to hold them off for as long as possible. Kutuzov himself, with the rest of the army and all the supply trains, took the road to Znaim.

Marching thirty miles through a stormy night across trackless hills, with hungry, poorly shod soldiers, and losing a third of his men as stragglers along the way, Bagration reached the Vienna-Znaim road at Hollabrünn a few hours ahead of the French approaching from Vienna. Kutuzov and his supply trains still had several days of marching before they could reach Znaim. So Bagration, with his four thousand hungry, exhausted men, would have to hold off the entire enemy army for days at Hollabrünn—which was clearly impossible. But a twist of fate made the impossible possible. The success of the trick that had handed the Vienna bridge to the French without a fight led Murat to try deceiving Kutuzov in the same way. When Murat encountered Bagration's small detachment on the Znaim road, he mistook it for Kutuzov's entire army. To ensure he could crush it completely, he waited for the rest of his troops still coming from Vienna, and in the meantime offered a three-day truce on the condition that both armies hold their positions without moving. Murat declared that peace negotiations were already underway, and that he was therefore proposing the truce to avoid unnecessary bloodshed. Count Nostitz, the Austrian general commanding the forward positions, believed Murat's envoy and pulled back, leaving Bagration's division exposed. Another envoy rode to the Russian lines to announce the peace talks and offer the Russian army a three-day truce. Bagration replied that he had no authority to accept or reject a truce and sent his adjutant to Kutuzov to report the offer.

A truce was Kutuzov's only chance to buy time, give Bagration's worn-out troops some rest, and let the baggage and heavy supply trains—whose movements were hidden from the French—advance at least one more stage toward Znaim. The truce offer was the only chance, and a completely unexpected one, of saving the army. As soon as he received the news, Kutuzov immediately dispatched Adjutant General Wintzingerode to the enemy camp. Wintzingerode was not merely to agree to the truce but also to propose terms of surrender—and meanwhile, Kutuzov sent his adjutants racing back to push the movement of the entire army's baggage trains along the Krems-Znaim road as fast as possible. Bagration's exhausted and hungry detachment, which alone was covering the movement of the supply trains and the whole army, had to remain in place facing an enemy eight times its size.

Kutuzov's expectation—that the surrender proposal (which committed him to nothing) would buy time for part of the transport to get through, and that Murat's mistake would soon be discovered—proved correct. As soon as Bonaparte, who was at Schönbrunn sixteen miles from Hollabrünn, received Murat's dispatch with the proposed truce and surrender terms, he saw through the ruse and wrote the following letter to Murat:

Bonaparte's adjutant rode at full gallop with this furious letter to Murat. Bonaparte himself, not trusting his generals, moved out with the entire Guard toward the battlefield, determined not to let a ready victim escape. And Bagration's four thousand men, meanwhile, cheerfully lit their campfires, dried and warmed themselves, and cooked porridge for the first time in three days—not one of them knowing or imagining what awaited them.

Between three and four in the afternoon, Prince Andrew—who had kept pressing Kutuzov for permission—arrived at Grunth and reported to Bagration. Bonaparte's aide-de-camp hadn't yet reached Murat's forces, and the battle hadn't begun. In Bagration's detachment, nobody had any clear picture of the larger situation. Some spoke of peace but didn't really believe it was possible; others talked about a battle but didn't believe it was actually imminent. Bagration, knowing that Bolkonski was one of Kutuzov's favorite and trusted adjutants, received him with special respect, explaining that there would probably be an engagement that day or the next, and giving him full freedom to either stay through the battle or join the rearguard and oversee the order of retreat, "which is also very important."
"There you have the pleasures of camp life, Prince," said the staff officer (in French).

Another company, a lucky one since not every unit had vodka, was gathered around a pockmarked, broad-shouldered sergeant major who tilted a small keg, filling one by one the canteen lids held out to him. The soldiers raised the lids to their lips with something like reverence, drained them, swished the vodka around in their mouths, and walked away with brightened faces, licking their lips and wiping them on the sleeves of their greatcoats. Every face was as calm as if all this were happening back home during a peaceful camp, not within sight of the enemy before a battle in which at least half of them would fall. Two soldiers held him down while two others lashed his bare back with switches. The man screamed in an unnatural, animal way. A heavy-set major paced up and down the line, ignoring the screams, and kept repeating:
"We'll make you dance the way we did under Suvorov," said Dolokhov (in French).

The regimental commander, a thin, frail-looking old man with a kind smile—his drooping eyelids covering more than half his eyes and giving him a gentle expression—rode up to Bagration and greeted him like a host welcoming an honored guest. He reported that his regiment had been attacked by French cavalry, and that although the attack had been repulsed, he'd lost more than half his men. He used the military term "repulsed" to describe what had happened, but in truth he did not himself know what had happened during that half hour to the troops entrusted to him, and could not say with certainty whether the attack had been repulsed or his regiment had been broken up. All he really knew was that at the start of the action, shells and bullets had begun flying all over his regiment, hitting his men. Then someone had shouted "Cavalry!" and his soldiers had started shooting. They were still shooting now—not at the cavalry, which had vanished, but at French infantry that had moved into the hollow and was firing at them. Prince Bagration looked at Tushin. He was clearly reluctant to distrust Bolkonski's passionate opinion, yet not quite able to fully accept it either. He nodded and told Tushin he could go. Prince Andrew walked out with him.

Many of his former bachelor friends were no longer in Petersburg. The Guards had gone to the front. Dolokhov had been demoted to the ranks. Anatole was somewhere in the provinces with the army. Prince Andrew was abroad. So Pierre had no chance to spend his evenings the way he used to, or to have intimate, heart-to-heart conversations with an older friend he respected. His entire time was consumed by dinners and balls, mostly spent at Prince Vasili's house in the company of the stout princess, his wife, and their beautiful daughter Helene.
In the early winter of 1805-06, Pierre received one of Anna Pavlovna's usual pink invitations, with a note added: 'You will find the beautiful Helene here, whom it is always a delight to see.'

When he read that line, Pierre felt for the first time that some connection that others could see had formed between him and Helene. The thought both alarmed him—as if some obligation were being placed on him that he couldn't fulfill—and pleased him as an intriguing possibility.

"Wait, I have something in mind for you this evening." She glanced at Helene and smiled. "My dear Helene, be kind to my poor aunt who adores you. Go keep her company for ten minutes. And so it won't be too boring, here is the dear count, who I'm sure won't refuse to go with you."
Pierre sincerely agreed about Helene's perfect manners. Whenever he thought of Helene, it was only of her beauty and her remarkable ability to appear silently dignified in any social setting.

The old aunt received the two young people in her corner but seemed more interested in hiding her adoration for Helene and showing her fear of Anna Pavlovna. She looked at her niece as if asking what to do with these visitors. As she left them, Anna Pavlovna touched Pierre's sleeve again: "I hope you won't say it's boring at my house again." She glanced at Helene.

Helene smiled with a look that said she couldn't imagine anyone seeing her without being enchanted. The aunt coughed, swallowed, and told Helene in French how pleased she was to see her, then turned to Pierre with the same greeting and the same look. In the middle of a halting, dull conversation, Helene turned to Pierre with the beautiful, radiant smile she gave everyone. Pierre was so used to that smile, and it meant so little to him, that he paid no attention. The aunt was talking about a collection of snuffboxes that had belonged to Pierre's father, Count Bezukhov, and showed them her own. Princess Helene asked to see the portrait of the aunt's husband on the lid.

He half stood up, meaning to walk around, but the aunt handed him the snuffbox across Helene's back. Helene leaned forward to make room and looked back with a smile. She was wearing, as always at evening parties, a dress cut very low at the front and back, in the fashion of the time. Her bust, which had always seemed like marble to Pierre, was so close that his nearsighted eyes couldn't help noticing the living warmth of her neck and shoulders, so near his lips that he would only have had to bend his head slightly to touch them. He felt the warmth of her body, smelled her perfume, and heard the creaking of her corset as she moved. He no longer saw her marble beauty as a complete whole unified with her dress—instead, he saw all the charm of her body barely concealed by her clothing. And once he had seen this, he couldn't unsee it, just as you can't restore an illusion you've seen through.

"So you've never noticed before how beautiful I am?" Helene seemed to say. "You hadn't realized I'm a woman? Yes, I am a woman who could belong to anyone—to you too," said her glance. And at that moment Pierre felt that Helene not only could but must be his wife, and that it couldn't be any other way.

She paused, as women always do after mentioning their age. "If you marry, that will be a different matter," she continued, her glance linking them both. Pierre didn't look at Helene and she didn't look at him. But she was just as terrifyingly close. He mumbled something and blushed.

In November 1805, Prince Vasili had to make an inspection tour of four different provinces. He had arranged this for himself so he could visit his neglected estates at the same time, pick up his son Anatole from his regiment, and take him to visit old Prince Bolkonski to arrange a match with the rich old man's daughter. But before leaving home for these new tasks, Prince Vasili had to settle things with Pierre, who had lately been spending whole days at home—that is, at Prince Vasili's house where he was staying—and had been absurd, excited, and foolish in Helene's presence (as a man in love should be), but had not yet proposed.

Six weeks after Anna Pavlovna's party, and after the sleepless night when Pierre had decided that marrying Helene would be a disaster and he should avoid her and leave, Pierre—despite that decision—had not left Prince Vasili's house. He felt with horror that in everyone's eyes he was being drawn closer to her every day, that he could no longer see her the way he used to, that he couldn't break away from her, and that although it would be terrible, he would have to tie his fate to hers. He might have been able to free himself, but Prince Vasili—who had rarely hosted gatherings before—now threw a party almost every evening at which Pierre had to be present unless he wanted to spoil everyone's enjoyment and disappoint their expectations. In the rare moments when he was home, Prince Vasili would take Pierre's hand in passing and draw it downward, or absent-mindedly offer his wrinkled, clean-shaven cheek for Pierre to kiss, saying: 'See you tomorrow,' or 'Come to dinner or I won't see you,' or 'I'm staying in just for your sake.' And although Prince Vasili, when he stayed in 'for Pierre's sake,' barely exchanged two words with him, Pierre felt he couldn't let him down. Every day he told himself the same thing: 'It's time I figured out who she really is. Was I wrong before, or am I wrong now? No, she's not stupid, she's a wonderful woman,' he sometimes told himself. 'She never makes a mistake, never says anything foolish. She says little, but what she says is always clear and simple—so she can't be stupid. She was never embarrassed and isn't embarrassed now, so she can't be a bad person!' He had often started thinking aloud or making reflections in her company, and she always responded either with a brief, appropriate remark—showing it didn't interest her—or with a silent look and smile that more clearly than anything demonstrated her superiority. She was right to consider all arguments meaningless compared to that smile.

On Helene's name day, a small gathering of 'just family'—as his wife put it—assembled for supper at Prince Vasili's. All these friends and relatives had been given to understand that the young woman's fate would be decided that evening. The guests took their seats at supper. Princess Kuragina, a stout, imposing woman who had once been beautiful, sat at the head of the table. On either side of her were the most important guests—an old general and his wife, and Anna Pavlovna Scherer. At the other end sat the younger and less important guests, along with family members, and there too sat Pierre and Helene, side by side. Prince Vasili wasn't eating supper; he circled the table in high spirits, sitting down with one guest after another and making casual, pleasant remarks to each—except to Pierre and Helene, whose presence he seemed not to notice. He kept the whole party lively. The wax candles burned brightly; the silver and crystal gleamed, as did the ladies' gowns and the gold and silver of the men's epaulettes. Servants in scarlet livery moved around the table; the clatter of plates, knives, and glasses blended with the animated buzz of several conversations. At one end, an old chamberlain was assuring an old baroness of his passionate love for her, at which she laughed. At the other end, someone was telling the story of some poor Mary Viktorovna's misfortunes. In the center, Prince Vasili held everyone's attention. With a playful smile, he was telling the ladies about last Wednesday's meeting of the Imperial Council, at which Sergei Kuzmich Vyazminitov, the new military governor general of Petersburg, had received and read the now-famous letter from Emperor Alexander to Sergei Kuzmich. In it, the Emperor said he was receiving declarations of loyalty from all sides, that the one from Petersburg gave him special pleasure, and that he was proud to lead such a nation and would strive to be worthy of it. Everywhere, new stories circulated about individual acts of heroism by Russian officers and soldiers at Austerlitz. One man had saved a regimental standard, another had killed five Frenchmen, a third had loaded five cannons single-handedly. People who didn't know Berg personally told how he had taken his sword in his left hand after being wounded in the right, and pressed forward. Of Bolkonski, nothing was said, and only those who knew him personally mourned that he had died so young, leaving behind a pregnant wife and an eccentric father.

Nesvitsky was there as a longtime club member. Pierre, who at his wife's insistence had let his hair grow and given up his spectacles, moved through the rooms in fashionable clothes but looking sad and listless. Here, as everywhere, he was surrounded by an atmosphere of deference to his wealth, and being accustomed to dominating such people, he treated them with distracted contempt.

Nicholas Rostov sat with Denisov and his new acquaintance Dolokhov near the middle of the table. Across from them sat Pierre, next to Prince Nesvitsky. Count Ilya Rostov, along with the other committee members, sat facing Bagration and, as the very embodiment of Moscow hospitality, served as the prince's host.

"To the health of our Sovereign, the Emperor!" he cried, and at that moment his kind eyes glistened with tears of joy and emotion. The band instantly struck up "Conquest's joyful thunder waken..." Everyone rose and shouted "Hurrah!" Bagration also stood and shouted "Hurrah!" in exactly the same voice he had used on the battlefield at Schon Grabern. Young Rostov's ecstatic voice rang out above the three hundred others. He nearly wept. "To the health of our Sovereign, the Emperor!" he roared, "Hurrah!" He drained his glass in one gulp and smashed it on the floor. Many followed his example, and the loud cheering went on for a long time. When the noise died down, the footmen swept away the broken glass and everyone sat down again, smiling at the racket they had made and exchanging remarks. The old count stood up again, glanced at a note beside his plate, and proposed another toast: "To the health of the hero of our last campaign, Prince Peter Ivanovich Bagration!" His blue eyes filled with tears once more. "Hurrah!" the three hundred voices cried again. But this time, instead of the band, a choir began singing a cantata composed by Paul Ivanovich Kutuzov:
Hearing that shout and seeing who it was directed at, Nesvitsky and the man sitting beside Pierre turned to him in alarm.

At the very instant he said those words, Pierre felt that the question of his wife's guilt — which had been torturing him all day — was finally and conclusively answered: yes, she was guilty. He hated her and was forever separated from her. Despite Denisov's plea that he stay out of it, Rostov agreed to serve as Dolokhov's second. After dinner, he discussed the arrangements for the duel with Nesvitsky, who was Pierre's second. Pierre went home, but Rostov, Dolokhov, and Denisov stayed on at the club until late, listening to the gypsy singers and other performers.

"I'll tell you the whole secret of dueling in two words. If you're going to fight a duel and you sit down to write your will and tender letters to your parents, thinking you might be killed — you're a fool and you're done for. But if you go with the firm intention of killing your opponent as quickly and surely as possible, then everything will be fine. That's what our bear hunter back in Kostroma used to tell me: 'Everyone's afraid of a bear,' he'd say, 'but once you see one, all your fear vanishes — your only thought is not to let him get away!' That's how it is with me. Until tomorrow, mon cher." (in French)
* À demain, mon cher.

The next morning, at eight o'clock, Pierre and Nesvitsky drove to the Sokolniki forest, where they found Dolokhov, Denisov, and Rostov already waiting. Pierre had the look of a man consumed by thoughts that had nothing to do with the matter at hand. His drawn face was sallow. He had obviously not slept. He kept looking around distractedly and squinting as if dazzled by the sun. He was entirely preoccupied with two thoughts: his wife's guilt, of which he no longer had the slightest doubt after his sleepless night, and the blamelessness of Dolokhov, who had no reason to protect the honor of a man who meant nothing to him. "I would probably have done the same in his place," Pierre thought. "Actually, I'm sure I would have. So why this duel? Why this killing? Either I'll kill him, or he'll hit me in the head, or the elbow, or the knee. Why can't I just leave — run away — disappear somewhere?" Such thoughts kept passing through his mind. But at those very moments he would ask, in a particularly calm, distracted tone that earned the respect of the onlookers, "Will this take much longer? Is everything ready?"
When everything was prepared — the sabers planted in the snow to mark the barriers and the pistols loaded — Nesvitsky walked up to Pierre.

"Then allow me to convey your regrets, and I'm sure your opponent will accept them," said Nesvitsky, who, like everyone else involved — and like everyone in such situations — still couldn't quite believe it had come to an actual duel. "You know, Count, it's far more honorable to admit a mistake than to let things become irreparable. There was no real insult on either side. Let me speak to them..."
"Sideways! Shield yourself with your pistol!" shouted Nesvitsky.

Pierre, with a gentle smile of pity and remorse, his arms and legs spread helplessly, stood with his broad chest facing Dolokhov directly and looked at him with sorrow. Denisov, Rostov, and Nesvitsky squeezed their eyes shut. At that same instant they heard a shot and Dolokhov's furious cry.
Nesvitsky stopped him and took him home.

"'I'm not that stupid.... Just you try.... You clear out of this,' she used to say (in French). Seeing how successful she was with young and old men and women, Pierre often couldn't understand why he didn't love her.
* Allez-vous promener

"It's all her fault," he told himself. "But what does that matter? Why did I tie myself to her? Why did I say 'I love you' (in French) to her — which was a lie, and worse than a lie? I'm guilty and must endure... what? A stain on my name? A lifelong misfortune? Oh, that's nonsense," he thought. "A stain on my name and honor — that's something separate from who I really am."
* Je vous aime

But the moment he imagined himself calmed by such thoughts, she suddenly came into his mind as she had been in those moments when he'd most strongly expressed his fake love for her, and he felt the blood rush to his heart and had to get up again and move around and smash and tear at whatever came to hand. "Why did I tell her 'I love you'?" he kept repeating to himself. And after saying it for the tenth time, Moliere's words came to him: "Mais que diable allait-il faire dans cette galère?" ("But what the devil was he doing in that galley?") — and he began to laugh at himself.

"If you won't answer, I'll tell you myself..." Helene continued. "You believe everything people tell you. You were told" — Helene laughed — "that Dolokhov was my lover," she said in French with her characteristic blunt directness, uttering the word amant as casually as any other word, "and you believed it! Well, what have you proved? What does this duel prove? That you're a fool, que vous êtes un sot, but everybody already knew that. What's going to happen now? I'll be the laughingstock of all Moscow. Everyone will say that you, drunk and clueless about what you were doing, challenged a man you were jealous of for no reason." Helene's voice rose and she grew more and more agitated. "A man who is better than you in every way..."

Helene's face became terrible. She shrieked and sprang aside. His father's nature showed itself in Pierre. He felt the thrill and ecstasy of rage. He hurled down the marble slab, shattering it, and lunging toward her with outstretched hands, he roared "Get out!" in such a terrible voice that the whole house heard it with horror. God knows what he would have done if Helene hadn't fled the room.
(Frühstück: breakfast.)

Another five days passed, and then the young Prince Nicholas Andreevich was baptized. The wet nurse held the coverlet with her chin while the priest used a goose feather to anoint the baby's small red, wrinkled soles and palms.

His grandfather, who was his godfather, trembling and afraid of dropping him, carried the infant around the battered tin font and handed him over to the godmother, Princess Mary. Prince Andrew sat in another room, faint with fear that the baby might be drowned in the font, and waited for the ceremony to end. He looked up joyfully at the baby when the nurse brought him over, and nodded his approval when she told him that the wax with the baby's hair had not sunk in the font but had floated.
"Nicholas, will you come to Iogel's? Please do!" said Natasha. "He invited you, and Vasili Dmitrich is coming too."
(Denisov.)
(To indicate he didn't want more tea.)

"You hate it. Then change it, purify yourself; and as you are purified, you will gain wisdom. Look at your life, my dear sir. How have you spent it? In wild debauchery, receiving everything from society and giving nothing in return. You became the owner of a great fortune. How have you used it? What have you done for your neighbor? Have you ever thought about your tens of thousands of slaves? Have you helped them physically or morally? No! You have profited by their labor to lead a dissolute life. That is what you have done. Have you chosen a role in which you could serve your neighbor? No! You have spent your life in idleness. Then you married, my dear sir — took on responsibility for guiding a young woman — and what have you done? You didn't help her find the path of truth, my dear sir. You pushed her into an abyss of deceit and misery. A man insulted you and you shot him, and you say you don't know God and hate your life. That's not surprising, my dear sir!"

Thanks to Anna Mikhaylovna's efforts, his own instincts, and the peculiarities of his reserved temperament, Boris had managed during his military service to position himself very advantageously. He was aide-de-camp to a very important personage, had been sent on a very important mission to Prussia, and had just returned as a special courier. He had thoroughly mastered that unwritten code he had been so pleased to discover at Olmutz — the code by which an ensign could outrank a general, and success in the service depended not on effort or work, or courage or perseverance, but simply on knowing how to get along with those who dispense rewards. He was often surprised at how rapidly he advanced and at others' inability to grasp these principles. As a result, his entire manner of life, all his old friendships, all his plans for the future, had completely changed. He was not rich, but would spend his last ruble to be better dressed than others, and would sooner deny himself many pleasures than be seen in a shabby carriage or an old uniform. He cultivated friendships only with those above him in position who might be useful. He liked Petersburg and looked down on Moscow. His memories of the Rostov household and his boyhood love for Natasha were unpleasant to him, and he had not once visited the Rostovs since the day he left for the army. To be at Anna Pavlovna's drawing room he considered an important career advance, and he immediately understood his role, letting his hostess make use of whatever interest he could offer. He himself carefully assessed each face, evaluating the potential for forming connections with each person present and the advantages that might result. He took the seat indicated beside the beautiful Helene and listened to the general conversation.

"Ah, my dear vicomte," Anna Pavlovna chimed in (in French), "L'Urope" — for some reason she pronounced it Urope, as if this were a specially refined French pronunciation she could permit herself when speaking with a Frenchman — "L'Urope ne sera jamais notre alliée sincère" ("Europe will never be our sincere ally").
* "Europe will never be our sincere ally."

"In short, having hoped to settle things by looking warlike, we find we've stumbled into an actual war — and what's more, a war on our own borders, with and for the King of Prussia. We have everything in perfect order; there's just one small thing missing — namely, a commander in chief. Since it was felt that the Austerlitz success might have been more decisive if the commander in chief hadn't been so young, all our octogenarians were reviewed, and of Prozorovski and Kamensky, the latter was chosen. The general arrives, Suvorov-style, in a peasant cart, and is greeted with cheers of joy and triumph.

"After Austerlitz!" said Prince Andrew darkly. "No, thank you. I've promised myself never to serve in the active Russian army again. And I won't — not even if Bonaparte were here at Smolensk threatening Bald Hills — even then I wouldn't serve in the Russian army! Well, as I was saying," he continued, regaining his composure, "now there's the recruiting. My father is chief of the Third District, and my only way of avoiding active service is to serve under him."

"Delighted to see you. I'm very glad to see you," she said to Pierre (in French) as he kissed her hand. She had known him as a child, and now his friendship with Andrew, his marital troubles, and above all his kind, simple face inclined her warmly toward him. She looked at him with her beautiful, radiant eyes, and seemed to say: "I like you very much, but please don't make fun of my people." After the first greetings they sat down.
* Charmée de vous voir. Je suis très contente de vous voir.
"Andrew!" said Princess Mary imploringly. "You must know that this is a woman," Prince Andrew said to Pierre (in French).
"Andrew, for God's sake!" Princess Mary repeated (in French).
* Il faut que vous sachiez que c'est une femme.
* Andrew, au nom de Dieu!
"But, my dear friend," said Prince Andrew (in French), "on the contrary, you should be grateful that I'm explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man."
* Mais, ma bonne amie, vous devriez au contraire m'être reconnaissante de ce que j'explique à Pierre votre intimité avec ce jeune homme.

"Oh sir, sir, what a sin! And you who have a son!" she began, her pallor flushing to vivid red. "Sir, what have you said? God forgive you!" And she crossed herself. "Lord forgive him! My dear, what does it mean?" she asked, turning to Princess Mary. She stood up and, nearly in tears, began gathering her things into her wallet. She was clearly frightened and ashamed to have accepted hospitality in a house where such things could be said, and at the same time sorry to lose the charity this house provided.

"Come, Pelageya, I was joking," said Pierre. "Princess, I give you my word, I didn't mean to offend her (in French). I meant nothing — I was only joking," he said, smiling shyly and trying to make amends. "It was all my fault, and Andrew was only joking."
* Princesse, ma parole, je n'ai pas voulu l'offenser.

"Wostov! How are you, how are you?" he called out in the same voice as at the regiment — but Rostov noticed sadly that beneath this familiar ease and energy, something new, sinister, and hidden showed in Denisov's expression and tone.

"Me — petition the Empewo'!" exclaimed Denisov in a voice that tried hard to recover its old fire but came out sounding like impotent irritation. "What for? If I were a wobber I'd ask for mercy, but I'm being court-martialed for bwinging wobbers to justice. Let them twy me — I'm not afwaid of anyone. I've served the Tsar and my countwy honowably and have not stolen! And am I to be degwaded? Listen, I'm w'iting to them stwaight: 'If I had wobbed the Tweasuwy...'"
"Haven't I said I'm not going to gwovel?" Denisov interrupted, and went back to reading his paper.

Boris was among the few present on the banks of the Niemen on the day the two Emperors met. He saw the raft decorated with monograms, saw Napoleon pass before the French Guards on the far bank, saw the thoughtful face of Emperor Alexander as he sat silently in a tavern on the riverbank awaiting Napoleon's arrival, and watched both Emperors board their boats and meet on the raft — Napoleon stepping forward quickly to greet Alexander and extending his hand — before they both disappeared into the pavilion. Since entering the highest circles, Boris had made it his habit to observe everything carefully and note it down. At the time of the Tilsit meeting, he asked about the names and uniforms of Napoleon's entourage and listened closely to every word spoken by important people. When the Emperors entered the pavilion, he checked his watch and remembered to check it again when Alexander emerged. The meeting had lasted one hour and fifty-three minutes. He recorded this that same evening among other facts he considered historically significant. Since the Emperor's suite was very small, being present at Tilsit for this interview was a matter of great importance for anyone who valued his career. Boris, having secured this advantage, felt his position was now firmly established. He had not only become known — people had grown used to him and accepted him. Twice he had carried out missions for the Emperor himself, so that the sovereign knew his face, and everyone at court, far from giving him the cold shoulder as they had at first when they considered him a newcomer, would now have been surprised had he been absent.
"No — I only wonder how you got away from your regiment. I'll be with you in a moment," he said (in French), answering someone who called him.
* Dans un moment je suis à vous.
"Will Your Majesty allow me to consult the colonel?" said Alexander, and he took a few quick steps toward Prince Kozlovsky, the battalion commander.
"To whom shall it be given?" Emperor Alexander asked Kozlovsky in Russian, in a low voice.
Kozlovsky scanned the ranks with a resolute eye, and his gaze swept over Rostov.

Count Kochubey didn't finish. He stood up, took Prince Andrew's arm, and went to meet a tall, bald, fair-haired man of about forty, with a large open forehead and a long face of unusual, peculiar whiteness, who was just entering. The newcomer wore a blue tailcoat with a cross on a ribbon around his neck and a star on his left breast. It was Speransky. Prince Andrew recognized him at once and felt a throb within him — as happens at critical moments of life. Whether it was respect, envy, or anticipation, he couldn't tell. Speransky's whole figure was of a distinctive type that made him instantly recognizable. In the society Prince Andrew frequented, he had never encountered anyone who combined such awkward, clumsy gestures with such calm self-possession; he had never seen such a resolute yet gentle expression as that in those half-closed, slightly moist eyes, or so firm a smile that expressed nothing in particular; nor had he heard such a refined, smooth, soft voice. Above all, he had never seen such delicate whiteness of face and hands — broad hands, but very plump, soft, and white. Such whiteness and softness Prince Andrew had only seen on the faces of soldiers who had been in the hospital a long time. This was Speransky, Secretary of State, the Emperor's reporter, and his companion at Erfurt, where he had met and talked with Napoleon more than once.

"I am an admirer of Montesquieu," replied Prince Andrew (in French), "and his idea that the principle of monarchies is honor strikes me as indisputable. Certain rights and privileges of the nobility seem to me a means of sustaining that sentiment."
* Le principe des monarchies est l'honneur me paraît incontestable. Certains droits et privilèges de la noblesse me paraissent être des moyens de soutenir ce sentiment.
* Si vous envisagez la question sous ce point de vue.
(The Illuminati sought to replace monarchical institutions with republican ones.)

Helene had been at Erfurt during the famous meeting of the Emperors and had brought back from there her connections with Napoleonic dignitaries. At Erfurt her success had been brilliant. Napoleon himself had noticed her in the theater and said of her (in French): "That's a superb creature." Her success as a beautiful and elegant woman did not surprise Pierre, for she had become even more attractive than before. What did surprise him was that during these last two years his wife had somehow acquired the reputation of being as charming and witty as she was beautiful. The distinguished Prince de Ligne wrote her eight-page letters. Bilibin saved up his best witticisms to deliver them in Countess Bezukhova's presence. To be received in the Countess Bezukhova's salon was considered a mark of intellectual distinction. Young men read books before attending Helene's evenings so they would have something to say in her salon, and secretaries of the embassy, and even ambassadors, confided diplomatic secrets to her, so that in a way Helene became a force. Pierre, who knew she was very stupid, sometimes attended her evenings and dinner parties — where politics, poetry, and philosophy were discussed — with a strange feeling of bewilderment and dread. At these parties he felt like a conjurer who always expects his trick to be found out. But whether because stupidity was exactly what was needed to run such a salon, or because the people being deceived found pleasure in the deception, the illusion was never exposed, and Helene Bezukhova's reputation as a lovely and clever woman became so firmly established that she could say the emptiest and most foolish things and everybody would go into raptures over every word, finding deep meaning in it that she herself never intended.
* C'est un superbe animal.
* (2) D'une femme charmante, aussi spirituelle que belle.

I got up late. On waking I lay in bed a long time, giving in to laziness. O God, help and strengthen me that I may walk in Your ways! Read the Scriptures, but without proper feeling. Brother Urusov came and we talked about worldly vanities. He told me about the Emperor's new projects. I began to criticize them, but remembered my rules and my benefactor's words — that a true Freemason should be a zealous worker for the state when his help is needed, and a quiet observer when not called upon to assist. My tongue is my enemy. Brothers G. V. and O. visited me and we had a preliminary talk about admitting a new Brother. They assigned me the duty of Rhetor. I feel weak and unworthy. Then our talk turned to interpreting the seven pillars and steps of the Temple, the seven sciences, the seven virtues, the seven vices, and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Brother O. was very eloquent. In the evening the admission took place. The new decoration of the premises added much to the magnificence of the spectacle. It was Boris Drubetskoy who was admitted. I nominated him and served as Rhetor. A strange feeling stirred in me the whole time I stood alone with him in the dark chamber. I caught myself harboring a feeling of hatred toward him which I tried in vain to overcome. That is exactly why I would like to save him from evil and lead him onto the path of truth, but ill thoughts of him would not leave me. It seemed to me that his purpose in joining the Brotherhood was merely to grow close to and win favor with members of our lodge. Apart from the fact that he had asked me several times whether N. and S. were members of our lodge (a question I could not answer), and that, by my observation, he is incapable of feeling any real respect for our holy order and is too absorbed in and satisfied with outward appearances to desire spiritual improvement, I had no real cause to doubt him — yet he struck me as insincere, and the whole time I stood alone with him in the dark temple, it seemed to me he was smiling contemptuously at my words, and I truly wanted to plunge the sword I held to his bare chest. I could not summon eloquence, nor could I frankly voice my doubts to the Brothers and the Grand Master. Great Architect of Nature, help me find the true path out of this labyrinth of lies!
* das soll mein Weib werden.
"I know! Cyril Matveich... but he's old."

On the thirty-first of December, New Year's Eve, 1809-10, an old grandee of Catherine's era was hosting a ball and midnight supper. The diplomatic corps and the Emperor himself were expected to attend.

The grandee's famous mansion on the English Quay blazed with countless lights. Police were posted at the brilliantly lit entrance, which was carpeted with red cloth, and not only gendarmes but dozens of police officers and even the police chief himself stood at the door. Carriages kept pulling away and new ones arriving, with footmen in red livery and plumed hats. From the carriages stepped men in uniforms, decorated with stars and ribbons, while ladies in satin and ermine carefully descended the carriage steps that were lowered for them with a clatter, then walked quickly and silently over the red carpet at the entrance.

Natasha looked in the mirrors and could not pick out her own reflection from the rest. Everything blurred into one brilliant procession. On entering the ballroom, the steady murmur of voices, footsteps, and greetings overwhelmed her, and the light and glitter dazzled her even more. The host and hostess, who had already been standing at the door for half an hour repeating the same phrase to each arrival — "Delighted to see you" (in French) — greeted the Rostovs and Peronskaya in the same manner.
* Charmé de vous voir.

But before he reached them, Pierre stopped beside a very handsome, dark-haired man of medium height in a white uniform, who was standing by a window talking to a tall man wearing decorations and a ribbon. Natasha immediately recognized the shorter, younger man in white: it was Bolkonski, who seemed to her much younger, happier, and better-looking than before.
"There's someone else we know — Bolkonski, do you see, Mama?" said Natasha, pointing out Prince Andrew. "You remember, he spent a night with us at Otradnoe."

"Oh, you know him?" said Peronskaya. "I can't stand him. He's the man of the moment right now (in French). And so proud! Takes after his father. He's hand in glove with Speransky, writing some kind of legislation. Just look how he treats the ladies! There's one speaking to him and he's turned away," she said, pointing at him. "I'd give him a piece of my mind if he treated me like that."
* Il fait à présent la pluie et le beau temps.

"Where is she?" asked Bolkonski. "Excuse me!" he added, turning to the baron, "we'll finish this conversation elsewhere — at a ball one must dance." He stepped forward in the direction Pierre had indicated. The despairing, dejected expression on Natasha's face caught his eye. He recognized her, guessed her feelings, saw that this was her debut, remembered their conversation at the window, and with an expression of pleasure approached Countess Rostova.

Berg smiled with a sense of superiority over his weak-natured wife and paused, reflecting that this dear wife of his was after all only a weak woman who could not understand everything that constitutes a man's dignity — what it means to be a man (in German). Vera, at the same time, smiled with a sense of superiority over her good, conscientious husband, who nevertheless understood life incorrectly, as in Vera's view all men did. Berg, judging by his wife, thought all women weak and foolish. Vera, judging by her husband alone and generalizing from that, believed that all men, though they understand nothing and are conceited and selfish, credit only themselves with common sense.
* ein Mann zu sein.
"Yes, you know — between cousins, closeness often leads to love. Le cousinage est un dangereux voisinage — cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood, don't you think?"

The day after her conversation with her mother, Natasha waited for Bolkonski all day, but he didn't come. It was the same on the second and third days. Pierre didn't come either, and Natasha, not knowing that Prince Andrew had gone to see his father, could not explain his absence.
"Mama! Bolkonski is here!" she said. "Mama, this is terrible, it's unbearable! I don't want... to be tormented! What am I supposed to do?..."

There was no formal betrothal ceremony, and Natasha's engagement to Bolkonski was not announced; Prince Andrew insisted on this. He said that since he was responsible for the delay, he alone should bear the burden of it; that he had given his word and was bound forever, but that he didn't wish to bind Natasha and was giving her complete freedom. If after six months she felt she didn't love him, she would have every right to reject him. Naturally neither Natasha nor her parents wanted to hear of this, but Prince Andrew was firm. He came to the Rostovs' every day, but didn't behave toward Natasha as an engaged man: he didn't use the intimate "thou" but addressed her as "you," and kissed only her hand. After the engagement, completely different relations sprang up between them — intimate, natural, and sincere. It was as if they hadn't known each other before. Both loved to recall how they had thought of each other when they were still nothing to one another; they felt themselves now to be entirely different people — then they had been artificial, now they were natural and genuine. At first the family felt somewhat constrained around Prince Andrew; he seemed like a man from another world. For a long time Natasha had to train the family to get used to him, proudly assuring them all that he only seemed different but was really just like everyone else, and that she wasn't afraid of him and nobody else should be either. After a few days they grew accustomed to him and went on with their usual way of life in his presence, and he took part in it. He could talk about estate management with the count, about fashion with the countess and Natasha, and about albums and needlework with Sonya. Sometimes the household, both among themselves and in his presence, marveled at how it had all come about and at the obvious signs that had foretold it: Prince Andrew's visit to Otradnoe, their coming to Petersburg, the resemblance between Natasha and Prince Andrew that the old nurse had noticed on his first visit, and Andrew's encounter with Nicholas in 1805, and many other incidents that seemed to prove it was all meant to be.

During that year after his son's departure, old Prince Nicholas Bolkonski's health and temper grew much worse. He became still more irritable, and it was Princess Mary who usually bore the brunt of his frequent fits of unprovoked anger. He seemed to search deliberately for her most sensitive spots in order to torment her mentally as cruelly as possible. Princess Mary had two passions and therefore two sources of joy — her nephew, little Nicholas, and religion — and these were the old prince's favorite targets for mockery and attack. Whatever the topic of conversation, he would steer it around to the superstitions of old maids or the pampering and spoiling of children. "You want to turn him" — little Nicholas — "into an old maid like yourself! A pity! Prince Andrew wants a son, not an old maid," he would say. Or, turning to Mademoiselle Bourienne, he would ask her in Princess Mary's presence how she liked their village priests and icons, and would joke about them.

Reading these letters, Nicholas felt a dread of being dragged away from the surroundings where, shielded from all of life's entanglements, he was living so calmly and quietly. He sensed that sooner or later he would have to plunge back into that whirlpool of life, with its embarrassments and problems to be sorted out, its accounts with stewards, quarrels and intrigues, its obligations, the social world, and Sonya's love and his promise to her. It was all impossibly difficult and complicated, and he replied to his mother in cold, formal letters in French, beginning "My dear Mama" and ending "Your obedient son," that said nothing about when he would return. In 1810 he received letters from his parents telling him of Natasha's engagement to Bolkonski, and that the wedding would be in a year because the old prince was making difficulties. This letter grieved and annoyed Nicholas. First, he was sorry that Natasha — for whom he cared more than for anyone else in the family — was being lost to the home; and second, from his hussar's point of view, he regretted not having been there to show that fellow Bolkonski that a connection with his family was no such great honor, and that if he loved Natasha he could do without his doddering father's permission. For a moment he wondered whether to apply for leave to see Natasha before her wedding, but then came the maneuvers, and his thoughts about Sonya, and the confusion of family finances — and Nicholas put it off again. But in the spring of that year he received a letter from his mother, written without his father's knowledge, and that letter persuaded him to return. She wrote that if he didn't come and take charge of things, their entire property would be sold at auction and they would all be left destitute. The count was so weak, trusted Mitenka so completely, and was so good-natured, that everyone took advantage of him and things were going from bad to worse. "For God's sake, I beg you, come at once if you don't want to make me and the whole family wretched," the countess wrote.

Her brother often wondered as he looked at her. She didn't seem at all like a girl in love and separated from her fiance. She was even-tempered, calm, and as cheerful as ever. This amazed Nicholas and even made him skeptical about Bolkonski's courtship. He couldn't quite believe that her fate was sealed, especially since he hadn't seen her with Prince Andrew. It always seemed to him that there was something not quite right about this planned marriage.

Within an hour the whole hunting party was assembled at the porch. Nicholas, with a stern and serious air that showed there was no time for trifles, walked past Natasha and Petya, who were trying to tell him something. He inspected every detail of the hunt, sent a pack of hounds and huntsmen ahead to find the quarry, mounted his chestnut Donets, whistled to his own leash of borzois, and set off across the threshing ground toward a field that led to the Otradnoe wood. The old count's horse, a sorrel gelding called Viflyanka, was led by his groom, while the count himself rode in a small trap to a spot reserved for him.

The old count, knowing his son's passion for the hunt, hurried so as not to be late, and the huntsmen had not yet reached their places when Count Ilya Rostov, cheerful, flushed, and with quivering cheeks, drove up with his black horses over the winter rye to the spot reserved for him, where a wolf might emerge. Having straightened his coat and fastened on his hunting knives and horn, he mounted his good, sleek, well-fed horse Viflyanka — which was turning gray, like himself. His carriage was sent home. Count Ilya Rostov, though not a keen sportsman at heart, knew the rules of the hunt well. He rode to the bushy edge of the road where he was to stand, settled his reins, got comfortable in the saddle, and — feeling he was ready — looked about with a smile.
"And you, Michael Nikanorovich?" he said, addressing "Uncle."
(The French shawl dance.)

"And such a one!" she said. But the moment she said it, a new train of thoughts and feelings arose in her. "What did Nicholas's smile mean when he said 'already chosen'? Is he glad or not? It's as if he thinks my Bolkonski wouldn't approve of or understand our fun here. But he would understand it all. Where is he right now?" she wondered, and her face suddenly grew serious. But this lasted only a second. "Don't dare think about it," she told herself, and sat down again, smiling, beside "Uncle," asking him to play something more.

Christmas came, and apart from the formal Mass, the solemn and tedious holiday congratulations from neighbors and servants, and the new outfits everyone wore, there were no special festivities — though the crisp frost of twenty degrees of frost Reaumur, the dazzling sunshine by day, and the starlit winter nights seemed to call for some celebration.

Stung by the word schemer, Nicholas raised his voice and told his mother he had never expected her to try to force him to sell his feelings — but that if that was how it was, he would say once and for all... But he didn't have time to say the decisive word — the word whose imminent arrival his mother could see coming in his face, and was awaiting with terror, and which might have remained a cruel memory between them forever. He didn't have time to say it because Natasha, with a pale, set face, came in through the door where she had been listening.

There was still no improvement in the countess's health, but postponing the trip to Moscow any longer was impossible. Natasha's trousseau had to be ordered and the house sold. Moreover, Prince Andrew was expected in Moscow, where old Prince Bolkonski was spending the winter, and Natasha was sure he had already arrived.

When, after a bachelor supper, he got up with his amiable, kindly smile and yielded to entreaties to go off somewhere with the revelers, shouts of delight and triumph arose among the young men. At balls he danced whenever a partner was needed. Young ladies, married and unmarried, liked him because he was equally friendly to all without making love to any of them, especially after supper. "He's charming; he has no sex," they said of him (in French).
* Il est charmant; il n'a pas de sexe.

At the beginning of winter, Prince Nicholas Bolkonski and his daughter moved to Moscow. At that time, enthusiasm for Emperor Alexander's regime had waned and a patriotic, anti-French sentiment prevailed. This, combined with the old prince's record, his intellect, and his eccentricity, immediately made Prince Nicholas Bolkonski an object of particular respect among Muscovites and the center of Moscow's opposition to the government.

Metivier, who came that morning with his congratulations, considered it proper in his capacity as doctor to force his way past the barrier (in French), as he explained to Princess Mary, and went in to see the prince. It happened that on this name-day morning the prince was in one of his worst moods. He had been going around the house since dawn finding fault with everyone and pretending not to understand what was said to him and not to be understood himself. Princess Mary knew this mood of quiet, absorbed grouchiness well — it generally built to an explosion of rage — and she went about all morning as though walking past a loaded gun, waiting for the inevitable shot. Until the doctor's arrival the morning had passed safely. After admitting the doctor, Princess Mary sat in the drawing room with a book near the door through which she could hear everything from the study.
* de forcer la consigne.

Boris, who had come to Moscow on leave a few days earlier, had been eager to be presented to Prince Nicholas Bolkonski and had managed to ingratiate himself so well that the old prince made an exception to his rule of not receiving bachelors.
"On that day I always go to pay my respects to the relics of Prince Nicholas Bolkonski."

Lopukhin and the old general occasionally joined in. Prince Bolkonski listened like a presiding judge receiving reports, now and then silently or with a brief word indicating that he was taking note. The tone of the conversation made clear that no one approved of what was happening in the political world. Stories were told that obviously confirmed the view that everything was going from bad to worse — but each speaker stopped, or was stopped, at the point where criticism might touch the sovereign himself.

"Other territories have been offered in exchange for the Duchy of Oldenburg," said Prince Bolkonski. "He shuffles dukes around the way I might move my serfs from Bald Hills to Bogucharovo or my Ryazan estates."

He said this because on his trip from Petersburg he had had the honor of being presented to the Duke. Prince Bolkonski glanced at the young man as if about to say something, but changed his mind — evidently considering him too young.

That winter the Karagins' house was the most pleasant and hospitable in Moscow. In addition to the formal evening and dinner parties, a large company, chiefly of men, gathered there every day, eating supper at midnight and staying till three in the morning. Julie never missed a ball, a promenade, or a play. Her dresses were always of the latest fashion. But despite all that, she seemed disillusioned about everything and told everyone that she didn't believe in friendship or love or any of the joys of life, and expected peace only "over there." She adopted the tone of one who has suffered a great disappointment, like a girl who has either lost the man she loved or been cruelly deceived by him. Though nothing of the kind had happened to her, she was regarded in that light, and had even herself come to believe that she had suffered much in life. This melancholy, which didn't prevent her from enjoying herself, didn't stop the young people who came to her house from having a good time. Every visitor paid tribute to the melancholy mood of their hostess, and then amused himself with society gossip, dancing, intellectual games, and rhyming games that were in fashion at the Karagins'. Only a few of these young men, among them Boris, entered more deeply into Julie's melancholy, and with these she had long private conversations about the vanity of all worldly things, and she showed them her albums filled with mournful sketches, maxims, and verses.
La mort est secourable et la mort est tranquille. Ah! contre les douleurs il n'y a pas d'autre asile. *
* Death gives relief and death is peaceful. Ah! from suffering there is no other refuge.

Aliment de poison d'une âme trop sensible, Toi, sans qui le bonheur me serait impossible, Tendre mélancholie, ah, viens me consoler, Viens calmer les tourments de ma sombre retraite, Et mêle une douceur secrète A ces pleurs que je sens couler. *

*Poisonous nourishment of a too sensitive soul, Thou, without whom happiness would for me be impossible, Tender melancholy, ah, come to console me, Come to calm the torments of my gloomy retreat, And mingle a secret sweetness With these tears that I feel to be flowing.

Anna Mikhaylovna, who often visited the Karagins, would play cards with the mother while carefully inquiring about Julie's dowry — she was to have two estates in Penza and the Nizhegorod forests. Anna Mikhaylovna regarded the refined sadness that united her son to the wealthy Julie with emotion and resignation to the Divine will.

Julie had long been expecting a proposal from her melancholy admirer and was ready to accept it; but some secret feeling of repulsion toward her, toward her desperate desire to get married, toward her artificiality, and a feeling of horror at giving up the possibility of real love, still held Boris back. His leave was running out. He spent every day and whole days at the Karagins', and every day on thinking it over told himself that he would propose tomorrow. But in Julie's presence, looking at her red face and chin (nearly always powdered), her moist eyes, and her expression of constant readiness to switch at once from melancholy to unnatural rapture at the prospect of married bliss, Boris could not bring himself to say the decisive words, though in his imagination he had long considered himself the owner of those Penza and Nizhegorod estates and had planned how to use the income from them. Julie saw Boris's indecision, and sometimes it occurred to her that she was repulsive to him, but her feminine self-deception immediately provided consolation, and she told herself that he was only shy from love. Her melancholy, however, began to turn into irritability, and not long before Boris's departure she formed a definite plan of action. Just as Boris's leave was running out, Anatole Kuragin appeared in Moscow, and naturally in the Karagins' drawing room, and Julie, suddenly dropping her melancholy, became cheerful and very attentive to Kuragin.

The idea of being made a fool of and of having thrown away that whole month of painful melancholy service to Julie, and of seeing all the revenue from the Penza estates — which he had already mentally allocated and put to proper use — fall into the hands of another, and especially into the hands of that idiot Anatole, stung Boris. He drove to the Karagins' with the firm intention of proposing. Julie met him in a gay, careless manner, spoke casually of how she had enjoyed yesterday's ball, and asked when he was leaving. Though Boris had come intentionally to speak of his love and therefore meant to be tender, he began speaking irritably about how easily women can switch from sadness to joy, and how their moods depend solely on who happens to be paying court to them. Julie was offended and replied that it was true that a woman needs variety, and the same thing over and over again would bore anyone.

At the end of January, old Count Rostov went to Moscow with Natasha and Sonya. The countess was still unwell and unable to travel, but it was impossible to wait for her recovery. Prince Andrew was expected in Moscow any day, the trousseau had to be ordered, and the estate near Moscow had to be sold. Besides, the chance to introduce his future daughter-in-law to old Prince Bolkonski while he was in Moscow couldn't be missed. The Rostovs' Moscow house had not been heated that winter, and as they had come only for a short time and the countess was not with them, the count decided to stay with Marya Dmitrievna Akhrosimova, who had long been urging them to accept her hospitality.

The next day, on Marya Dmitrievna's advice, Count Rostov took Natasha to call on Prince Nicholas Bolkonski. The count did not set out cheerfully on this visit — at heart he was afraid. He clearly remembered his last meeting with the old prince at the time of the enrollment, when in reply to a dinner invitation he had been forced to listen to an angry scolding for not having provided his full quota of men. Natasha, on the other hand, having put on her best dress, was in the highest spirits. "They can't help liking me," she thought. "Everybody always has liked me, and I'm so willing to do anything they want, so ready to be fond of him — for being his father — and of her — for being his sister — that there's no reason for them not to like me..."

Natasha at that moment felt so softened and tender that it wasn't enough for her to love and know she was loved — she wanted now, at once, to embrace the man she loved, to speak and hear from him words of love such as filled her heart. While she sat in the carriage beside her father, pensively watching the streetlamp lights flickering on the frozen window, she felt still sadder and more in love, and forgot where she was going and with whom. Having fallen into the line of carriages, the Rostovs' carriage drove up to the theater, its wheels squeaking over the snow. Natasha and Sonya, holding up their dresses, jumped out quickly. The count got out with the help of the footmen, and, passing among the men and women entering and the program sellers, all three of them walked along the corridor to the first row of boxes. Through the closed doors the music was already audible.
"The Karagins, Julie — and Boris with them. You can tell at once that they're engaged..."

At a moment when everything was quiet before a new song, a door leading to the stalls on the side nearest the Rostovs' box creaked, and the steps of a late arrival were heard. "There's Kuragin!" whispered Shinshin. Countess Bezukhova turned smiling to the newcomer, and Natasha, following the direction of that look, saw an exceptionally handsome adjutant approaching their box with a self-assured yet courteous air. This was Anatole Kuragin, whom she had seen and noticed long ago at the ball in Petersburg. He was now in an adjutant's uniform with one epaulet and a shoulder knot. He moved with a restrained swagger that would have been ridiculous had he not been so good-looking and had his handsome face not worn such an expression of good-humored satisfaction and gaiety. Though the performance was going on, he walked deliberately down the carpeted aisle, his sword and spurs slightly jingling and his handsome, perfumed head held high. Having looked at Natasha, he approached his sister, laid his well-gloved hand on the edge of her box, nodded to her, and leaning forward asked a question, gesturing toward Natasha.

"Dear count, you must let me look after your daughters! Though I'm not staying here long this time — nor are you — I'll try to give them a good time. I had already heard a lot about you in Petersburg and wanted to get to know you," she said to Natasha with her perfect, lovely smile. "I'd heard about you from my page, Drubetskoy. Have you heard he's getting married? And also from my husband's friend Bolkonski, Prince Andrew Bolkonski," she went on with special emphasis, implying that she knew about his relationship to Natasha. To get better acquainted she asked that one of the young ladies should come into her box for the rest of the performance, and Natasha moved over to it.

"And do you know, Countess," he said, suddenly addressing her as an old familiar acquaintance, "we're organizing a costume tournament; you ought to take part in it! It will be great fun. We're all meeting at the Karagins'! Please come! No, really, eh?" said he.

"At first I didn't like it much, because what makes a city pleasant is the pretty women (in French), isn't that so? But now I like it very much indeed," he said, looking at her meaningfully. "You'll come to the costume tournament, Countess? Do come!" and putting out his hand toward her bouquet and lowering his voice, he added, "You will be the prettiest there. Do come, dear countess, and give me this flower as a pledge!"
* ce sont les jolies femmes.

After Mass, when they had finished their coffee in the dining room where the slipcovers had been removed from the furniture, a servant announced that the carriage was ready, and Marya Dmitrievna rose with a stern air. She wore her best shawl, the one she used for paying calls, and announced that she was going to see Prince Nicholas Bolkonski to have it out with him about Natasha.

"Well, friends, I've now thought the whole matter over and this is my advice," she began. "Yesterday, as you know, I went to see Prince Bolkonski. Well, I had a talk with him... He got it into his head to start shouting, but I'm not one to be shouted down. I said what I had to say!"
"And Bolkonski?" she asked.

On the day the count left, Sonya and Natasha were invited to a big dinner party at the Karagins', and Marya Dmitrievna took them there. At the party Natasha again met Anatole, and Sonya noticed that she spoke to him, trying not to be overheard, and that all through dinner she was more agitated than ever. When they got home, Natasha was the first to begin the explanation Sonya expected.
"Oh, Sonya, if you knew him as I do! He said... He asked me what I had promised Bolkonski. He was glad I was free to refuse him."
"But you haven't refused Bolkonski?" said she.
"Perhaps I have. Perhaps it's all over between me and Bolkonski. Why do you think so badly of me?"

"She will run away with him!" thought Sonya. "She's capable of anything. There was something especially desperate and determined in her face today. She cried as she said goodbye to Uncle," Sonya remembered. "Yes, that's it — she means to elope with him. But what am I to do?" she thought, recalling all the signs that clearly indicated Natasha had some terrible intention. "The count is away. What am I to do? Write to Kuragin demanding an explanation? But what obliges him to reply? Write to Pierre, as Prince Andrew asked me to in case of some misfortune?... But perhaps she really has already refused Bolkonski — she sent a letter to Princess Mary yesterday. And Uncle is away..." To tell Marya Dmitrievna, who had such faith in Natasha, seemed terrible to Sonya. "Well, anyway," thought Sonya as she stood in the dark corridor, "now or never I must prove that I remember the family's goodness to me and that I love Nicholas. Yes! If I don't sleep for three nights I won't leave this corridor, and I will hold her back by force and not let the family be disgraced," she thought.

When he returned to Moscow, Pierre was handed a letter from Marya Dmitrievna asking him to come see her on a matter of great importance relating to Andrew Bolkonski and his fiancee. Pierre had been avoiding Natasha because it seemed to him that his feelings for her were stronger than a married man's should be toward his friend's fiancee. Yet some fate constantly threw them together.

Pierre raised his shoulders and listened open-mouthed to what was told him, scarcely able to believe his own ears. That Prince Andrew's deeply loved fiancee — the same Natasha Rostova who used to be so charming — should give up Bolkonski for that fool Anatole who was already secretly married (as Pierre knew), and should be so in love with him as to agree to run away with him, was something Pierre could not conceive or imagine.

After hearing the details of Anatole's marriage from Pierre, and venting her fury against Anatole in a stream of abuse, Marya Dmitrievna told Pierre why she had sent for him. She was afraid that the count or Bolkonski, who might arrive at any moment, if they found out about this affair (which she hoped to hide from them) might challenge Anatole to a duel, and she therefore asked Pierre to tell his brother-in-law in her name to leave Moscow and not dare let her set eyes on him again. Pierre — only now grasping the danger to the old count, Nicholas, and Prince Andrew — promised to do as she wished. Having briefly and precisely explained what she wanted, she sent him to the drawing room.
Pierre met the old count, who seemed nervous and upset. That morning Natasha had told him she had refused Bolkonski.
"Yes, you are a great friend of Bolkonski's — no doubt she wants to send him a message," said the count. "Oh dear! Oh dear! How happy it all was!"

Old Prince Bolkonski had heard all the rumors circulating in the town from Mademoiselle Bourienne and had read the note to Princess Mary in which Natasha had broken off her engagement. He seemed in better spirits than usual and awaited his son with great impatience.

"Peter Kirilovich," she began rapidly, "Prince Bolkonski was your friend — is your friend," she corrected herself. (It seemed to her that everything that had once been must now be different.) "He told me once to turn to you..."
"Home!" said Pierre, and despite twenty-two degrees of frost, Fahrenheit, he threw open the bearskin cloak from his broad chest and breathed in the air with joy.

From the end of 1811, an intensified buildup and concentration of the forces of Western Europe began, and in 1812 these forces — millions of men, counting those transporting and feeding the army — moved from the west eastward to the Russian frontier, toward which since 1811 Russian forces had been similarly drawn. On June twelfth, 1812, the forces of Western Europe crossed the Russian frontier and war began — that is, an event took place contrary to human reason and to human nature.
