Millions of men committed against one another such innumerable crimes, frauds, betrayals, thefts, forgeries, counterfeiting, burglaries, arson, and murders as in whole centuries are not recorded in the annals of all the law courts of the world, but which those who committed them did not at the time regard as crimes.

What produced this extraordinary event? What were its causes? The historians tell us with naive assurance that its causes were the wrongs inflicted on the Duke of Oldenburg (whose duchy Napoleon had annexed), the failure to observe the Continental System (Napoleon's trade embargo), the ambition of Napoleon, the firmness of Alexander, the mistakes of the diplomats, and so on.

We can understand that the matter appeared that way to contemporaries. It naturally seemed to Napoleon that the war was caused by England's intrigues (as in fact he said on the island of St. Helena). It naturally seemed to members of the English Parliament that the cause of the war was Napoleon's ambition; to the Duke of Oldenburg, that the cause was the violence done to him; to businessmen, that the cause was the Continental System which was ruining Europe. It seemed to the generals and old soldiers that the main reason for the war was the necessity of giving them employment; to the legitimists of that day, that it was the need of restoring les bons principes (good principles). And it seemed to the diplomats that it all resulted from the fact that the alliance between Russia and Austria in 1809 had not been sufficiently well concealed from Napoleon, and from the clumsy wording of Memorandum No. 178, a diplomatic dispatch. It is natural that these and a countless and infinite number of other reasons — the number depending on the endless diversity of viewpoints — presented themselves to the people of that day; but to us, to posterity, who view the event in all its magnitude and perceive its plain and terrible meaning, these causes seem inadequate. To us it is incomprehensible that millions of Christian men killed and tortured each other either because Napoleon was ambitious or Alexander was firm, or because England's policy was astute or the Duke of Oldenburg was wronged. We cannot grasp what connection such circumstances have with the actual fact of slaughter and violence. Why, because the Duke was wronged, thousands of men from the other side of Europe killed and ruined the people of Smolensk and Moscow and were killed by them.

Had Napoleon not taken offense at the demand that he should withdraw beyond the Vistula, and not ordered his troops to advance, there would have been no war; but had all his sergeants objected to serving a second term, there could have been no war either. Nor could there have been a war had there been no English intrigues and no Duke of Oldenburg, had Alexander not felt insulted, and had there not been an autocratic government in Russia. Nor could there have been a war without the Revolution in France and the dictatorship and Empire that followed it, or without all the things that produced the French Revolution, and so on. Without each of these causes nothing could have happened. So all these causes — myriads of causes — combined to bring it about. And so there was no single cause for that event, but it had to occur because it had to. Millions of men, abandoning their human feelings and reason, had to march from west to east to slay their fellows, just as some centuries earlier hordes of men had come from the east to the west, slaying their fellows.

The actions of Napoleon and Alexander, on whose words the event seemed to depend, were as little voluntary as the actions of any soldier drawn into the campaign by lot or by conscription. This could not be otherwise, for in order that the will of Napoleon and Alexander (on whom the event seemed to depend) should be carried out, the concurrence of innumerable circumstances was needed, without any one of which the event could not have taken place. It was necessary that millions of men in whose hands lay the real power — the soldiers who fired, or transported provisions and guns — should consent to carry out the will of these weak individuals, and should have been induced to do so by an infinite number of diverse and complex causes.

Each man lives for himself, using his freedom to achieve his personal aims, and feels with his whole being that he can now do or refrain from doing this or that action. But as soon as he has done it, that action performed at a certain moment in time becomes irrevocable and belongs to history, in which it has not a free but a predestined significance.

There are two sides to the life of every man: his individual life, which grows freer the more abstract its interests are, and his elemental hive life, in which he inevitably obeys laws laid down for him.

Though Napoleon at that time, in 1812, was more convinced than ever that it depended on him whether to shed (or not to shed) the blood of his peoples (in French) — as Alexander expressed it in the last letter he wrote him — he had never been so much in the grip of inevitable laws, which compelled him, while thinking that he was acting on his own free will, to perform for the hive life — that is, for history — whatever had to be performed.
* Verser (ou ne pas verser) le sang de ses peuples.

The people of the west moved eastward to slay their fellow men, and by the law of coincidence thousands of minute causes aligned and combined to produce that movement and war. There were complaints about the failure to observe the Continental System, the Duke of Oldenburg's wrongs, and the movement of troops into Prussia — undertaken (as it seemed to Napoleon) solely to secure an armed peace. There was the French Emperor's love and habit of war coinciding with his people's inclinations, the allure of the grand preparations, the expenditure on those preparations and the need to recoup them, and the intoxicating honors he received in Dresden. There were the diplomatic negotiations, too, which contemporaries believed were conducted with a sincere desire for peace but which only wounded the self-love of both sides — and millions of other causes that adapted themselves to the event or coincided with it.

Nothing is the cause. All this is merely the coincidence of conditions in which all vital organic and elemental events occur. And the botanist who finds that the apple falls because the cellular tissue decays and so forth is equally right with the child who stands under the tree and says the apple fell because he wanted to eat it and prayed for it. Equally right or wrong is he who says Napoleon went to Moscow because he wanted to, and perished because Alexander desired his destruction. And equally right or wrong is he who says that an undermined hill weighing a million tons fell because the last laborer struck it for the last time with his pickaxe. In historic events, the so-called great men are labels giving names to events, and like labels they have only the smallest connection with the event itself.
Every act of theirs, which appears to them an act of their own will, is in a historical sense involuntary and is related to the whole course of history and predestined from eternity.
* Viva il re!

Murat's face beamed with foolish satisfaction as he listened to "Monsieur de Bal-macheve." But royauté oblige — royalty has its obligations! And he felt it incumbent on him, as a king and an ally, to discuss state affairs with Alexander's envoy. He dismounted, took Balashev's arm, and moving a few steps away from his suite, which waited respectfully, began to walk up and down with him, trying to speak meaningfully. He mentioned that the Emperor Napoleon had been offended by the demand that he withdraw his troops from Prussia, especially when that demand became publicly known and the dignity of France was thereby insulted.
* "Royalty has its obligations."

In the year 1812, when news of the war with Napoleon reached Bucharest — where Kutuzov had been living for two months, spending his days and nights with a Wallachian woman — Prince Andrew asked Kutuzov to transfer him to the Western Army. Kutuzov, who was already tired of Bolkonski's activity, which seemed to reproach his own idleness, very readily let him go and gave him a mission to Barclay de Tolly.

Prince Andrew found Barclay de Tolly, to whom he had been assigned, on the bank of the Drissa. As there was not a single town or large village in the vicinity of the camp, the immense number of generals and courtiers accompanying the army were living in the best houses of villages on both sides of the river, over a radius of six miles. Barclay de Tolly was quartered nearly three miles from the Emperor. He received Bolkonski stiffly and coldly and told him in his foreign accent that he would mention him to the Emperor for a decision on his assignment, but asked him meanwhile to remain on his staff. Anatole Kuragin, whom Prince Andrew had hoped to find with the army, was not there. He had gone to Petersburg, but Prince Andrew was glad to hear this. His mind was occupied with the affairs of the center that was conducting a gigantic war, and he was glad to be free for a while from the distraction caused by thoughts of Kuragin. During the first four days, while no duties were required of him, Prince Andrew rode all around the fortified camp and, using his own knowledge and his conversations with experts, tried to form a definite opinion about it. But the question of whether the camp was advantageous or not remained unresolved in his mind. Already from his military experience and from what he had seen in the Austrian campaign, he had reached the conclusion that in war the most carefully considered plans have no significance and that everything depends on how unexpected movements of the enemy — which cannot be foreseen — are met, and on how and by whom the whole matter is handled. To understand this last point, Prince Andrew, using his position and connections, tried to grasp the character of the army's leadership and of the men and factions involved, and he arrived at the following picture of the situation.

While the Emperor had still been at Vilna, the forces had been divided into three armies. First, the army under Barclay de Tolly; second, the army under Bagration; and third, the one commanded by Tormasov. The Emperor was with the first army, but not as commander in chief. In the orders issued, it was not stated that the Emperor would take command, only that he would be with the army. The Emperor moreover had with him not a commander in chief's staff but the imperial headquarters staff. In attendance on him was the head of the imperial staff, Quartermaster General Prince Volkonsky, as well as generals, imperial aides-de-camp, diplomatic officials, and a large number of foreigners — but not the army staff. Besides these, there were in attendance on the Emperor without any definite assignments: Arakcheev, the former Minister of War; Count Bennigsen, the senior general by rank; the Grand Duke Tsarevich Constantine Pavlovich; and Count Rumyantsev, the Chancellor. There were also Stein, a former Prussian minister; Armfeldt, a Swedish general; Pfuel, the chief author of the plan of campaign; Paulucci, an adjutant general and Sardinian émigré; Wolzogen — and many others. Though these men held no military position in the army, their standing gave them influence, and often a corps commander, or even the commander in chief, did not know in what capacity he was questioned by Bennigsen, the Grand Duke, Arakcheev, or Prince Volkonsky, or was given this or that piece of advice, and did not know whether a certain order received in the form of advice came from the man who gave it or from the Emperor, and whether it had to be carried out or not. But this was only the surface; the essential significance of the Emperor's presence and of all these people, from a courtier's perspective (and in an Emperor's vicinity all became courtiers), was clear to everyone. It was this: the Emperor did not take the title of commander in chief but controlled all the armies; the men around him were his assistants. Arakcheev was a faithful enforcer of order who served as the sovereign's bodyguard. Bennigsen was a landowner in the Vilna province who appeared to be doing the honors of the district but was actually a good general, useful as an adviser and ready to replace Barclay. The Grand Duke was there because it suited him. The former Minister Stein was there because his advice was valuable and Emperor Alexander held him in high personal esteem. Armfeldt bitterly hated Napoleon and was a general full of self-confidence — a quality that always influenced Alexander. Paulucci was there because he was bold and decisive in speech. The adjutants general were there because they always accompanied the Emperor, and lastly and chiefly, Pfuel was there because he had drawn up the plan of campaign against Napoleon and, having persuaded Alexander to believe in its effectiveness, was directing the whole business of the war. With Pfuel was Wolzogen, who expressed Pfuel's thoughts in a more comprehensible way than Pfuel himself — who was a harsh, bookish theorist, self-confident to the point of despising everyone else — could manage.

The second faction was the direct opposite of the first; as always, one extreme was met by representatives of the other. Its members demanded an advance from Vilna into Poland and freedom from all prearranged plans. Besides advocating bold action, this group also represented nationalism, which made them still more one-sided in the dispute. They were Russians: Bagration, Ermolov (who was beginning to come to prominence), and others. At that time a famous joke of Ermolov's was circulating: as a great favor he had petitioned the Emperor to make him a German. The men of this faction, remembering Suvorov, the Russian general, said that what one had to do was not to reason or stick pins in maps, but fight, beat the enemy, keep him out of Russia, and not let the army get demoralized.

Of a fourth opinion the most conspicuous representative was the Tsarevich, who could not forget his disillusionment at Austerlitz, where he had ridden out at the head of the Guards in his helmet and cavalry uniform as to a review, expecting to crush the French gallantly, but had unexpectedly found himself in the front line and had narrowly escaped amid the general confusion. The men of this faction had both the quality and the defect of frankness in their opinions. They feared Napoleon, recognized his strength and their own weakness, and openly said so. They said: "Nothing but sorrow, shame, and ruin will come of all this! We have abandoned Vilna and Vitebsk and shall abandon Drissa. The only sensible thing left is to make peace as soon as possible, before we are thrown out of Petersburg."

The fifth faction consisted of supporters of Barclay de Tolly, not so much of the man as of the minister of war and commander in chief. "Be he what he may" (they always began like that), "he is an honest, practical man and we have nobody better. Give him real power, for war cannot be waged successfully without unity of command, and he will show what he can do, as he did in the war in Finland. If our army is well organized and strong and has retreated to Drissa without suffering any defeats, we owe this entirely to Barclay. If Barclay is now replaced by Bennigsen, all will be lost, for Bennigsen showed his incapacity already in 1807."

The sixth faction, the Bennigsenites, said on the contrary that there was at any rate no one more active and experienced than Bennigsen: "Twist about as you may, you'll have to come to Bennigsen in the end. Let the others make mistakes now!" said they, arguing that our retreat to Drissa was a most shameful reverse and an unbroken chain of blunders. "The more mistakes that are made the better. At least it will be understood sooner that things can't go on like this. What is needed is not some Barclay or other, but a man like Bennigsen, who proved himself in 1807 and to whom Napoleon himself gave credit — a man whose authority would be willingly accepted, and Bennigsen is the only such man."

The seventh faction consisted of the sort of people who are always to be found, especially around young sovereigns, and of whom there were particularly many around Alexander — generals and imperial aides-de-camp passionately devoted to the Emperor not merely as a monarch but as a man, adoring him sincerely and selflessly as Rostov had done in 1805, and who saw in him not only all the virtues but all human capabilities as well. These men, though delighted with the sovereign's refusal to command the army, nevertheless blamed him for such excessive modesty and only desired and insisted that their adored sovereign should abandon his diffidence and openly announce that he would take personal command of the army, gather a commander in chief's staff around him, and — consulting experienced theoreticians and practical men as needed — lead the troops himself, whose spirits would thereby be raised to the highest pitch.

The eighth and largest group, which outnumbered the others as ninety-nine to one, consisted of men who desired neither peace nor war, neither an advance nor a defensive camp at Drissa or anywhere else, neither Barclay nor the Emperor, neither Pfuel nor Bennigsen, but only the one most essential thing — as much advantage and pleasure for themselves as possible. In the troubled waters of conflicting and intersecting intrigues that swirled around the Emperor's headquarters, it was possible to succeed in many ways unthinkable at other times. A man who simply wanted to keep his lucrative post would today agree with Pfuel, tomorrow with his opponent, and the day after — merely to avoid responsibility or to please the Emperor — would declare that he had no opinion at all on the matter. Another who wished to gain some advantage would attract the Emperor's attention by loudly advocating the very thing the Emperor had hinted at the day before, and would argue and shout at the council, beating his chest and challenging those who disagreed to duels, thereby proving his readiness to sacrifice himself for the common good. A third, in the absence of opponents, between two councils, would simply ask for a special bonus for his faithful services, well knowing that at such a moment people would be too busy to refuse. A fourth, while seemingly overwhelmed with work, would often come accidentally under the Emperor's eye. A fifth, to achieve his long-cherished aim of dining with the Emperor, would stubbornly argue for or against some newly emerging opinion and produce arguments more or less convincing and correct to that end.

All the men of this group were fishing for rubles, decorations, and promotions, and in this pursuit they watched only the weathercock of imperial favor; as soon as they noticed it turning in any direction, this whole drone population of the army began blowing hard that way, making it all the harder for the Emperor to turn it elsewhere. Amid the uncertainties of the situation, with the threat of serious danger lending a peculiarly menacing character to everything, amid this vortex of intrigue, egotism, conflicting views and feelings, and the diversity of nationalities among these people, this eighth and largest group — the people preoccupied with personal gain — introduced great confusion and obscurity into the common task. Whatever question arose, a swarm of these drones, without having finished buzzing about the previous topic, flew to the new one and by their noise drowned out and obscured the voices of those who were arguing honestly.

From among all these factions, just at the time Prince Andrew reached the army, another — a ninth — was being formed and beginning to raise its voice. This was the party of older, reasonable men experienced and capable in state affairs, who, without sharing any of those conflicting opinions, were able to take a detached view of what was happening at headquarters and to consider ways out of this muddle, indecision, intricacy, and weakness.

The men of this faction said and thought that the problems stemmed mainly from the Emperor's presence in the army with his military court and the resulting indefinite, conditional, and unstable fluctuation of relations, which was appropriate at court but harmful in an army; that a sovereign should reign but not command the army, and that the only solution was for the Emperor and his court to leave; that the mere presence of the Emperor paralyzed the action of fifty thousand men needed to guarantee his personal safety; and that the worst commander in chief acting independently would be better than the best one hampered by the presence and authority of the monarch.

Just at the time Prince Andrew was living idly at Drissa, Shishkov, the Secretary of State and one of the chief representatives of this faction, wrote a letter to the Emperor which Arakcheev and Balashev agreed to sign. In this letter, taking advantage of the permission given him by the Emperor to discuss the general course of affairs, he respectfully suggested — on the plea that it was necessary for the sovereign to rouse the people of the capital to a warlike spirit — that the Emperor should leave the army.

This stirring of the people by their sovereign, and his call to them to defend their country—the very incitement which was the chief cause of Russia's triumph, insofar as it was produced by the Tsar's personal presence in Moscow—was suggested to the Emperor, and accepted by him, as a pretext for leaving the army.

This letter had not yet been presented to the Emperor when Barclay, one day at dinner, informed Bolkonski that the sovereign wished to see him personally, to question him about Turkey, and that Prince Andrew was to present himself at Bennigsen's quarters at six that evening.

Prince Andrew arrived at Bennigsen's quarters — a moderate-sized country gentleman's house situated on the very banks of the river. Neither Bennigsen nor the Emperor was there, but Chernyshev, the Emperor's aide-de-camp, received Bolkonski and told him that the Emperor, accompanied by General Bennigsen and Marquis Paulucci, had gone out a second time that day to inspect the Drissa fortifications, about whose suitability serious doubts were beginning to arise.

Prince Andrew's eyes were still following Pfuel out of the room when Count Bennigsen entered hurriedly, and nodding to Bolkonski but not pausing, went into the study, giving instructions to his adjutant as he went. The Emperor was following him, and Bennigsen had hurried ahead to make some preparations and be ready to receive the sovereign. Chernyshev and Prince Andrew went out onto the porch, where the Emperor, who looked fatigued, was dismounting. Marquis Paulucci was talking to him with particular intensity, and the Emperor, with his head tilted to the left, was listening with a displeased expression. The Emperor moved forward, clearly wanting to end the conversation, but the flushed and excited Italian, ignoring etiquette, followed him and kept talking.
Without paying attention to the end of the Italian's remarks, and as though not hearing them, the Emperor recognized Bolkonski and addressed him warmly.

The discussions dragged on, and the longer they lasted, the more heated the disputes became — culminating in shouts and personal attacks — and the less possible it was to reach any general conclusion. Prince Andrew, listening to this babel of languages and to these conjectures, plans, refutations, and outbursts, felt nothing but amazement at what they were all saying. A thought that had long since and often occurred to him during his military service — the idea that there is not and cannot be any science of war, and that therefore there can be no such thing as military genius — now struck him as an obvious truth. "What theory and science can apply to a matter whose conditions and circumstances are unknown and cannot be defined, especially when the strength of the forces involved cannot be measured? No one was or is able to foresee what position our army or the enemy's will be in tomorrow, and no one can gauge the real strength of any given detachment. Sometimes — when there is no coward at the front to shout 'We're cut off!' and start running, but instead a brave and cheerful fellow who shouts 'Hurrah!' — a force of five thousand is worth thirty thousand, as at Schön Grabern, while at other times fifty thousand flee from eight thousand, as at Austerlitz. What science can govern a matter in which, as in all practical affairs, nothing can be precisely determined and everything depends on countless conditions whose significance reveals itself only at a particular moment that no one can predict? Armfeldt says our army is cut in half, and Paulucci says we have the French between two fires; Michaud says the Drissa camp is worthless because the river is behind it, while Pfuel says that is exactly what makes it strong; Toll proposes one plan, Armfeldt another — and they are all good and all bad, because the merits of any proposal can only be seen at the moment of execution. And why do they all talk of 'military genius'? Is a man a genius because he can order bread to be brought up at the right time and tell soldiers to go right or left? It is only because military leaders are surrounded by pomp, power, and crowds of sycophants who flatter authority by attributing to it qualities of genius it does not possess. The best generals I have known were, on the contrary, stupid or absent-minded men. Bagration was the best — Napoleon himself admitted it. And Napoleon himself! I remember his smug, self-satisfied face on the field of Austerlitz. Not only does a good commander not need any special qualities — on the contrary, he needs the absence of the highest and best human attributes: love, poetry, tenderness, and philosophic, questioning doubt. He should be narrow-minded, firmly convinced that what he is doing is enormously important (otherwise he will lack the necessary patience), and only then will he be a brave leader. God forbid that he should be humane, that he should love or feel pity, or think about what is just and unjust. It is no wonder that a theory of their 'genius' was invented for them long ago, because they hold power! The success of a military action depends not on them but on the man in the ranks who shouts 'We're lost!' or who shouts 'Hurrah!' And only in the ranks can one serve with the assurance of being truly useful."

She heard, or thought she heard, the names Kuragin and Bolkonski. But she was always imagining that. It always seemed to her that everyone who looked at her was thinking only of what had happened to her. With a sinking heart, miserable as she always was now in a crowd, Natasha in her lilac silk dress trimmed with black lace walked—as women can—with all the more poise and dignity the greater the pain and shame in her soul. She knew for certain that she was pretty, but this no longer gave her satisfaction as it used to. On the contrary, it tormented her more than anything lately, especially on this bright, hot summer day in town. "It's Sunday again—another week gone," she thought, remembering that she had been here the Sunday before, "and always the same life that is no life, and the same surroundings in which it used to be so easy to live. I'm pretty, I'm young, and I know that now I am good. I used to be bad, but now I know I am good," she thought, "and yet my best years are slipping by and are no good to anyone." She stood by her mother's side and exchanged nods with acquaintances nearby. Out of habit she sized up the ladies' dresses, criticized the posture of a woman standing close by who wasn't crossing herself properly but in a cramped way, and again she thought with annoyance that she herself was being judged and was judging others, and suddenly, at the sound of the service, she felt horrified at her own sinfulness, horrified that the former purity of her soul was once again lost.

Among these letters was one from Nicholas Rostov to his father. Pierre took it, and Rostopchin also gave him the Emperor's appeal to Moscow—just printed—the latest army orders, and his own most recent bulletin. Scanning the army orders, Pierre found in one of them, in the lists of killed, wounded, and decorated, the name of Nicholas Rostov, awarded a Saint George's Cross of the Fourth Class for courage shown in the Ostrovna affair, and in the same dispatch the name of Prince Andrew Bolkonski, appointed to command a regiment of light infantry. Though he didn't want to remind the Rostovs of Bolkonski, Pierre couldn't resist making them happy with the news of their son's decoration, so he sent the printed army order and Nicholas's letter to the Rostovs, keeping the appeal, the bulletin, and the other orders to bring with him to dinner.

"I don't know myself," Natasha answered quickly, "but I wouldn't want to do anything you disapproved of. I trust you completely. You don't know how important you are to me, how much you've done for me..." She spoke rapidly and didn't notice how Pierre flushed at her words. "I saw in that same army order that he—Bolkonski"—she whispered the name quickly—"is in Russia, and back in the army. What do you think?" She was speaking hurriedly, obviously afraid her composure might fail. "Will he ever forgive me? Won't he always hold bitter feelings toward me? What do you think? What do you think?"

"Excuse me, your excellency," he began. (He knew the senator well but thought it necessary to address him formally on this occasion.) "Though I don't agree with the gentleman"—he hesitated, wanting to say "my very honorable opponent"—"with the gentleman whom I have not the honor of knowing, I believe the nobility have been summoned not merely to express sympathy and enthusiasm but also to consider the means by which we can help our Fatherland! I believe," he went on, warming to his subject, "that the Emperor himself would not be satisfied to find in us merely owners of serfs whom we are willing to hand over for his service, and cannon fodder (in French) we are ready to make of ourselves—and not to obtain from us any co-co-counsel."
* Chair à canon.

Alexander refused negotiations because he felt himself personally insulted. Barclay de Tolly tried to command the army in the best way because he wanted to fulfill his duty and earn fame as a great commander. Rostov charged the French because he couldn't resist the urge to gallop across a level field. In the same way, the countless people who took part in the war acted according to their personal characteristics, habits, circumstances, and aims. They were moved by fear or vanity, they rejoiced or were outraged, they reasoned, imagining they knew what they were doing and did it of their own free will. But they were all involuntary tools of history, carrying on a work hidden from them but understandable to us. Such is the inevitable fate of men of action, and the higher they stand in the social hierarchy, the less free they are.

Providence compelled all these men, striving to achieve personal aims, to further the accomplishment of an immense result that none of them at all expected—neither Napoleon, nor Alexander, nor still less any of those who did the actual fighting.

The cause of the destruction of the French army in 1812 is clear to us now. No one will deny that it was, on the one hand, their advance into the heart of Russia late in the season without any preparation for a winter campaign, and on the other, the character given to the war by the burning of Russian towns and the hatred of the enemy this aroused among the Russian people. But no one at the time foresaw what now seems so obvious. It was the only way an army of eight hundred thousand men — the best in the world and led by the best general — could be destroyed: in conflict with a raw army of half its numerical strength, led by inexperienced commanders, as the Russian army was. Not only did no one foresee this, but on the Russian side every effort was made to hinder the only thing that could save Russia, while on the French side, despite Napoleon's experience and so-called military genius, every effort was directed toward pushing on to Moscow at the end of summer—that is, toward doing the very thing that was bound to lead to destruction.

In historical works on 1812, French writers are very fond of saying that Napoleon sensed the danger of extending his line, that he sought a battle, and that his marshals advised him to stop at Smolensk, and of making similar claims to show that even then the danger of the campaign was understood. Russian authors are even more fond of telling us that from the very start a Scythian war plan was adopted to lure Napoleon into the depths of Russia, and this plan is attributed by some to Pfuel, by others to a certain Frenchman, by others to Toll, and by others again to Alexander himself—pointing to notes, plans, and letters that contain hints of such a strategy. But all these hints at what happened, from both the French side and the Russian, are advanced only because they happen to fit the event. Had the event not occurred, these hints would have been forgotten, as we have forgotten the thousands and millions of contrary hints and expectations that circulated at the time but have now been forgotten because events proved them wrong. There are always so many conjectures about the outcome of any event that however it may end, there will always be people to say: "I said then that it would be so," quite forgetting that among their innumerable conjectures, many pointed in the opposite direction.

Conjectures as to Napoleon's awareness of the danger of extending his line, and on the Russian side about luring the enemy into the depths of Russia, are clearly of this kind, and only by great stretching can historians attribute such conceptions to Napoleon and his marshals, or such plans to the Russian commanders. All the facts flatly contradict these conjectures. Throughout the entire war, there was no wish on the Russian side to draw the French into the heart of the country; on the contrary, from the moment the French entered Russia, everything was done to stop them. And not only was Napoleon not afraid to extend his line, but he welcomed every step forward as a triumph and did not seek battle as eagerly as in his former campaigns, but very lazily.

At the very start of the war our armies were divided, and our only aim was to unite them—though uniting the armies was no advantage if we intended to retreat and lure the enemy deeper into Russia. Our Emperor joined the army to encourage it to defend every inch of Russian soil and not to retreat. The enormous fortified camp at Drissa was built according to Pfuel's plan, with no intention of retreating further. The Emperor reproached the commanders in chief for every step they fell back. He could not bear the idea of letting the enemy even reach Smolensk, much less could he contemplate the burning of Moscow, and when our armies did unite, he was displeased that Smolensk had been abandoned and burned without a major battle being fought under its walls.

The facts show plainly that Napoleon did not foresee the danger of advancing on Moscow, nor did Alexander and the Russian commanders think of luring Napoleon on—quite the opposite. The luring of Napoleon into the depths of the country was not the result of any plan, for no one believed it possible; it resulted from a most complex web of intrigues, aims, and desires among those who took part in the war and had no understanding whatever of the inevitable outcome, or of the one way to save Russia. Everything came about by chance. The armies were divided at the start of the campaign. We tried to unite them, with the clear intention of giving battle and checking the enemy's advance, and by this effort to unite them while avoiding battle with a much stronger enemy—necessarily retreating at an acute angle—we led the French on to Smolensk. But we withdrew at an acute angle not only because the French advanced between our two armies; the angle became still more acute and we withdrew still farther, because Barclay de Tolly was an unpopular foreigner disliked by Bagration (who would come under his command), and Bagration, commanding the second army, tried to postpone the junction and avoid coming under Barclay's authority as long as he could. Bagration was slow in effecting the junction—though it was the chief aim of all at headquarters—because, as he claimed, he was putting his army at risk on this march, and it was better for him to withdraw more to the left and south, harassing the enemy from flank and rear and recruiting men from Ukraine for his army; and it seems he planned this in order to avoid serving under the detested foreigner Barclay, whose own rank was lower than Bagration's.
The Emperor was with the army to encourage it, but his presence and ignorance of what steps to take, and the enormous number of advisers and plans, destroyed the first army's energy and it retired.

The intention was to make a stand at the Drissa camp, but Paulucci, aiming to become commander in chief, suddenly turned his energy to influencing Alexander, and Pfuel's entire plan was abandoned and the command given to Barclay. But since Barclay didn't inspire confidence, his power was limited. The armies were divided, there was no unity of command, and Barclay was unpopular; but from this confusion, division, and the unpopularity of the foreign commander in chief, there resulted, on the one hand, indecision and the avoidance of battle (which we could not have refrained from had the armies been united and had someone other than Barclay been in command), and on the other, an ever-increasing indignation against the foreigners and a rising patriotic fervor.

Barclay stood for caution. The Tsarevich hinted at treachery and demanded a general engagement. Lubomirsky, Bronnitsky, Wlocki, and the others of that group stirred up so much trouble that Barclay, under the pretext of sending papers to the Emperor, dispatched these Polish adjutant generals to Petersburg and plunged into open conflict with Bennigsen and the Tsarevich.

Despite his higher rank, Bagration — in this contest of magnanimity — took orders from Barclay. But having submitted, he agreed with him less than ever. By the Emperor's orders, Bagration reported directly to Alexander. He wrote to Arakcheev, the Emperor's confidant: "It must be as my sovereign pleases, but I cannot work with the Minister" (meaning Barclay). "For God's sake send me somewhere else, if only to command a regiment. I can't stand it here. Headquarters are so full of Germans that a Russian cannot exist and nothing makes any sense. I thought I was truly serving my sovereign and the Fatherland, but it turns out I am serving Barclay. I confess I have no desire to."

The swarm of Bronnitskys and Wintzingerodes and their kind further embittered the relations between the commanders in chief, and even less unity resulted. Preparations were made to fight the French in front of Smolensk. A general was sent to survey the position. This general, who hated Barclay, rode off to visit a friend of his, a corps commander, and having spent the day with him, returned to Barclay and condemned, as unsuitable from every point of view, the battleground he hadn't seen.
Bald Hills, Prince Nicholas Bolkonski's estate, lay forty miles east of Smolensk and two miles from the main road to Moscow.

That same evening the prince gave his instructions to Alpatych. Dessalles asked to see Princess Mary and told her that, since the prince was not well and was taking no steps to ensure his safety, and since Prince Andrew's letter made it clear that staying at Bald Hills might be dangerous, he respectfully advised her to send a letter with Alpatych to the Provincial Governor at Smolensk, asking about the state of affairs and the extent of the danger to Bald Hills. Dessalles wrote this letter for Princess Mary, she signed it, and it was given to Alpatych with instructions to hand it to the Governor and return as quickly as possible if there was danger.
"To his Honor Baron Asch, from General-in-Chief Prince Bolkonski," he announced with such solemnity and importance that the official turned to him and took the letters.

"With our kind of business, how can we just leave?" said Ferapontov. "We'd have to pay seven rubles a cartload to Dorogobuzh, and I tell them it's not Christian to charge that! Selivanov, now, he made a good deal last Thursday—sold flour to the army at nine rubles a sack. Will you have some tea?" he added.

Among the countless categories that can be applied to the phenomena of human life, one may distinguish between those where substance matters most and those where form does. To the latter—as distinct from village, country, provincial, or even Moscow life—we may assign Petersburg life, and especially the life of its salons. That salon life is unchanging. Since 1805 we had made peace and quarreled again with Bonaparte and had made constitutions and unmade them again, but the salons of Anna Pavlovna and Helene remained just as they had been—the one seven and the other five years before. At Anna Pavlovna's they spoke with puzzlement of Bonaparte's successes, just as before, and saw in them and in the subservience shown to him by the European sovereigns a malicious conspiracy whose sole purpose was to cause unpleasantness and anxiety to the court circle that Anna Pavlovna represented. And in Helene's salon, which Rumyantsev himself honored with his visits, regarding Helene as a remarkably intelligent woman, they spoke with the same ecstasy in 1812 as in 1808 of the "great nation" and the "great man" and regretted our rift with France, a rift which, according to them, ought to be promptly ended by peace.

Lately, since the Emperor's return from the army, there had been some excitement in these rival salon circles and some demonstrations of hostility between them, but each camp kept to its own line. In Anna Pavlovna's circle, only those Frenchmen who were deep-rooted legitimists were admitted, and patriotic views were expressed: that one shouldn't attend the French theater and that maintaining the French troupe was costing the government as much as a whole army corps. The war's progress was eagerly followed, and only the most flattering reports about our army were circulated. In the French circle of Helene and Rumyantsev, reports of the enemy's cruelty and of the war were challenged, and all Napoleon's attempts at conciliation were discussed. In that circle they frowned on those who advised hurried preparations for moving the court and the girls' educational institutions under the Dowager Empress's patronage to Kazan. In Helene's circle, the war was regarded as a series of formal demonstrations that would very soon end in peace. The view that prevailed there was Bilibin's—he was now quite at home in Helene's house, which every clever man was obliged to visit—that matters would be settled not by gunpowder, but by those who had invented it. In that circle, the Moscow enthusiasm (news of which had reached Petersburg along with the Emperor's return) was ridiculed sarcastically and very cleverly, though with great caution.

Soon after the Emperor's return, Prince Vasili, in a conversation about the war at Anna Pavlovna's, severely criticized Barclay de Tolly but was undecided as to who ought to be appointed commander in chief. One of the visitors, usually referred to as "a man of great merit," having described how he had that day seen Kutuzov—the newly chosen chief of the Petersburg militia—presiding over the enrollment of recruits at the Treasury, cautiously ventured to suggest that Kutuzov would be the man to satisfy all requirements.

"I've talked and talked at the Assembly of the Nobility," Prince Vasili interrupted, "but they did not listen to me. I told them his election as chief of the militia would not please the Emperor. They did not listen to me."

This was perfectly correct on the twenty-fourth of July. But on the twenty-ninth of July, Kutuzov was given the title of Prince. This might indicate a wish to get rid of him, and so Prince Vasili's opinion remained valid, though he was not now in any hurry to express it. But on the eighth of August, a committee consisting of Field Marshal Saltykov, Arakcheev, Vyazmitinov, Lopukhin, and Kochubey met to consider the progress of the war. This committee concluded that our failures were due to a lack of unified command, and though its members were aware of the Emperor's dislike of Kutuzov, after brief deliberation they agreed to recommend his appointment as commander in chief. That same day Kutuzov was appointed commander in chief with full powers over the armies and over the entire region they occupied.

"Well, have you heard the great news? Prince Kutuzov is field marshal! All disagreements are over! I am so glad, so delighted! At last we have a man!" he said, glancing sternly and significantly around at everyone in the drawing room.
"But, Prince, they say he's blind!" he said, reminding Prince Vasili of his own words.
"Eh? Nonsense! He sees well enough," said Prince Vasili quickly, in a deep voice with a slight cough—the voice and cough he always used to dismiss difficulties.

"He sees well enough," he added. "And what I'm so pleased about is that our sovereign has given him full powers over all the armies and the whole region—powers no commander in chief has ever had before. He's a second autocrat," he concluded with a triumphant smile.

"They say the Emperor was reluctant to give Kutuzov those powers. They say he blushed like a girl to whom La Fontaine's Joconde is read, when he said to Kutuzov: 'Your Emperor and the Fatherland award you this honor.'"

"Oh, no, no!" warmly rejoined Prince Vasili, now unwilling to yield Kutuzov to anyone; in his opinion Kutuzov was not only admirable but was adored by everybody. "No, that's impossible," he said, "for our sovereign valued him so highly before."

After Smolensk, Napoleon sought a battle beyond Dorogobuzh at Vyazma, and then at Tsarevo-Zaimishche, but it happened that due to a combination of innumerable circumstances, the Russians could not give battle until they reached Borodino, seventy miles from Moscow. From Vyazma, Napoleon ordered a direct advance on Moscow.

Moscow, the Asiatic capital of this great empire, the sacred city of Alexander's people, Moscow with its countless churches shaped like Chinese pagodas (in French)—this Moscow gave Napoleon's imagination no rest. On the march from Vyazma to Tsarevo-Zaimishche, he rode his light bay bobtailed horse accompanied by his Guards, his bodyguard, his pages, and his aides-de-camp. Berthier, his chief of staff, dropped behind to question a Russian prisoner captured by the cavalry. Followed by the interpreter Lelorgne d'Ideville, he overtook Napoleon at a gallop and reined in his horse with an amused expression.
* Moscou, la capitale asiatique de ce grand empire, la ville sacrée des peuples d'Alexandre, Moscou avec ses innombrables églises en forme de pagodes chinoises.

The interpreter translated these words without the final phrase, and Bonaparte smiled. "The young Cossack made his mighty interlocutor smile," says Thiers. After riding a few paces in silence, Napoleon turned to Berthier and said he wanted to see how the news that he was talking to the Emperor himself—to that very Emperor who had inscribed his immortally victorious name on the Pyramids—would affect this child of the Don. (in French)

After Alpatych's return from Smolensk, the old prince seemed suddenly to wake from a dream. On reaching home, Pierre told Evstafey—his head coachman, who knew everything, could do anything, and was known to all Moscow—that he would leave that night for the army at Mozhaysk, and ordered him to send his saddle horses ahead. Why and how were the battles of Shevardino and Borodino given and accepted? Why was the battle of Borodino fought? There was not the slightest sense in it for either the French or the Russians. Its immediate result for the Russians was, and was bound to be, that we were brought closer to the destruction of Moscow—which we feared more than anything in the world; and for the French, its immediate result was that they were brought closer to the destruction of their whole army—which they feared more than anything in the world. The outcome was completely obvious, and yet Napoleon offered and Kutuzov accepted the battle.

If the commanders had been guided by reason, it would seem obvious to Napoleon that by advancing thirteen hundred miles and fighting with a probability of losing a quarter of his army, he was marching toward certain destruction; and it would have been equally clear to Kutuzov that by accepting battle and risking the loss of a quarter of his army, he would certainly lose Moscow. For Kutuzov this was as mathematically clear as a simple rule in checkers: if I have one piece fewer than my opponent and keep trading pieces evenly, I will certainly lose, and so I should stop trading. Say my opponent has sixteen pieces and I have fourteen—I am only one-eighth weaker than he is. But if we go on trading and I lose thirteen more pieces to his thirteen, he ends up three times as strong as I am.

Before the battle of Borodino our strength relative to the French was about five to six, but after the battle it was little more than one to two: before the battle we had a hundred thousand against a hundred and twenty thousand; afterward, barely fifty thousand against a hundred thousand. Yet the shrewd and experienced Kutuzov accepted the battle, while Napoleon, supposedly a commander of genius, offered it—losing a quarter of his army and lengthening his lines of communication even further. If we are told he expected to end the campaign by capturing Moscow, as he had ended a previous campaign by capturing Vienna, there is much evidence to the contrary. Napoleon's own historians tell us that from Smolensk onward he wanted to stop, that he knew the danger of his extended position, and that he knew the occupation of Moscow would not end the campaign, for at Smolensk he had seen what condition the Russians were leaving their own towns in—left to him—and he had received not a single reply to his repeated announcements of his wish to negotiate.

In giving and accepting battle at Borodino, Kutuzov acted involuntarily and irrationally. But later, to fit what had occurred, historians provided cleverly crafted evidence of the foresight and genius of the generals who, of history's blind tools, were the most enslaved and involuntary.

The ancients left us model heroic poems in which the heroes supply the entire interest of the story, and we still cannot accustom ourselves to the fact that, in our era, history written in that same heroic mode is meaningless.

On the other question—how the battle of Borodino and the preceding battle of Shevardino were fought—there also exists a definite, well-known, but quite false account. All the historians describe the affair as follows:

The Russians did not seek the best position; on the contrary, during the retreat they passed many positions better than Borodino. They did not stop at any of them because Kutuzov did not wish to occupy a position he had not chosen himself, because the popular demand for battle had not yet been expressed strongly enough, because Miloradovich had not yet arrived with the militia, and for many other reasons. The fact is that other positions they had passed were stronger, and the position at Borodino (where the battle was fought), far from being strong, was no more of a position than any other spot one might find in the Russian Empire by sticking a pin into the map at hazard.

Not only did the Russians not fortify the position on the field of Borodino to the left of and at right angles to the highway (the position where the battle took place), but never until the twenty-fifth of August, 1812, did they even consider that a battle might be fought there. This is shown, first, by the fact that there were no entrenchments there by the twenty-fifth, and those begun on the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth were never completed; and second, by the position of the Shevardino Redoubt. That redoubt was quite senseless in front of the position where the battle was accepted. Why was it more heavily fortified than any other point? And why were all efforts exhausted and six thousand men sacrificed defending it until late at night on the twenty-fourth? A Cossack patrol would have sufficed to observe the enemy. Third, as proof that the position where the battle was fought had not been planned, and that the Shevardino Redoubt was not an advanced post of that position, there is this: until the twenty-fifth, both Barclay de Tolly and Bagration were convinced the Shevardino Redoubt was the left flank of the position. Kutuzov himself, in his report written hastily after the battle, calls the Shevardino Redoubt the left flank of the position. Only much later, when reports on the battle of Borodino were written at leisure, was the incorrect and extraordinary claim invented—probably to justify the mistakes of a commander in chief who had to be portrayed as infallible—that the Shevardino Redoubt had been an advanced post (whereas in reality it was simply a fortified point on the left flank), and that the battle of Borodino was fought by us on a pre-selected, entrenched position (whereas it was fought on a quite unexpected and almost unfortified spot).

Napoleon, riding to Valuevo on the twenty-fourth, did not see (as the history books claim) the Russian position from Utitsa to Borodino (he could not have seen that position because it did not exist), nor did he see an advanced post of the Russian army. Instead, while pursuing the Russian rearguard, he came upon the left flank of the Russian position—at the Shevardino Redoubt—and unexpectedly for the Russians moved his army across the Kolocha. The Russians, not having time to begin a general battle, pulled back their left wing from the position they had intended to hold and took up a new position that had not been planned and was not fortified. By crossing the Kolocha to the left of the highway, Napoleon shifted the entire coming battle from right to left, as seen from the Russian side, and moved it onto the plain between Utitsa, Semenovsk, and Borodino—a plain no more advantageous as a position than any other in Russia. It was there that the entire battle of the twenty-sixth of August took place.

Had Napoleon not ridden out on the evening of the twenty-fourth to the Kolocha, and had he not then ordered an immediate attack on the redoubt, but instead begun the attack the next morning, then no one would have doubted that the Shevardino Redoubt was the left flank of our position. The battle would have taken place where we expected it. In that case, we would probably have defended the Shevardino Redoubt—our left flank—even more stubbornly. We would have attacked Napoleon in the center or on the right, and the battle would have been fought on the twenty-fifth, in the position we had intended and fortified. But the attack on our left flank came instead in the evening, after the retreat of our rearguard—that is, immediately after the fight at Gridneva. Because of this, and because the Russian commanders did not wish, or were not in time, to begin a general engagement that same evening, the first and chief action of the battle of Borodino was already lost on the twenty-fourth. This loss obviously led to the loss of the battle fought on the twenty-sixth.

Not only was the Russian army on the twenty-sixth defended by weak, unfinished entrenchments, but the disadvantage of that position was increased by the fact that the Russian commanders—not having fully grasped what had happened, namely the loss of our position on the left flank and the shifting of the entire forthcoming battlefield from right to left—maintained their extended position from the village of Novoe to Utitsa, and consequently had to shift their forces from right to left during the battle. So throughout the entire battle, the Russians opposed the entire French army launched against our left flank with only half as many men. (Poniatowski's action against Utitsa and Uvarov's on the right flank against the French were separate actions from the main battle.) So the battle of Borodino was not fought at all as it has been described (in an effort to conceal our commanders' mistakes, even at the cost of diminishing the glory due to the Russian army and people). The battle of Borodino was not fought on a pre-chosen, entrenched position with forces only slightly weaker than the enemy's. Rather, as a result of the loss of the Shevardino Redoubt, the Russians fought the battle of Borodino on an open and almost unfortified position, with forces only half as numerous as the French. Under those conditions, it was not merely unthinkable to fight for ten hours and achieve an indecisive result—it was unthinkable to keep the army even from complete collapse and rout.

"So as not to lay waste the country we were leaving to the enemy," said Prince Andrew with venomous irony. "It's very sound: you can't allow the land to be pillaged or accustom the troops to looting. At Smolensk too he calculated correctly that the French might outflank us since they had larger forces. But he couldn't understand this," cried Prince Andrew in a shrill voice that seemed to escape him involuntarily: "he couldn't understand that there, for the first time, we were fighting for Russian soil, and that there was a spirit in the men such as I had never seen before, and that we had held the French for two days, and that that success had increased our strength tenfold. He ordered us to retreat, and all our efforts and losses went for nothing. He didn't intend to betray us; he tried to do his best; he thought out everything carefully—and that is exactly why he's unfit. He's unfit now precisely because he plans everything very thoroughly and precisely, as every German must. How can I explain it?... Well, say your father has a German valet, and the valet is splendid and satisfies your father's needs better than you could—then it's fine to let him serve. But if your father is mortally ill, you'll send the valet away and attend to your father with your own clumsy, unpracticed hands, and will comfort him better than a skilled stranger could. That's how it's been with Barclay. While Russia was healthy, a foreigner could serve her and be a splendid minister; but the moment she's in danger, she needs one of her own kin. But in your Club they've been calling him a traitor! They've slandered him as a traitor, and the only result will be that later, ashamed of their false accusations, they'll make him out to be a hero or genius instead of a traitor—and that will be even more unjust. He is an honest and very meticulous German."
"A skillful commander?" said Pierre. "Well, one who foresees all possibilities... and foresees the enemy's intentions."

"Yes," replied Prince Andrew, "but with this little difference: in chess you can think over each move as long as you like and aren't limited by time, and with this further difference too: in chess, a knight is always stronger than a pawn, and two pawns are always stronger than one. In war, though, a battalion is sometimes stronger than a division and sometimes weaker than a company. The relative strength of bodies of troops can never be known to anyone. Believe me," he continued, "if things depended on plans made by the staff, I would be there making plans. But instead I have the honor of serving here in the regiment with these gentlemen, and I believe that on us—not on those others—tomorrow's battle will depend... Success never depends, and never will depend, on position, equipment, or even numbers—and least of all on position."

Prince Andrew glanced at Timokhin, who looked at his commander in alarm and confusion. In contrast to his former reserved taciturnity, Prince Andrew now seemed stirred up. He apparently couldn't stop himself from expressing the thoughts that had suddenly occurred to him.

"A battle is won by those who firmly resolve to win it! Why did we lose the battle of Austerlitz? Our losses were nearly equal to the French, but very early we told ourselves we were losing the battle—and we lost it. And we said so because we had nothing to fight for there, we wanted to get away from the battlefield as fast as possible. 'We've lost, so let's run,' and we ran. If we hadn't said that till evening, God knows what might have happened. But tomorrow we won't say it! You talk about our position—the left flank weak, the right flank overextended," he went on. "That's all nonsense, there's nothing of the kind. But what awaits us tomorrow? A hundred million most diverse chances that will be decided in an instant by whether our men or theirs run or don't run, and whether this man or that man is killed. Everything being done now is just play. The fact is that those men you've been riding around the position with don't just fail to help—they actually hinder. They're only concerned with their own petty interests."

"At such a moment!" Prince Andrew repeated. "To them it's only a moment affording opportunities to undermine a rival and earn an extra cross or ribbon. For me, tomorrow means this: a Russian army of a hundred thousand and a French army of a hundred thousand have met to fight, and the point is that these two hundred thousand men will fight, and whichever side fights more fiercely and spares itself less will win. And if you want to know: whatever happens, whatever blunders those at the top may make, we will win tomorrow's battle. Tomorrow, happen what may, we will win!"

"If there were none of this magnanimity in war, we would go to war only when it was worth going to certain death, as now. Then there would be no war because some Paul Ivanovich had offended some Michael Ivanovich. And when there was a war like this one, it would be real war! Then all these Westphalians and Hessians whom Napoleon is dragging along would not follow him into Russia, and we would not go fight in Austria and Prussia without knowing why. It all comes down to this: get rid of the falsehood and let war be war and not a game. As it is now, war is the favorite pastime of the idle and frivolous. The military profession is the most highly honored."

"But what is war? What is needed for success in warfare? What are the habits of the military? The aim of war is murder; the methods of war are spying, treachery, and their encouragement, the ruin of a country's inhabitants, robbing them or stealing to feed the army, and fraud and falsehood called military craft. The habits of the military class are the absence of freedom—that is, discipline—plus idleness, ignorance, cruelty, debauchery, and drunkenness. And in spite of all this, it is the highest class, respected by everyone. All the kings except the Chinese wear military uniforms, and the man who kills the most people gets the highest rewards."

For some time he stood in silence, wondering whether he should follow him or go away. "No, he doesn't want it!" Pierre decided. "And I know that this is our last meeting!" He sighed deeply and rode back to Gorki.

He closed his eyes. One image succeeded another in his imagination. On one of them he dwelt long and joyfully. He vividly recalled an evening in Petersburg. Natasha, with an animated, excited face, was telling him how she had gone looking for mushrooms the previous summer and had gotten lost in the big forest. She described the depths of the forest, her feelings, and a conversation with a beekeeper she met, incoherently and constantly interrupting her story to say: "No, I can't! I'm not telling it right; no, you don't understand," though he encouraged her by saying that he did understand, and he really had understood all she wanted to say. But Natasha was not satisfied with her own words: she felt they didn't convey the passionately poetic feeling she had experienced that day and wished to convey. "He was such a delightful old man, and it was so dark in the forest... and he had such kind... No, I can't describe it," she had said, flushed and excited. Prince Andrew smiled now the same happy smile as he had then when he looked into her eyes. "I understood her," he thought. "I not only understood her, but it was that inner, spiritual force—that sincerity, that openness of soul—that very soul of hers, which seemed bound by her body—it was that soul I loved in her... loved so deeply and happily..." and suddenly he remembered how his love had ended. "He didn't need anything like that. He neither saw nor understood anything of the kind. He only saw in her a pretty, fresh young girl with whom he didn't deign to join his fate. And I?... and he is still alive and happy!"

The original Russian line along the river Kolocha had been disrupted by the capture of the Shevardino Redoubt on the twenty-fourth, and part of the line—the left flank—had been pulled back. That part was not entrenched, and in front of it the ground was more open and level than elsewhere. It was obvious to anyone, military or civilian, that this was where the French should attack. It would seem that no great deliberation was needed to reach this conclusion, nor any particular care or trouble on the part of the Emperor and his marshals, nor was there any need of that special and supreme quality called genius which people are so ready to attribute to Napoleon; yet the historians who described the event later, and the men who surrounded Napoleon at the time, and Napoleon himself, all thought otherwise.

Napoleon rode across the plain, surveyed the terrain with a profound air and in silence, nodded approvingly or shook his head dubiously, and without explaining to the generals around him the deep course of reasoning behind his decisions, merely gave them his final conclusions as commands. Having heard a suggestion from Davout (now called the Prince of Eckmühl) to turn the Russian left wing, Napoleon said it should not be done, without explaining why. General Compans (who was to attack the flèches) proposed leading his division through the woods, and Napoleon agreed. The so-called Duke of Elchingen (Ney), though, ventured to remark that a move through the woods was dangerous and might throw the division into disorder.

After inspecting the terrain opposite the Shevardino Redoubt, Napoleon pondered briefly in silence and then indicated where two batteries should be set up by the morrow to act against the Russian entrenchments, and where the field artillery should be positioned in line with them.
After giving these and other orders, he returned to his tent, and the dispositions for the battle were written down from his dictation.
At dawn the two new batteries established during the night on the plain occupied by the Prince of Eckmühl will open fire on the opposing batteries of the enemy.

At the same time the commander of the artillery of the 1st Corps, General Pernetti, with thirty cannon of Compans's division and all the howitzers of Dessaix's and Friant's divisions, will move forward, open fire, and overwhelm with shellfire the enemy's battery, against which will operate:
24 guns of the Guard artillery, 30 guns of Compans's division,

The commander of the artillery of the 3rd Corps, General Fouché, will place the howitzers of the 3rd and 8th Corps, sixteen in all, on the flanks of the battery that is to bombard the entrenchment on the left, which will have forty guns in all directed against it.
General Compans will move through the wood to seize the first fortification.

The Viceroy will occupy the village and cross by its three bridges, advancing to the same heights as Morand's and Gérard's divisions, which under his command will be directed against the redoubt and fall into line with the rest of the forces.
All this must be done in good order (le tout se fera avec ordre et méthode), retaining troops in reserve as far as possible.
September 6, 1812 (New Style).

These dispositions, which are very obscure and confused if one allows oneself to regard the arrangements without religious awe of Napoleon's genius, related to Napoleon's orders to deal with four points—four different orders. Not one of them was, or could be, carried out.

The dispositions say first that the batteries placed at the spot Napoleon chose, together with Pernetti's and Fouché's guns, which were to come in line with them, 102 guns in all, were to open fire and shower shells on the Russian flèches and redoubts. This could not be done, because from the spots Napoleon selected, the projectiles did not carry to the Russian works, and those 102 guns fired into the air until the nearest commander, contrary to Napoleon's instructions, moved them forward.

The second order was that Poniatowski, advancing on the village through the wood, should turn the Russian left flank. This could not be done and was not done, because Poniatowski, advancing on the village through the wood, met Tuchkov there blocking his way, and could not and did not turn the Russian position.

The third order was: General Compans will move through the wood to seize the first fortification. Compans's division did not seize the first fortification but was driven back, because on emerging from the wood it had to re-form under grapeshot, of which Napoleon was unaware.

The fourth order was: The Viceroy will occupy the village (Borodino) and cross by its three bridges, advancing to the same heights as Morand's and Gérard's divisions (for whose movements no directions are given), which under his command will be directed against the redoubt and fall into line with the rest of the forces.

As far as one can make out—not so much from this unintelligible sentence as from the attempts of the Viceroy to execute the orders given him—he was to advance from the left through Borodino to the redoubt while Morand's and Gérard's divisions advanced simultaneously from the front.

All of this, like the other parts of the disposition, was not and could not be executed. After passing through Borodino, the Viceroy was driven back to the Kolocha and could get no farther; while Morand's and Gérard's divisions did not take the redoubt but were beaten back, and the redoubt was only captured at the end of the battle by cavalry (something probably unforeseen and unheard of by Napoleon). So not one of the orders in the disposition was, or could be, carried out. But the dispositions state that after the fight begins in this manner, orders will be given according to the enemy's movements—and so it might be supposed that Napoleon would make all necessary adjustments during the battle. But this was not and could not be done, because throughout the entire battle Napoleon was so far away that (as later became clear) he could not know the course of the battle, and not one of his orders during the fight could be carried out.
"She's been wounded!" said the adjutant. "In the right foreleg above the knee. A bullet, no doubt. Congratulations, Count — your baptism of fire!"

The marshals and generals, who were closer to the fighting but, like Napoleon, did not participate in the actual combat and only occasionally came within musket range, made their own decisions without consulting Napoleon and issued orders about where and how to fire, where cavalry should charge and infantry should run. But even their orders were rarely carried out, and then only partially. For the most part, things happened contrary to their commands. Soldiers ordered to advance ran back when met with grapeshot; soldiers ordered to hold their ground suddenly rushed forward or backward when Russians appeared unexpectedly before them, and cavalry charged without orders in pursuit of fleeing Russians. In this way two cavalry regiments galloped through the Semenovsk hollow, and as soon as they reached the crest turned around and galloped back at full speed. The infantry moved the same way, sometimes running to entirely different places than ordered. All commands about moving guns, sending infantry to fire, or dispatching horsemen to ride down Russian infantry were given by the officers on the spot nearest the units, without consulting Ney, Davout, or Murat, much less Napoleon. They didn't fear punishment for disobeying orders or acting on their own initiative, because in battle what's at stake is the dearest thing of all — one's own life — and sometimes safety seems to lie in running back, sometimes in running forward. These men in the thick of battle acted on the impulse of the moment. In reality, however, all these movements forward and backward did not improve or alter the position of the troops, and accomplished little harm on their own; the actual damage — the maiming and killing — was done by the balls and bullets flying over the fields where these men floundered about. The moment they left the zone of fire, their commanders in the rear re-formed them, restored discipline, and marched them back into the killing zone, where, under the influence of mortal fear, they broke discipline again and rushed about at random.

Napoleon silently shook his head. Assuming the refusal referred only to the victory and not to lunch, Monsieur de Beausset respectfully and playfully observed that there was no reason to skip lunch when one could have it.

The Russians didn't make that effort because they were not the attackers. At the start of the battle they had stood blocking the road to Moscow, and they were still doing so at the end. But even if the Russians had wanted to drive the French from their positions, they couldn't have made this final push — all the Russian troops had been broken up, and there was no part of the Russian army that had not suffered in the battle. Though still holding their ground, they had lost ONE HALF of their men.

The more the Russian army retreated, the more fiercely a spirit of hatred for the enemy flared up, and as it fell back, the army grew and consolidated. At Borodino, a collision occurred. Neither army was shattered, but the Russian army retreated immediately after the clash — as inevitably as a ball recoils after striking another that carries greater momentum. And with equal inevitability, the ball of the invasion, which had advanced with such momentum, rolled on for some distance, even though the collision had stripped it of all its power.

The Russians retreated eighty miles — beyond Moscow — and the French reached Moscow, where they came to a standstill. For five weeks there was not a single battle. The French didn't move. Like a bleeding, mortally wounded animal licking its wounds, they remained inert in Moscow for five weeks. Then suddenly, for no fresh reason, they fled back — dashing for the Kaluga road, and after a victory (at Malo-Yaroslavets, where the field of battle again remained theirs) without fighting a single serious engagement, they fled even faster toward Smolensk, beyond Smolensk, beyond the Berezina, beyond Vilna, and farther still.

On the evening of August 26, Kutuzov and the entire Russian army were convinced that the Battle of Borodino was a victory. Kutuzov reported this to the Emperor. He gave orders to prepare for a fresh battle to finish off the enemy, and did so not to deceive anyone but because he knew the enemy had been beaten — as everyone who had taken part in the battle knew.

It was impossible to fight before information was gathered, the wounded collected, ammunition supplies replenished, the dead counted, new officers appointed to replace those killed, and the men had eaten and slept. And meanwhile, the very next morning, the French army advanced on its own, carried forward by its own momentum, which seemed now to be growing in inverse proportion to the square of the distance from its goal. Kutuzov wanted to attack the next day, and the whole army wanted the same. But wanting to attack is not enough — there must also be the possibility of doing so, and that possibility did not exist. It was impossible not to retreat one day's march, and then in the same way it was impossible not to retreat another day's march, and a third, and at last, on September 1, when the army drew near Moscow — despite the powerful feelings that had risen in every rank — circumstances forced it to retreat beyond Moscow. And the troops made one final day's march and abandoned Moscow to the enemy.

For people accustomed to thinking that campaign plans and battles are made by generals — as any of us, sitting over a map in a study, can imagine how we'd have arranged things in this or that battle — certain questions arise: Why didn't Kutuzov do this or that during the retreat? Why didn't he take up a position before reaching Fili? Why didn't he retreat at once by the Kaluga road, abandoning Moscow? And so on. People who think this way forget, or don't know, the inevitable constraints that always limit any commander in chief. The activity of a commander in chief bears no resemblance to what we imagine when sitting comfortably at our desks studying a campaign on a map, with known numbers of troops on each side in a known location, starting from a given moment. A commander in chief never deals with the beginning of any event — the starting point from which we always view it. He is always in the midst of a series of shifting events, and at no moment can he grasp the full significance of what is happening. From moment to moment the event takes shape imperceptibly, and at every moment of this continuous, uninterrupted shaping of events the commander in chief finds himself in the midst of a most complex web of intrigues, worries, contingencies, authorities, projects, counsels, threats, and deceptions, constantly forced to respond to countless questions that conflict with one another.

A commander in chief's job might seem to be simply choosing one of these proposals. But he cannot even do that. Events and time do not wait. For instance, on the twenty-eighth it is suggested to him that he cross to the Kaluga road, but just then an adjutant gallops up from Miloradovich asking whether to engage the French or retreat. An order must be given him at once, that instant. And the order to retreat carries us past the turn to the Kaluga road. After the adjutant comes the commissary general asking where the stores are to be taken, then the head of hospitals asking where to send the wounded, then a courier from Petersburg with a letter from the sovereign refusing to contemplate abandoning Moscow. The commander in chief's rival — the man undermining him (and there are always several such men, not just one) — presents a new plan diametrically opposed to the Kaluga road idea. The commander in chief himself needs sleep and refreshment to maintain his energy. A respected general overlooked in the distribution of awards comes to complain. Local residents beg for protection. An officer sent to inspect the area comes in and gives a report quite contrary to what was said by the officer previously sent; and a spy, a prisoner, and a general back from reconnaissance all describe the enemy's position differently. People accustomed to misunderstanding or forgetting these inevitable constraints describe, for instance, the army's position at Fili and assume the commander in chief could freely decide on September 1 whether to abandon or defend Moscow — whereas with the Russian army less than four miles away, no such question existed. When had it been decided?
