"How glad I am you've come. You're tired. Won't you have some tea?" Natasha went up to her. "You've improved in looks and grown more manly," continued the countess, taking her daughter's hand.

Princess Mary postponed her departure. Sonya and the count tried to take Natasha's place but couldn't. They saw that she alone was able to restrain her mother from unreasoning despair. For three weeks Natasha stayed constantly at her mother's side, sleeping on a lounge chair in her room, making her eat and drink, and talking to her endlessly, because the mere sound of her tender, caressing tones soothed her mother.

A spiritual wound, caused by a tearing of the spiritual body, is like a physical wound. Strange as it may seem, just as a deep wound may heal until its edges join, physical and spiritual wounds alike can only heal completely through a vital force from within.

Natasha's wound healed in that way. She had believed her life was over, but her love for her mother unexpectedly showed her that the essence of life—love—was still active within her. Love awoke, and so did life.

Prince Andrew's last days had drawn Princess Mary and Natasha together; this new sorrow brought them closer still. Princess Mary postponed her departure and for three weeks looked after Natasha as though she were a sick child. The last weeks spent in her mother's bedroom had strained Natasha's physical strength.

"Is she like him?" thought Natasha. "Yes, like and yet not like. But she is quite original, strange, new, and unknown. And she loves me. What is in her heart? Everything good. But how? What is her mind like? What does she think about me? Yes, she is wonderful!"
"Mary," she said timidly, drawing Princess Mary's hand toward her, "Mary, you mustn't think I'm wicked. You don't, do you? Mary darling, how I love you! Let's be quite, quite friends."
And Natasha, embracing her, began kissing her face and hands, making Princess Mary feel shy but happy by this demonstration of her feelings.

From that day a tender and passionate friendship—the kind that exists only between women—was established between Princess Mary and Natasha. They were constantly kissing and saying tender things to each other and spent most of their time together. When one left the room, the other grew restless and hurried to rejoin her. Together they felt more in harmony with each other than either felt with herself when alone. A feeling stronger than friendship arose between them—an exclusive feeling of life being possible only in each other's presence.

Sometimes they were silent for hours; other times, after they were already in bed, they would begin talking and continue until morning. They spoke mostly of the distant past. Princess Mary told of her childhood, her mother, her father, and her dreams; and Natasha, who had previously turned away from that life of devotion, submission, and the poetry of Christian self-sacrifice with passive incomprehension, now—feeling bound to Princess Mary by affection—learned to love her past too and to understand a side of life that had been entirely foreign to her. She did not think of applying submission and self-denial to her own life, for she was used to seeking other kinds of joy; but she understood and loved those previously incomprehensible virtues in someone else. For Princess Mary, listening to Natasha's stories of childhood and youth, an equally new and previously unknown side of life opened up: a belief in life and its pleasures.

Just as before, they never mentioned him, so as not to lower (as they felt) their exalted feelings by putting them into words. But this silence gradually—without their realizing it—caused them to begin forgetting him.

One day she went quickly upstairs and found herself out of breath. Without thinking, she immediately invented a reason to go back down, and then, testing her strength, ran upstairs again, carefully noting the result.

She did not know, and would not have believed, that beneath the layer of slime that seemed to her impenetrable, covering her soul, delicate young shoots of grass were already sprouting. They would take root and so cover with their living green the grief that weighed her down that it would soon no longer be seen or noticed. The wound had begun to heal from within.

After the encounter at Vyazma—where Kutuzov had been unable to hold back his troops in their eagerness to overwhelm and cut off the enemy, and so on—the farther movement of the fleeing French and the Russians pursuing them continued as far as Krasnoe without a battle. The flight was so rapid that the Russian army pursuing the French could not keep up; cavalry and artillery horses broke down, and the information about French movements was never reliable.

To understand the degree of exhaustion of the Russian army, you only need to grasp clearly the meaning of one fact: while losing no more than five thousand killed and wounded after Tarutino, and fewer than a hundred prisoners, the Russian army that had left Tarutino a hundred thousand strong reached Krasnoe with only fifty thousand.

The rapid Russian pursuit was just as destructive to our army as the French flight was to theirs. The only difference was that the Russian army moved voluntarily, with no such threat of destruction as hung over the French, and that sick Frenchmen were left behind in enemy hands while sick Russians were left among their own people. The main cause of Napoleon's army wasting away was the speed of its movement, and convincing proof of this is the corresponding decline of the Russian army.

As far as it was in his power, Kutuzov did not try to check the French movement, though that was what Petersburg and the Russian generals wanted. Instead, as he had at Tarutino and Vyazma, he directed all his efforts toward speeding the retreat along while easing the movement of our army.

But besides this, since the army's exhaustion and enormous reduction from the speed of the advance had become obvious, another reason for slackening the pace and delaying presented itself: the aim of the Russian army was to pursue the French. The French route was unknown, so the closer our troops trod on their heels, the greater the distance they had to cover. Only by keeping some distance back could they cut across the French zigzag path. All the artful maneuvers suggested by our generals meant fresh movements of the army and a lengthening of its marches, whereas the only sensible objective was to shorten those marches. To this end, Kutuzov directed his efforts throughout the entire campaign from Moscow to Vilna—not casually or intermittently, but so consistently that he never once deviated from it.

Kutuzov felt and knew—not through reasoning or military science, but with the whole of his Russian being—what every Russian soldier felt: that the French were beaten, that the enemy was fleeing and must be driven out; but at the same time he, like his soldiers, understood all the hardship of this march, the rapidity of which was unparalleled for such a time of the year.

But the generals—especially the foreign ones in the Russian army—wanted to distinguish themselves, astonish someone, and for some reason capture a king or a duke. Any battle now would be horrible and senseless, yet to them this seemed the perfect time to fight and conquer somebody. Kutuzov merely shrugged his shoulders when one after another they presented him with maneuver plans for soldiers who were ill-shod, insufficiently clad, and half-starved—soldiers who within a month, without fighting a single battle, had dwindled to half their original number and who, at the best, if the flight continued, would have to go a greater distance than they had already traversed before they reached the frontier.

Toll wrote out a battle plan: "The first column will march to such and such a place," and so on. And as usual, nothing happened according to plan. Prince Eugene of Wurttemberg fired from a hilltop over the French crowds running past and demanded reinforcements that never arrived. The French, avoiding the Russians, scattered and hid in the forest by night, making their way around as best they could, and continued their flight.

Miloradovich, who said he did not want to know anything about the commissary affairs of his detachment and could never be found when needed—this man who styled himself chevalier sans peur et sans reproche, "the knight without fear and without reproach," and who loved to parley with the French—sent envoys demanding their surrender, wasted time, and didn't do what he was ordered to do.
* Knight without fear and without reproach.

And the cavalry, with spurs and sabers urging on horses that could barely move, trotted with great effort to the column presented to them—that is, to a crowd of Frenchmen frozen stiff, frostbitten, and starving—and the column that had been presented to them threw down its arms and surrendered, as it had long been anxious to do.

These men, carried away by their passions, were nothing more than blind tools of the most melancholy law of necessity, yet they considered themselves heroes and imagined they were accomplishing a most noble and honorable deed. They blamed Kutuzov, saying that from the very start of the campaign he had prevented them from defeating Napoleon, that he thought of nothing but satisfying his passions and would not advance from the Linen Factories because he was comfortable there, that he had stopped the advance at Krasnoe because he quite lost his head on learning Napoleon was there, and that he probably had an understanding with Napoleon and had been bribed, and so on and so on.

Not only his contemporaries, carried away by their passions, but posterity and history itself have acclaimed Napoleon as grand, while Kutuzov is described by foreigners as a crafty, dissolute, weak old courtier, and by Russians as something indefinite—a sort of puppet useful only because he had a Russian name.

In 1812 and 1813, Kutuzov was openly accused of blundering. The Emperor was dissatisfied with him. And in a history recently written by order of the Highest Authorities, it is stated that Kutuzov was a cunning court liar, frightened of the name of Napoleon, and that by his blunders at Krasnoe and the Berezina he deprived the Russian army of the glory of a complete victory over the French.
(History of the Year 1812. The character of Kutuzov and reflections on the unsatisfactory results of the battles at Krasnoe, by the historian Bogdanovich.)

Such is the fate—not of great men ("grands hommes") whom the Russian mind does not acknowledge—but of those rare and always solitary individuals who, perceiving the will of Providence, submit their personal will to it. The hatred and contempt of the crowd is the punishment for those who discern the higher laws.

For Russian historians, strange and terrible to say, Napoleon—that most insignificant tool of history, who never anywhere, even in exile, showed human dignity—Napoleon is the object of adulation and enthusiasm; he is grand. But Kutuzov—the man who, from the beginning to the end of his activity in 1812, never once wavered by word or deed from Borodino to Vilna, gave an example of self-sacrifice unmatched in history, along with a living awareness of the future significance of what was happening—Kutuzov seems to them something indefinite and pitiful, and when they speak of him and of the year 1812, they always seem a little ashamed.

Kutuzov never spoke of "forty centuries looking down from the Pyramids," of the sacrifices he was making for the fatherland, or of what he intended or had accomplished. In general he said nothing about himself, struck no poses, always appeared to be the simplest and most ordinary of men, and said the simplest and most ordinary things. He wrote letters to his daughters and to the writer Madame de Stael, read novels, enjoyed the company of pretty women, joked with generals, officers, and soldiers, and never contradicted anyone who tried to prove anything to him. When Count Rostopchin galloped up to Kutuzov at the Yauza bridge and personally accused him of causing Moscow's destruction, saying: "How was it you promised not to abandon Moscow without a battle?" Kutuzov replied: "And I shall not abandon Moscow without a battle"—though Moscow was already abandoned. When Arakcheev, coming from the Emperor, told him that Ermolov ought to be appointed chief of artillery, Kutuzov replied: "Yes, I was just saying so myself"—though a moment before he had said the exact opposite. What did it matter to him—who then alone amid a senseless crowd understood the whole tremendous significance of what was happening—what did it matter to him whether Rostopchin attributed the calamities of Moscow to him or to himself? Still less could it matter who was named chief of artillery.

But that man, so careless with his words, never once during his entire period of activity uttered a single word inconsistent with the one aim toward which he worked throughout the whole war. Obviously, despite himself, in the most diverse circumstances, he repeatedly expressed his real thoughts with the bitter conviction that he would not be understood. Beginning with the battle of Borodino, from which point his disagreement with those around him began, he alone said that Borodino was a victory, and he repeated this both verbally and in his dispatches and reports until his death. He alone said that the loss of Moscow is not the loss of Russia. In reply to Lauriston's proposal of peace, he said: There can be no peace, for such is the people's will. He alone, during the French retreat, said that all our maneuvers are useless, that everything is being accomplished of itself better than we could desire, that the enemy must be offered a "golden bridge", that the battles at Tarutino, Vyazma, and Krasnoe were unnecessary, that they needed to keep enough strength to reach the border, and that he would not sacrifice a single Russian for ten Frenchmen.

Nor do his words alone prove that only he understood the meaning of the events. His actions—without the slightest deviation—were all directed toward one and the same threefold end: (1) to brace all his strength for the conflict with the French, (2) to defeat them, and (3) to drive them out of Russia, while minimizing as far as possible the suffering of our people and our army.

This procrastinator Kutuzov, whose motto was "Patience and Time," this enemy of decisive action, gave battle at Borodino and invested the preparations for it with unparalleled solemnity. This same Kutuzov, who before the battle of Austerlitz had predicted it would be lost, alone and against everyone else declared to his dying day that Borodino was a victory—despite generals' assurances that the battle was lost, and despite the unprecedented fact that an army had had to retreat after winning it. He alone, throughout the entire retreat, insisted that battles, which were useless then, should not be fought, and that a new war should not be begun, and that the Russian frontier should not be crossed.

It is easy now to understand the significance of these events, now that they and their results lie before us, provided we refrain from attributing to the actions of the masses aims that existed only in the heads of a dozen people.
The source of that extraordinary power of penetrating the meaning of the events then occurring lay in the national feeling that he possessed in full purity and strength.

Only the recognition that he possessed this feeling caused the people, in such a strange manner and contrary to the Tsar's wish, to choose him—an old man in disfavor—as their representative in the national war. And only that feeling placed him on the highest human pedestal from which he, the commander in chief, devoted all his powers not to slaying and destroying men but to saving them and showing them pity.
That simple, modest, and therefore truly great figure could not be cast in the false mold of a European hero—the supposed ruler of men—that history has invented.
To a lackey no man can be great, for a lackey has his own conception of greatness.
"Hey, Sixth Company! You devils! Lend a hand... You may want us one of these days."
"Vive Henri Quatre! Vive ce roi valiant! — Long live Henry the Fourth! Long live that brave king!" sang Morel, winking. "Ce diable à quatre... — That rowdy devil..."

"Qui eut le triple talent, De boire, de battre, Et d'être un vert galant — who had a triple talent—for drinking, for fighting, and for being a charming fellow..."

The French army melted away at the steady rate of a mathematical progression, and the crossing of the Berezina—about which so much has been written—was only one intermediate stage in its destruction, not at all the decisive episode of the campaign. If so much has been and still is written about the Berezina, on the French side this is only because at the broken bridge across that river, the calamities their army had been previously enduring were suddenly concentrated at one moment into a tragic spectacle that remained in every memory. On the Russian side, it's simply because in Petersburg—far from the actual fighting—a plan (again one of Pfuel's) had been devised to catch Napoleon in a strategic trap at the Berezina River. Everyone assured himself that everything would go according to plan, and therefore insisted that it was the Berezina crossing that destroyed the French army. In reality, the results of the crossing were far less disastrous to the French—in guns and men lost—than Krasnoe had been, as the numbers show.

The sole importance of the Berezina crossing lies in the fact that it plainly and undeniably proved the fallacy of all the plans to cut off the enemy's retreat and the soundness of the only possible course of action—the one Kutuzov and the general mass of the army had demanded—simply to follow the enemy. The French mob fled at ever-increasing speed, all its energy directed toward reaching its goal. It fled like a wounded animal, and it was impossible to block its path. This was shown not so much by its arrangements for crossing as by what happened at the bridges. When the bridges collapsed, unarmed soldiers, civilians from Moscow, and women with children who were traveling with the French—all carried forward by vis inertiæ—pressed forward into boats and into the ice-covered water and did not surrender.

That impulse was reasonable. The condition of both fugitives and pursuers was equally miserable. As long as they stayed with their own people, each could hope for help from comrades and hold a defined place among them. But those who surrendered—while remaining in that same wretched condition—dropped to a lower level in any claim on the necessities of life. The French didn't need to be told that half the prisoners—whom the Russians didn't know what to do with—perished of cold and hunger despite their captors' desire to save them. They sensed it could not be otherwise. The most compassionate Russian commanders, those favorably disposed toward the French—even the Frenchmen in the Russian service—could do nothing for the prisoners. The French perished from the very conditions to which the Russian army itself was exposed. It was impossible to take bread and clothing from our hungry and indispensable soldiers to give to Frenchmen who, though not harmful, or hated, or guilty, were simply unnecessary. Some Russians even did that, but they were exceptions.

Certain destruction lay behind the French, but ahead lay hope. Their ships had been burned; there was no salvation except in collective flight, and on that the whole strength of the French was concentrated.

The farther they fled, the more wretched became the plight of the remnant—especially after the Berezina, on which (in consequence of the Petersburg plan) the Russians had placed such high hopes—and the more heated grew the passions of the Russian commanders, who blamed one another and above all Kutuzov. Anticipation that the failure of the Petersburg Berezina plan would be attributed to Kutuzov led to growing dissatisfaction, contempt, and ridicule. The ridicule and contempt were expressed, of course, in respectful form, making it impossible for him to ask wherein he was to blame. They didn't talk seriously to him; when reporting or asking for his approval, they appeared to be fulfilling a regrettable formality while winking behind his back and trying to mislead him at every turn.

Because they couldn't understand him, all these people assumed it was useless to talk to the old man. He would never grasp the profundity of their plans, they thought; he would answer with his phrases (which they thought were mere phrases) about a "golden bridge" and the impossibility of crossing the frontier with a mob of ragged men, and so forth. They had heard all that before. And everything he said—that they needed to wait for supplies, that the men had no boots—was so simple, while what they proposed was so complex and clever, that it was evident that he was old and stupid, and that they, though not in command, were military geniuses.
"On account of your bouts of ill health, would Your Excellency be so good as to proceed to Kaluga upon receipt of this, there to await further commands and appointments from His Imperial Majesty."

But after Bennigsen's departure, the Grand Duke Tsarevich Constantine Pavlovich joined the army. He had participated at the beginning of the campaign but had subsequently been removed from the army by Kutuzov. Now, returning to the army, he informed Kutuzov of the Emperor's displeasure at the poor success of our forces and the slowness of their advance. The Emperor intended to join the army personally in a few days.

The old man was experienced in both court and military affairs. This was the same Kutuzov who in August had been chosen commander in chief against the sovereign's wishes, who had removed the Grand Duke and heir apparent from the army, and who on his own authority and contrary to the Emperor's will had decided to abandon Moscow. Now he instantly understood that his day was over, his role played out, and the power he supposedly held was no longer his. And he understood this not merely from the court's attitude. He saw, on the one hand, that the military business in which he had played his part was finished, and he felt his mission was accomplished. At the same time, he began to feel the physical weariness of his aged body and the need for physical rest.

On November twenty-ninth, Kutuzov entered Vilna—his "dear Vilna," as he called it. Twice during his career he had been governor of Vilna. In that wealthy city, which had not been damaged, he found old friends and associations as well as the comforts of life he had so long been deprived of. And he suddenly turned from the cares of army and state, and as far as the passions seething around him allowed, immersed himself in the quiet life he had once known, as if all that was taking place and all that had still to be done in the realm of history did not concern him at all.

Chichagov was one of the most zealous "cutters-off" and "breakers-up." He had first wanted to effect a diversion in Greece, then in Warsaw, but never wished to go where he was actually sent. He was noted, too, for his bold manner of speaking to the Emperor, and he considered Kutuzov indebted to him—because when he was sent to conclude peace with Turkey in 1811, independently of Kutuzov, he had found the peace already made, and he acknowledged to the Emperor that the credit belonged to Kutuzov. This Chichagov was the first to meet Kutuzov at the castle where the latter was to stay. In undress naval uniform, with a dirk, and holding his cap under his arm, he handed Kutuzov a garrison report and the keys to the city. The contemptuously respectful attitude of the younger men toward the old man in his dotage was expressed to the highest degree by the behavior of Chichagov, who knew of the accusations being leveled at Kutuzov.
In conversation with Chichagov, Kutuzov happened to mention that the vehicles packed with china captured from him at Borisov had been recovered and would be restored to him.

"You mean to imply that I have nothing to eat from.... On the contrary, I can supply you with everything, even if you want to throw dinner parties," Chichagov replied warmly, trying with every word to prove his own integrity and therefore imagining Kutuzov was driven by the same concern.
Kutuzov, shrugging his shoulders, replied with his subtle, penetrating smile: "I meant merely to say what I said."

Contrary to the Emperor's wishes, Kutuzov kept the greater part of the army in Vilna. Those around him said he became extraordinarily slack and physically feeble during his stay. He attended to army business reluctantly, left everything to his generals, and while waiting for the Emperor to arrive led a dissipated life.

A courier who galloped to the castle in advance, in a troika with three foam-flecked horses, shouted "Coming!" and Konovnitsyn rushed into the vestibule to inform Kutuzov, who was waiting in the hall porter's little lodge.

A minute later, the old man's large, heavy figure in full-dress uniform—his chest covered with orders and a sash wrapped around his stomach—waddled out onto the porch. He put on his hat with its peaks to the sides, and holding his gloves in his hand, walked with effort sideways down the steps to street level, taking in his hand the report he had prepared for the Emperor.

From the force of fifty years' habit, all this had a physically agitating effect on the old general. He carefully and hastily felt himself all over, readjusted his hat, and pulling himself together, drew himself upright. At the very moment the Emperor stepped down from the sleigh and looked up at him, Kutuzov handed over the report and began speaking in his smooth, ingratiating voice.

The Emperor swept a rapid glance over Kutuzov from head to foot, frowned for an instant, but immediately composed himself, stepped forward, extended his arms, and embraced the old man. This embrace too, because of a long-standing impression related to his innermost feelings, had its usual effect on Kutuzov, and he gave a sob.

When alone with the field marshal, the Emperor expressed his dissatisfaction at the slowness of the pursuit and the mistakes made at Krasnoe and the Berezina, and informed him of his intentions for a future campaign abroad. Kutuzov made no rejoinder or remark. The same submissive, expressionless look with which he had listened to the Emperor's orders on the field of Austerlitz seven years before settled on his face now.

Suddenly he appeared to remember. A barely perceptible smile flashed across his puffy face, and bowing low and respectfully, he took the object from the tray. It was the Order of St. George, First Class.

It would be hard to explain why and where ants rush when their anthill has been destroyed: some hauling away bits of debris, larvae, and dead bodies, others streaming back to the hill, or why they bump into each other, chase one another, and fight. But it would be equally hard to explain what drove people to swarm back to Moscow after the French had gone. And just as when you watch ants around their ruined hill, despite the destruction of the hill, the tenacity, energy, and sheer number of the swarming insects show that something indestructible and immaterial—the real strength of the colony—still exists—so too Moscow in October, despite the absence of any authorities, churches, treasures, or houses, was still the same Moscow it had been in August. Everything was destroyed except something intangible yet powerful and indestructible.

The longer the French plundering continued, the more both Moscow's wealth and the plunderers' strength were destroyed. But the Russian plundering that accompanied the reoccupation of the capital had the opposite effect: the longer it continued and the more people took part in it, the more rapidly Moscow's wealth and its ordinary life were restored.

Within a week, the peasants who had come with empty carts to haul away plunder were stopped by the authorities and forced to cart dead bodies out of the city instead. Other peasants, hearing what had happened to their neighbors, brought in cartloads of rye, oats, and hay, undercutting each other's prices until they fell below what they had been before. Crews of carpenters hoping for high wages arrived daily, and on all sides new houses were going up and burned ones were being repaired. Merchants set up shop in makeshift stalls. Restaurants and inns opened in fire-damaged buildings. The clergy resumed services in many of the churches that had escaped the fire. Donors contributed looted church furnishings that had been recovered. Officials set up their small offices with writing desks and filing cabinets in small rooms. The higher authorities and the police organized the distribution of goods left behind by the French. The owners of houses in which a great deal of property from other buildings had been gathered complained of the unfairness of having everything taken to the Faceted Palace in the Kremlin, while others argued that the French had brought things from different houses to one location, and it was therefore unfair to let the owner of that house keep everything found in it. People cursed the police and bribed them; made out estimates ten times the real value for government stores that had perished in the fire; and appeals for help were made. And Count Rostopchin wrote proclamations.

"No, it's just the surprise," Pierre thought. But as soon as he tried to resume the conversation he'd been having with Princess Mary, he glanced again at Natasha, and a deeper flush spread across his face, and an even stronger wave of joy and agitation seized his heart. He grew confused in what he was saying and stopped in the middle of a sentence.

"She's come to stay with me," said Princess Mary. "The count and countess will be here in a few days. The countess is in a dreadful state, but Natasha herself needed to see a doctor. They insisted she come with me."
"Yes—is there a single family free of sorrow now?" said Pierre, turning to Natasha. "You know it happened on the very day we were rescued. I saw him. What a wonderful boy he was!"
Natasha looked at him, and in answer to his words her eyes widened and lit up.
"What can anyone say, what can anyone think, to console you?" said Pierre. "Nothing! Why did a boy like that, so splendid, so full of life, have to die?"
"Yes, these days it would be hard to live without faith..." Princess Mary remarked.
"Yes, yes, that's really true," Pierre broke in quickly.
"Why is it true?" Natasha asked, looking straight into Pierre's eyes.
"How can you even ask why?" said Princess Mary. "Just the thought of what's waiting for us..."
Natasha, without waiting for Princess Mary to finish, looked questioningly at Pierre again.
"And because," Pierre went on, "only someone who believes there's a God ruling us can bear a loss like hers—and... like yours."
Natasha had already opened her mouth to say something, but stopped herself. Pierre hurriedly turned away from her and went back to questioning Princess Mary about his friend's last days.

Pierre's awkwardness had almost worn off by now, but at the same time he felt that his freedom had vanished completely. He felt that there was now a judge over his every word and action, and that this judge's verdict mattered to him more than the verdict of the whole rest of the world put together. As he spoke, he found himself weighing what impression his words would make on Natasha. He wasn't saying things on purpose to please her, but whatever he said, he looked at it through her eyes.

Princess Mary—reluctantly, as people usually do in such cases—began telling him about the state she'd found Prince Andrew in. But Pierre's face, trembling with feeling, and his eager, restless questions, gradually drew her into details she had dreaded recalling even for her own sake.

"Yes, yes, and then...?" Pierre kept saying, leaning toward her with his whole body, listening eagerly to her story. "Yes, yes... so he grew calm, gentler? With his whole soul he'd always wanted just one thing—to be truly good—so he couldn't have been afraid of dying. Whatever faults he had—if he had any—weren't really his fault. So he did soften?... What a wonderful thing that he saw you again," he added, turning suddenly to Natasha and looking at her with eyes full of tears.
Natasha's face twitched. She frowned and lowered her eyes for a moment. She hesitated, unsure whether to speak.

"Yes, that was happiness," she said at last, in her quiet voice with its deep, chesty tone. "For me, it truly was happiness." She paused. "And he... he... he said he'd been wishing for it at the very moment I walked into the room...."
Natasha's voice broke. She flushed, pressed her clasped hands against her knees, then, with a visible effort at control, lifted her head and began speaking quickly.

"We knew nothing about it when we left Moscow. I didn't dare ask about him. Then suddenly Sonya told me he was traveling with us. I had no idea, I couldn't imagine what state he was in—all I wanted was to see him, to be with him," she said, trembling, breathing fast.

And without letting them interrupt, she went on to tell them what she had never told anyone before—everything she had lived through during those three weeks of the journey and of their time at Yaroslavl.

Pierre listened to her with his lips parted, his tear-filled eyes fixed on her. As he listened he wasn't thinking about Prince Andrew, or about death, or about what she was actually telling him. He listened to her and felt only pity for her—for what she was suffering right now, in the telling.
Princess Mary, frowning as she fought back her own tears, sat beside Natasha and heard, for the first time, the story of those last days of her brother's love for Natasha, and Natasha's for him.
Clearly Natasha needed to tell that story—painful as it was, and joyful too.
She talked on, mixing the most trivial details in with the innermost secrets of her heart, and it seemed as if she would never stop. Several times she repeated the same thing twice.
Dessalles' voice came from outside the door, asking whether little Nicholas could come in to say good night.
"Well, that's all of it—everything," said Natasha.

She got up quickly just as Nicholas came in, almost ran to the door hidden behind the curtains, struck her head on it, and rushed out of the room with a groan of pain or grief—it was hard to tell which.
Pierre stared at the door she had vanished through, and couldn't understand why he suddenly felt utterly alone in the world.
Princess Mary pulled him out of his daze by drawing his attention to her nephew, who had come into the room.

In that moment of tenderness, young Nicholas's face—which looked so much like his father's—moved Pierre so deeply that after kissing the boy he got up quickly, pulled out his handkerchief, and went to the window. He meant to say goodbye to Princess Mary, but she wouldn't let him go.
"No—Natasha and I sometimes don't go to sleep until after two, so please don't leave. I'll have supper brought up. Go on down, we'll join you in a moment."
Before Pierre left the room, Princess Mary told him: "This is the first time she's talked about him like that."

Pierre was shown into the large, brightly lit dining room; a few minutes later he heard footsteps, and Princess Mary came in with Natasha. Natasha was calm, though a serious, grave expression had settled on her face again. All three of them now felt that awkwardness that usually follows a serious, heartfelt talk. It's impossible to go back to the same subject, talking about trifles feels awkward, and yet the urge to talk is there, so silence feels like an affectation. They went to the table without a word. The footmen pulled the chairs back and pushed them in again. Pierre unfolded his cold napkin and, determined to break the silence, looked from Natasha to Princess Mary. They had evidently both come to the same decision: both their eyes shone with the quiet satisfaction of an admission that alongside sorrow, life also holds joy.

"Will you have some vodka, Count?" asked Princess Mary, and those words suddenly banished the shadows of the past. "Now tell us about yourself," she said. "People say such unbelievable things about you."

"Yes," Pierre answered, with the smile of mild irony that had become habitual to him now. "They even tell me things I never dreamed happened to me! Mary Abramovna invited me to her house and kept telling me what had happened to me, or ought to have happened to me. Stepan Stepanych also instructed me on how I ought to tell the story of my adventures. In general I've noticed it's very easy to become an interesting man—I'm an interesting man now—people invite me over and tell me all about myself."
Natasha smiled and was about to say something.
"We were told," Princess Mary broke in, "that you lost two million rubles in Moscow. Is that true?"
"Yet I'm three times as rich as I was before," Pierre replied.
Even though his situation had actually changed now that he'd decided to pay off his wife's debts and rebuild his houses, Pierre still insisted he had become three times as rich as before.
"What I've definitely gained is freedom," he began seriously, but didn't go on, realizing the subject was too self-centered.
"And are you building?"
"Yes. Savelich says I must!"

"Tell me—did you already know about the countess's death when you decided to stay behind in Moscow?" asked Princess Mary, and immediately flushed, realizing that her question, coming right after his talk of freedom, gave his words a meaning he perhaps hadn't intended.

"No," Pierre answered, apparently not at all bothered by the meaning Princess Mary had given his words. "I heard about it in Oryol, and you can't imagine how it shook me. We weren't a model couple," he added quickly, glancing at Natasha and noticing the curiosity on her face about how he'd speak of his wife, "but her death shook me terribly. When two people quarrel, they're both always somewhat to blame, and your own guilt suddenly feels much heavier once the other person is no longer alive to answer it. And then a death like that... with no friends near her, no comfort! I feel very, very sorry for her," he finished, pleased to see a look of glad approval on Natasha's face.
"So, you're an eligible bachelor again," said Princess Mary.
Pierre suddenly flushed crimson and for a long while tried not to look at Natasha. When he finally risked a glance her way, her face seemed cold, stern—almost contemptuous, he thought.
"And is it true you actually saw and spoke with Napoleon, the way we've heard?" said Princess Mary.
"No, not once! Everyone seems to imagine that being taken prisoner means becoming Napoleon's guest. Not only did I never see him, I never even heard anything about him—I was in far lower company!"
Supper ended, and Pierre, who at first had refused to talk about his captivity, was gradually drawn into telling the story.
"But it's true you stayed behind in Moscow to kill Napoleon?" Natasha asked with a faint smile. "I guessed as much back when we met at the Sukharev Tower—remember?"
Pierre admitted it was true, and from there, drawn on gradually by Princess Mary's questions and especially by Natasha's, he gave a detailed account of everything that had happened to him.

At first he spoke with the mild, amused irony that had become his habit toward everyone, and especially toward himself, but when he came to describing the horrors and suffering he had witnessed, he got carried away without meaning to, and began speaking with the suppressed feeling of a man reliving strong impressions in the act of recalling them.

Princess Mary, with a gentle smile, kept looking from Pierre to Natasha and back. In the whole story she saw only Pierre and his goodness. Natasha, leaning on her elbow, her expression constantly shifting with the story, watched Pierre with an attention that never wandered—clearly living through everything he described right alongside him. Not just her look, but her exclamations and the brief questions she asked, showed Pierre that she understood exactly what he was trying to convey. It was clear she grasped not only what he said, but also what he wanted to say and couldn't put into words. Pierre's account of the incident with the child and the woman—the one he'd been arrested for trying to protect—went like this: "It was an awful sight—children abandoned, some of them right in the flames... One was snatched out just in front of me... and there were women who'd had their things ripped off them, their earrings torn right out of their ears..." he flushed and grew flustered. "Then a patrol arrived and arrested every man there—every man, that is, who wasn't looting—and I was one of them."
"I'm sure you're not telling us everything—I'm sure you did something..." said Natasha, then paused and added, "something brave?"
Pierre went on. When he reached the execution he wanted to skip over the horrible details, but Natasha insisted he leave nothing out.
Pierre began to tell them about Karataev, then stopped. By now he had risen from the table and was pacing the room, Natasha following him with her eyes. Then he added:
"No—you can't understand what I learned from that man, that illiterate, simple man."
"Yes, yes, go on!" said Natasha. "Where is he now?"
"They killed him almost right in front of me."
And Pierre, his voice shaking the whole time, went on to describe the last days of the retreat, Karataev's illness, and his death.

He told the story of his adventures in a way he'd never let himself recall them before. He now saw, as it were, a new meaning in everything he had lived through. Now that he was telling it all to Natasha, he felt that particular pleasure a man feels when women listen to him—not the clever women who listen either to remember what they hear so they can use it to sharpen their own minds and repeat it later, or who want to fold it into some idea of their own and immediately offer their own clever remarks, ready-made in their little mental workshop—but the pleasure that comes from real women, gifted with the capacity to take in and absorb the very best a man has to show of himself. Natasha, without realizing it, was pure attention: she didn't miss a word, didn't miss a single quiver in Pierre's voice, not a look, not a twitch of a muscle in his face, not a single gesture. She caught his unfinished sentences in mid-flight and took them straight into her open heart, sensing the hidden meaning behind all of Pierre's inner struggle.

Princess Mary understood his story and felt for him, but by now something else had caught her full attention. She saw the possibility of love and happiness between Natasha and Pierre, and the first flicker of that thought filled her heart with gladness.
It was three in the morning. The footmen came in, their faces sad and stern, to change the candles, but no one noticed them.

Pierre finished his story. Natasha went on looking at him closely with bright, attentive, animated eyes, as though trying to make out something more that he had perhaps left unsaid. Pierre, in a happy, embarrassed confusion, glanced at her now and then, trying to think what to say next to start a new subject. Princess Mary stayed silent. None of them noticed that it was three in the morning and long past time for bed.

"People talk about misfortune and suffering," Pierre remarked, "but if right now someone asked me: 'Would you rather go back to being what you were before you were taken prisoner, or live through all of it again?'—then for heaven's sake, give me captivity and horsemeat again! We imagine that once we're thrown out of our usual ruts, everything is lost, but it's exactly then that something new and good begins. As long as there's life, there's happiness. There's so much, so much still ahead of us. I'm saying this to you," he added, turning to Natasha.
"Yes, yes," she said, answering something else entirely. "I too would wish for nothing but to live it all again from the start."
"That's not true, not true!" cried Pierre. "I'm not to blame for being alive and wanting to live—and neither are you."
Suddenly Natasha bowed her head, covered her face with her hands, and began to cry.
Pierre rose and took his leave.
Princess Mary and Natasha met as usual in the bedroom. They talked about what Pierre had told them. Princess Mary didn't say what she thought of Pierre, and Natasha didn't speak of him either.
"Well, good night, Mary!" said Natasha. "You know, I'm often afraid that by not talking about him"—she meant Prince Andrew—"for fear of not doing justice to our feelings, we're forgetting him."
Princess Mary sighed deeply, which was her way of admitting Natasha had a point, but she didn't say so out loud.
"Is it possible to forget him?" she said.

"It did me so much good to tell it all today. It was hard, painful—but good, so good!" said Natasha. "I'm sure he really loved him. That's why I told him... Was it all right?" she added, suddenly blushing.
"To tell Pierre? Oh, yes. What a wonderful man he is!" said Princess Mary.

"Do you know, Mary..." Natasha suddenly said, with a mischievous smile Princess Mary hadn't seen on her face in a long time, "he's grown somehow so clean, so smooth, so fresh—as if he'd just stepped out of a Russian bathhouse; do you know what I mean? Out of a moral bathhouse. Isn't that true?"
"Yes," Princess Mary answered. "He's changed a great deal for the better."
"With a short coat and his hair cropped short; just as if—well, just as if he'd come straight from the baths... Papa used to..."
"I understand now why he"—meaning Prince Andrew—"liked no one the way he liked him," said Princess Mary.
"Yes, and yet he's completely different from him. They say men become friends precisely when they're completely different. That must be true. He really is nothing like him—in anything."
And that same mischievous smile lingered on her face for a long time afterward, as if it had simply been forgotten there.

It was a long time before Pierre could fall asleep that night. He paced up and down his room, one moment turning some difficult problem over in his mind and frowning, the next suddenly shrugging his shoulders and wincing, and then smiling happily.

He was thinking about Prince Andrew, about Natasha, about their love—one moment jealous of her past, the next reproaching himself for that very feeling. It was already six in the morning, and he was still pacing the room.

"Well, what am I supposed to do if it can't be avoided? What am I to do? It's clearly meant to be," he said to himself, and undressing hastily, got into bed—happy and agitated, but without a trace of hesitation or doubt.
"Strange, impossible as this kind of happiness seems, I have to do everything in my power so that she and I become husband and wife," he told himself.
A few days earlier Pierre had decided to leave for Petersburg on Friday. When he woke up on Thursday, Savelich came in to ask about packing for the trip.

"What, to Petersburg? What's Petersburg? Who's even in Petersburg?" he asked himself, though only inwardly. "Oh, right—a long time ago, before all this happened, I did mean to go to Petersburg for some reason," he thought. "Why, though? Well, maybe I'll go anyway. What a good man he is, so attentive, remembering everything," he thought, looking at Savelich's old face, "and what a pleasant smile he has!"
"So, Savelich, you still don't want to accept your freedom?" Pierre asked him.
"What good is freedom to me, your excellency? We lived under the late count—God rest his soul!—and we've lived under you too, and never once been wronged."
"And what about your children?"
"The children will get along just the same. With masters like this, a person can live."
"If I may say so, your excellency, that would be a fine thing."
"How easily he takes it," thought Pierre. "He has no idea how frightening it is, how dangerous. Too soon, or too late... it's terrible!"

"No, I'll put it off for now. I'll let you know later. Forgive me for the trouble I've caused you," said Pierre, and seeing Savelich smile, he thought: "But how odd that he doesn't know there's no Petersburg for me now, that this other matter has to be settled first! But he probably knows it perfectly well, and is only pretending not to. Should I talk it over with him, see what he thinks?" Pierre wondered. "No—another time."
At breakfast Pierre told his cousin, the princess, that he had visited Princess Mary the day before and had met there—"Guess who? Natasha Rostova!"
The princess seemed to see nothing more remarkable in that than if he'd mentioned running into Anna Semyonovna.
"I've seen Princess Mary," she replied. "I heard they were arranging a match for her with young Rostov. It would be a very good thing for the Rostovs—they say the family's utterly ruined."
"No—I mean, do you actually know Natasha Rostova?"
"I heard about that business of hers at the time. It was a great pity."
"No, she either doesn't understand or she's pretending," Pierre thought. "Better not say anything more to her about it."
The princess had also had provisions packed for Pierre's journey.
"How kind everyone is," thought Pierre. "What's strange is that they should still bother with these things now, when it can't possibly matter to them anymore. And all for my sake!"
That same day the Chief of Police came to see Pierre, inviting him to send someone to the Faceted Palace to collect property that was to be returned to its owners that day.

"And this man too," thought Pierre, studying the Chief of Police's face. "What a fine-looking, kind officer. Imagine troubling himself over such trifles now! And people actually say he's dishonest, that he takes bribes. What nonsense! Besides, why shouldn't he take bribes? That's how he was raised, and everyone does it. But what a kind, pleasant face, and how he smiles when he looks at me."

As he drove through the streets past the burned-out houses, he found himself struck by the beauty of the ruins. The jagged chimney stacks and crumbling walls of the burned quarters of the city, stretching out and half-hiding one another, reminded him of the Rhine and of the Colosseum. The cabmen he passed and their fares, the carpenters cutting timber for new houses with their axes, the women peddlers, the shopkeepers—all of them looked at him with bright, cheerful eyes that seemed to say: "Ah, there he is! Let's see what comes of it!"

At the entrance to Princess Mary's house Pierre found himself doubting whether he had really been there the night before, whether he had really seen and talked with Natasha. "Maybe I imagined it; maybe I'll walk in and there won't be anyone there." But he had barely stepped into the room before he felt her presence with his whole being, in the loss of his sense of freedom. She was wearing the same black dress with its soft folds, her hair done the same way as the day before, and yet she was completely different. If she had looked like this when he'd walked in the day before, he could not for a single moment have failed to recognize her.

She looked the way he had known her almost as a child, and later as Prince Andrew's fiancée. A bright, questioning light shone in her eyes, and her face wore a friendly, strangely mischievous expression.
Pierre had dinner with them and would have stayed the whole evening, but Princess Mary was going to vespers, so Pierre left the house along with her.

The next day he came early, had dinner, and stayed the whole evening. Though Princess Mary and Natasha were clearly glad to see their visitor, and though all of Pierre's interest was now centered on that house, by evening they had talked their way through everything, and the conversation kept drifting from one trivial topic to another and repeatedly breaking off. He stayed so long that Princess Mary and Natasha exchanged glances, clearly wondering when he would leave. Pierre noticed this but still couldn't go. He felt uneasy and embarrassed, but he sat on because he simply could not bring himself to get up and say goodbye.
Princess Mary, seeing no end to it, was the first to rise, and complaining of a headache, began saying good night.
"So you're off to Petersburg tomorrow?" she asked.

"No, I'm not going," Pierre answered quickly, in a tone of surprise, almost offense. "Yes... no... to Petersburg? Tomorrow—but I won't say goodbye just yet. I'll come by in case you have any errands for me," he said, standing in front of Princess Mary, turning red, but making no move to leave.

Natasha gave him her hand and went out. Princess Mary, instead of leaving, sank into an armchair and looked at him with a stern, searching gaze from her deep, radiant eyes. The tiredness she had shown so plainly before had vanished completely now. With a long, deep sigh, she seemed to be settling in for a long talk.
The moment Natasha left the room, Pierre's confusion and awkwardness vanished instantly, replaced by eager excitement. He quickly pulled an armchair closer to Princess Mary.

"Yes, I wanted to tell you," he said, answering her look as though she had spoken aloud. "Princess, help me! What should I do? Can I hope? Princess, my dear friend, listen! I know everything. I know I'm not worthy of her, I know it's impossible to speak of it now. But I want to be a brother to her. No—not that. I don't want that, I can't..."
He stopped and rubbed his face and eyes with his hands.

"Well," he went on, with a visible effort to control himself and put his thoughts in order. "I don't know when I began to love her, but I have loved her, and only her, my whole life, and I love her so much that I can't imagine life without her. I can't propose to her right now, but the thought that maybe someday she could be my wife—and that I might be letting that chance slip away... that chance... it's unbearable. Tell me, can I hope? Tell me what I should do, dear princess!" he added after a pause, and touched her hand when she didn't answer.
"I've been thinking over what you told me," Princess Mary answered. "Here's what I'll say. You're right that speaking to her of love right now..."

Princess Mary stopped herself. She had been about to say that speaking of love was out of the question, but she stopped, because she had seen from the sudden change in Natasha two days earlier that far from being hurt if Pierre spoke of his love, it was exactly what she wanted.
"Speaking to her now just wouldn't do," the princess said all the same.
"But what should I do?"
Pierre looked straight into Princess Mary's eyes.
"I know that she loves—will love you," Princess Mary corrected herself.
Before she had even finished the sentence, Pierre had leapt up and seized Princess Mary's hand with a startled expression.
"What makes you say that? You think I may hope? You really think...?"
"Yes, I think so," said Princess Mary, smiling. "Write to her parents, and leave the rest to me. I'll tell her when the time is right. I want it to happen, and my heart tells me it will."
"No, it can't be! How happy I am! But it can't be.... How happy I am! No, it can't be!" Pierre kept repeating, kissing Princess Mary's hands.
"Go to Petersburg—that will be for the best. And I'll write to you," she said.

The next day Pierre came to say goodbye. Natasha was less animated than she'd been the day before, but that day, whenever Pierre looked at her, he sometimes felt as if he were dissolving, as if neither he nor she existed at all anymore, as if nothing existed but happiness itself. "Is it possible? No, it can't be," he told himself with every glance, every gesture, every word that filled his soul with joy.
When, saying goodbye, he took her thin, slender hand, he couldn't help holding it a little longer than he should have.

"Is it possible that this hand, this face, these eyes, all this wealth of feminine charm that still feels so strange to me, is it possible that one day it will be mine forever, as familiar to me as I am to myself?... No, that's impossible!..."
"Goodbye, Count," she said aloud. "I'll look forward so much to your return," she added in a whisper.

And those simple words, her look, and the expression on her face as she said them, gave Pierre two months' worth of endless memories, interpretations, and happy daydreams. "'I'll look forward so much to your return....' Yes, yes, how exactly did she say it? Yes—'I'll look forward so much to your return.' Oh, how happy I am! What is happening to me? How happy I am!" Pierre kept saying to himself.
There was nothing in Pierre's soul now anything like what had tormented him during his courtship of Helene.

He didn't repeat to himself, with that sickening flush of shame, the words he'd said, or ask, "Oh, why didn't I say that?" or "What on earth made me say 'Je vous aime'?" On the contrary, he now went back over every word he or Natasha had spoken, picturing every detail of her face, her smile, and he didn't want to change or add a single thing—only to go over it again and again. There wasn't a shadow of doubt in his mind anymore about whether what he'd set out to do was right. Only one terrible doubt sometimes crossed his mind: "Wasn't it all a dream? Could Princess Mary be mistaken? Am I not being too conceited, too sure of myself? I believe all this—and then suddenly Princess Mary tells her, and she's bound to smile and say: 'How strange! He must be fooling himself. Doesn't he know he's just a man, only a man, while I...? I'm something entirely different, something higher.'"

That was the only doubt that kept troubling Pierre. He wasn't making any plans now. The happiness in front of him seemed so unimaginable that if he could only reach it, it would be the end of everything—everything would be complete.

A joyful, unexpected kind of madness, the sort he'd never thought himself capable of, took hold of him. The whole meaning of life—not just his own life, but the whole world's—now seemed to him to be centered in his love and in the possibility of being loved by her. At times it seemed to him that everyone around him was occupied with exactly one thing: his future happiness. Sometimes it seemed to him that other people were all just as pleased as he was, and were only pretending to be busy with other things to hide it. In every word, every gesture, he saw hints of his own happiness. He often surprised the people he met with his meaningfully happy looks and smiles, which seemed to hint at some secret understanding between him and them. And when he realized that people might not actually be aware of his happiness, he felt sorry for them with his whole heart, and wanted somehow to explain to them that whatever was occupying them was a trivial, frivolous thing, not worth a moment's attention.

When people suggested he go into government service, or when the war or general political matters came up, discussed on the assumption that everyone's welfare hinged on this or that turn of events, he would listen with a mild, pitying smile, and surprise people with his strange remarks. But at this time he saw everyone—both the people who, as he imagined, understood the real meaning of life, which was to say, what he himself was feeling, and the unfortunate ones who clearly didn't understand it—all lit by the glow of the feeling shining within him, and effortlessly, without even trying, he saw in every single person he met everything good in them, everything worth loving.

When he went through his dead wife's affairs and papers, her memory stirred nothing in him but pity that she had never known the happiness he now knew. Prince Vasili, who, having landed a new post and some fresh decorations, was especially full of himself these days, struck Pierre now as a pitiable, good-natured old man, much to be felt sorry for.

Often, later in life, Pierre looked back on this period of blissful madness. Every view he formed of people and circumstances during this time stayed true for him ever afterward. Not only did he never renounce them later on, but whenever he was in doubt or torn between conflicting feelings, he would go back to the views he'd held during this time of his madness, and they always turned out to be right.

"I may have seemed strange, odd, back then," he thought, "but I wasn't as mad as I looked. Actually I was wiser then, and saw more clearly than at any other time, and understood everything worth understanding in life—because... because I was happy."

Pierre's madness consisted in this: he no longer waited, as he used to, to discover in people the particular traits he called "good qualities" before he loved them. His heart now overflowed with love on its own, and by loving people without a reason, he found undeniable reasons to love them.

After Pierre left that first evening, when Natasha had said to Princess Mary with a gaily mocking smile, "He looks just—just as if he'd come out of a Russian bathhouse—in a short coat, his hair cropped short," something hidden, something Natasha herself didn't know was there, but couldn't be held back, woke up in her soul.

Everything about her—her face, her walk, her look, her voice—suddenly changed. To her own surprise, a force of life and a hope of happiness rose to the surface and demanded to be satisfied. From that evening on, she seemed to have forgotten everything that had happened to her. She no longer complained about her situation, didn't say a word about the past, and no longer feared to make happy plans for the future. She spoke little about Pierre, but whenever Princess Mary brought him up, a long-extinguished light would rekindle in her eyes, and her lips would curve into a strange smile.

The change in Natasha surprised Princess Mary at first, but once she understood what it meant, it grieved her. "Could she really have loved my brother so little that she can forget him this quickly?" she wondered, turning the change over in her mind. But whenever she was actually with Natasha, she wasn't upset with her, and she didn't reproach her. This reawakened force of life that had taken hold of Natasha was so clearly irrepressible, so clearly unexpected even to Natasha herself, that in her presence Princess Mary felt she had no right to reproach her, even inwardly.
Natasha gave herself over so fully and openly to this new feeling that she didn't even try to hide the fact that she was no longer sad, but bright and cheerful.
When Princess Mary came back to her room after her late-night talk with Pierre, Natasha met her on the threshold.
"He's spoken? Yes? He's spoken?" she kept repeating.
And a joyful yet almost pained expression, one that seemed to be asking forgiveness for her own joy, settled over Natasha's face.

Understandable and touching as the look Natasha gave her seemed to Princess Mary, and sorry as she felt for Natasha's agitation, those words stung her for a moment. She thought of her brother, and of his love.
"But what's to be done? She can't help it," the princess thought.
And with a sad, rather stern expression, she told Natasha everything Pierre had said. On hearing that he was going to Petersburg, Natasha was stunned.
"To Petersburg!" she repeated, as if she couldn't understand it.
But then, noticing the grief on Princess Mary's face, she guessed the reason for that sadness, and suddenly burst into tears.
"Mary," she said, "tell me what I should do! I'm afraid of being a bad person. Whatever you tell me, I'll do it. Just tell me...."
"Do you love him?"
"Then why are you crying? I'm happy for you," said Princess Mary, who, because of those tears, forgave Natasha's happiness completely.
"It won't be right away—someday. Just think how much fun it will be when I'm his wife and you marry Nicholas!"
"Natasha, I've asked you not to talk about that. Let's talk about you instead."
They sat in silence for a while.
"But why does he have to go to Petersburg?" Natasha suddenly asked, and then hurried to answer her own question. "No, no, he has to... Yes, Mary, he has to...."

Seven years had passed. The storm-tossed sea of European history had settled back within its shores and seemed to have grown calm. But the mysterious forces that move humanity—mysterious because the laws governing their motion are unknown to us—went on working.

Though the surface of the sea of history looked motionless, the movement of humanity went on as unceasingly as the flow of time. Various groups of people formed and dissolved; the coming formation and dissolution of kingdoms, and the displacement of peoples, was being prepared.

The sea of history was no longer being driven spasmodically from shore to shore the way it had been before. It was seething in its depths. Historical figures were no longer being carried by the waves from one shore to another, as they had been. Now they seemed to spin in place. The historical figures who stood at the head of armies, and who had once reflected the movement of the masses by ordering wars, campaigns, and battles, now reflected that restless movement through political and diplomatic combinations, laws, and treaties.
Historians call this activity on the part of historical figures "the reaction."

In dealing with this period they severely condemn the historical figures who, in their view, caused what they call the reaction. All the well-known people of that era—from Alexander and Napoleon to the writer Madame de Staël, the churchman Photius, the philosophers Schelling and Fichte, and the writer Chateaubriand, and the rest—pass before their severe tribunal and are either acquitted or condemned, depending on whether they are judged to have served progress or reaction.

According to these accounts, a reaction took place in Russia too at that time, and the chief culprit was Alexander I—the same man who, by their own account, had been the chief cause of the liberal movement at the start of his reign, and the savior of Russia.
There is no one in Russian letters today, from schoolboy essayist to learned historian, who doesn't throw his little stone at Alexander for what he did wrong during this stretch of his reign.

"He should have acted this way here, and that way there. In this instance he did well, in that instance badly. He behaved admirably at the start of his reign and during 1812, but he behaved badly by granting Poland a constitution, by forming the Holy Alliance, by handing power over to his minister Arakcheev, by favoring Golitsyn and mysticism, and later the statesman Shishkov and Photius. He also behaved badly by meddling in the affairs of the active army, and by disbanding the Semenov regiment, a guards regiment."
It would take a dozen pages to list every reproach the historians level at him, all of it drawn from their knowledge of what is good for humanity.
What do these reproaches mean?

Don't the very actions the historians praise Alexander I for—his liberal moves at the start of his reign, his struggle against Napoleon, the firmness he showed in 1812 and in the campaign of 1813—flow from the same sources? Those sources are the circumstances of his birth, his education, his life, the things that made him the man he was. And isn't it from those same sources that the actions they blame him for also flowed—the Holy Alliance, the restoration of Poland, the reaction of 1820 and after?
What does the substance of these reproaches come down to?

It comes down to this. A historical figure like Alexander I stands on the very highest peak of human power, with the blinding light of history trained on him. He is a man exposed to the strongest influences there are—the intrigue, the flattery, the self-deception that power inevitably brings with it. He is a man who at every moment of his life felt himself responsible for everything happening across Europe. And he is a living man, not an invented character, a man who like every other man had his personal habits, passions, impulses toward goodness, beauty, and truth. Though not lacking in virtue—even the historians don't deny him that—this man did not hold the same idea of what was good for humanity fifty years ago that a present-day professor holds, a professor who has spent his whole life since youth doing nothing but study, which is to say, reading books and lectures and taking notes on them.

But even granting that Alexander I was mistaken, fifty years ago, in his view of what was good for the people, we're forced to assume something else as well. The historian sitting in judgment on Alexander will, after enough time has passed, turn out to have been mistaken in his view of what's good for humanity. This assumption isn't just natural, it's unavoidable, because if you watch the movement of history, you see that opinion about what's good for mankind shifts every year, with every new writer, so that what looked good ten years ago looks bad now, and the reverse. What's more, we find flatly contradictory views held at one and the same time about what counts as good and bad in history: some people count granting Poland a constitution and forming the Holy Alliance as praiseworthy acts of Alexander's, while others count the very same acts as blameworthy.

The activity of Alexander, or of Napoleon, can't be called either useful or harmful, because there's no way to say what it was useful or harmful for. If that activity displeases someone, it's only because it doesn't line up with that person's limited idea of what's good. I might judge the preservation of my father's house in Moscow, the glory of Russian arms, the prosperity of the universities of Petersburg and elsewhere, the freedom of Poland, the greatness of Russia, the balance of power in Europe, or some particular kind of European culture called "progress" to be good or bad. But whichever way I judge it, I have to admit that beyond all these things, the actions of every historical figure have other, more general purposes that I cannot see.

But let's grant, for argument's sake, that what we call science can reconcile all these contradictions and does possess an unchanging standard of good and bad by which to judge historical figures and events. Let's say Alexander could have done everything differently. Let's say that, guided by the very people who blame him now—people who claim to know the ultimate goal humanity is moving toward—he could have arranged everything according to the program his present-day accusers would hand him: nationality, freedom, equality, progress. Let's say that, I think, covers it. Let's assume this program was achievable, that it had already been worked out at the time, and that Alexander had acted on it. What, then, would have become of the activity of everyone who opposed the government's prevailing tendency at that time—activity that the historians themselves judge to have been good and beneficial? That activity would not have existed. There would have been no life. There would have been nothing.
If we accept that human life can be governed by reason, then the possibility of life is destroyed.

Historians assume that great men lead humanity toward certain goals: the greatness of Russia or of France, the balance of power in Europe, the spread of the ideas of the Revolution, general progress, or anything else. If we make that same assumption, there's no way to explain the facts of history without bringing in the ideas of chance and genius.

If the goal of the European wars at the start of the nineteenth century had been the aggrandizement of Russia, that goal could have been reached without all the wars that came before it, and without the invasion. If the goal was the aggrandizement of France, that could have been reached without the Revolution and without the Empire. If the goal was spreading ideas, the printing press could have done that job far better than warfare. If the goal was the progress of civilization, it's easy enough to see that there are other, more expedient ways of spreading civilization than by destroying wealth and human lives.
Why did it happen this way, and not some other way?
Because that's how it happened! "Chance created the situation; genius made use of it," says history.

The words "chance" and "genius" don't point to any real, existing thing, and so they can't be defined. They only mark a certain stage in our understanding of phenomena. I don't know why some particular event happens; I think I can't know it; so I do not try to know it, and I call it chance. I see a force producing effects that go beyond the reach of ordinary human power; I don't understand why this is happening, and I call it genius.

To a flock of rams, the one ram that the shepherd drives every evening into a separate pen to be fed, and that grows twice as fat as the rest, must look like a genius. And it must seem an astonishing coincidence of genius with a whole run of extraordinary chances that this particular ram—the one that, instead of going into the general fold every evening, goes into a special pen full of oats—that this very ram, now bursting with fat, ends up slaughtered for meat.

But all the rams would have to do is stop assuming that everything that happens to them happens purely for the sake of their sheepish goals; they'd only have to admit that whatever happens to them might also have purposes beyond their understanding, and right away they'd see a unity, a coherence, in everything that happened to that fattened ram. Even without knowing what purpose they were being fattened for, they would at least know that nothing that happened to the ram happened by accident, and they would no longer need the ideas of chance or genius.

We have to give up our claim to make out some purpose we can immediately grasp, and admit that the ultimate purpose lies beyond our understanding. Only then can we see the sequence running through the experiences of historical figures, and grasp the cause behind the effects they produce—effects out of all proportion to ordinary human capacities. And once we do that, the words "chance" and "genius" become unnecessary.

We need only admit that we don't know the purpose behind the European convulsions. All we know are the facts: the murders, first in France, then in Italy, in Africa, in Prussia, in Austria, in Spain, and in Russia. And we need only admit that the movements from west to east and from east to west form the essence and the point of these events. Once we admit that, we won't just have no need to see extraordinary ability and genius in Napoleon and Alexander—we'll be unable to see them as anything but men like other men. And we won't need to reach for chance to explain the small events that made these men what they were, but it will be plain that every one of those small events was inevitable.

By giving up any claim to know the ultimate purpose, we'll see clearly that no one could imagine a blossom or a seed better suited to any given plant than the ones it produces. In just the same way, it's impossible to imagine any two people more perfectly fitted, down to the smallest detail, for the purpose they had to fulfill, than Napoleon and Alexander, with all their antecedents.

The fundamental, essential meaning of the European events of the early nineteenth century lies in the movement of the mass of European peoples from west to east, and afterward from east to west. The movement from west to east came first. For the peoples of the west to be able to make their warlike march to Moscow, three things had to happen: (1) they had to form themselves into a military group of a size large enough to withstand a collision with the warlike military group of the east; (2) they had to throw off all established traditions and customs; and (3) during their military march they had to have at their head a man who could justify to himself, and to them, the deceptions, the robberies, and the murders that this march would require.

And starting with the French Revolution, the old, inadequately sized group was broken apart, along with the old habits and traditions, and step by step a new group was formed, larger in scale, with new customs and new traditions, and a man was produced who would stand at the head of the coming movement and carry the responsibility for everything it would take.

A man emerges—by what look like the strangest chances—from all the seething French factions. He has no convictions, no habits, no traditions, not even a name; he is not even a Frenchman. Without attaching himself to any one of the factions, he is carried forward into a position of prominence.

The ignorance of his colleagues, the weakness and insignificance of his opponents, the bluntness of his lies, and this man's dazzling, self-assured limitations raise him to the head of the army. The brilliant qualities of the soldiers sent to Italy, his opponents' reluctance to fight, and his childish daring and self-confidence win him military fame. Countless so-called chances follow him wherever he goes. Falling out of favor with the rulers of France turns to his advantage. His attempts to escape his predestined path fail: he is refused a place in the Russian service, and the post he seeks in Turkey comes to nothing. During the war in Italy he comes to the brink of destruction several times, and each time is saved in some unexpected way. And thanks to various diplomatic considerations, the Russian armies—the very ones that might have destroyed his prestige—never turn up on the scene until he is already gone.

When he comes back from Italy he finds the government in Paris in the middle of falling apart—a process in which everyone attached to it is inevitably swept away and destroyed. And by chance, a way out of this dangerous position presents itself, in the form of a pointless, senseless expedition to Africa. Once again so-called chance goes with him. Impregnable Malta surrenders without a shot. His most reckless schemes are crowned with success. The enemy fleet, which afterward would not let a single boat slip past, lets his entire army through. In Africa a whole series of outrages are committed against a nearly unarmed population. And the men who commit these crimes, above all their leader, convince themselves that this is admirable, that this is glory—it resembles Caesar, it resembles Alexander the Great, and so it must be good.

This ideal of glory and grandeur consists not merely in seeing nothing wrong in whatever one does, but in taking pride in every crime one commits, treating it as if it carried some incomprehensible supernatural meaning. It was this ideal, destined to guide this man and everyone around him, that found room to develop in Africa. Whatever he attempts succeeds. The plague does not touch him. The cruelty of murdering prisoners is never held against him as a fault. His childish, reckless, needless, and shameful departure from Africa, abandoning his comrades in the middle of their troubles, is chalked up to his credit, and once again the enemy fleet twice lets him slip past. And when, drunk on the crimes he has carried off so successfully, he reaches Paris, the collapse of the republican government—which a year earlier might have finished him—has now gone as far as it can go, and his arrival there, a newcomer with no ties to any faction, can only lift him higher. And though he himself has no plan, he is quite ready to step into his new role.
He had no plan, he was afraid of everything, but the factions snatched at him and demanded that he take part.

He alone—with his ideal of glory and grandeur, worked out in Italy and Egypt, his insane self-worship, his boldness in crime, his bluntness in lying—he alone was capable of justifying what had to be done.
