She talked only because she had a physical need to exercise her tongue and lungs. She cried the way a child cries, because her nose needed clearing, and so on. What is a goal, for people in full vigor, was for her plainly nothing but a pretext.
So, in the mornings—especially if she had eaten something rich the day before—she would feel a need to be angry, and would seize on the handiest pretext: Belova's deafness.
She would begin saying something to her, in a low voice, from the far end of the room.
And when Belova answered, "Oh yes, they've come," she would mutter angrily: "Good Lord! How stupid and deaf she is!"

Another pretext would be her snuff, which would seem too dry, or too damp, or not ground fine enough. After these fits of irritation her face would turn yellow, and her maids knew, by unfailing signs, exactly when Belova would be deaf again, the snuff damp again, and the countess's face yellow again. Just as she needed to work off her ill temper, so too she sometimes needed to exercise her still-surviving faculty of thought—and the pretext for that was a game of patience. When she needed to cry, the late count would serve as pretext. When she wanted to be agitated, Nicholas and his health would be the pretext, and when she felt the need to speak spitefully, Countess Mary would serve. When her vocal organs needed exercise, usually around seven o'clock, once she had rested after dinner in a darkened room, the pretext would be retelling the same old stories over and over to the same listeners.

The old lady's condition was understood by the whole household, though no one ever spoke of it aloud, and everyone made every possible effort to see to her needs. Only in a rare glance, exchanged with a sad smile between Nicholas, Pierre, Natasha, and Countess Mary, was their shared understanding of her condition ever expressed.

But those glances said something more besides: they said that she had already played her part in life, that what they now saw before them was not the whole of her, that all of them must one day become like her, and that they were glad to give way to her, to hold themselves back for the sake of this once-precious person, once as full of life as they themselves now were, but now so much to be pitied. "Memento mori," said those glances.
Only the truly heartless, the stupid ones in that household, and the very young children failed to understand this, and steered clear of her.

When Pierre and his wife came into the drawing room, the countess was in one of her usual moods, the kind that needed the mental effort of a game of patience, and so—though out of sheer habit she greeted him with the words she always used whenever Pierre or her son came back after an absence: "High time, my dear, high time! We were all tired of waiting for you. Well, thank God!" and received her presents with another of her customary remarks: "It's not the gift that matters, my dear, but that you gave it to me, an old woman..."—still, it was plain she was not really pleased at Pierre's arrival just then, since it drew her attention away from the unfinished game.

She finished her game of patience before she even examined the presents. They consisted of a card box of splendid workmanship, a bright-blue Sèvres teacup painted with shepherdesses and fitted with a lid, and a gold snuffbox with the count's portrait on the lid, which Pierre had commissioned from a miniaturist in Petersburg. The countess had long wanted a box of just that kind, but, not wanting to cry just then, she glanced indifferently at the portrait and gave her chief attention to the card box.

"Thank you, my dear, you've cheered me up," she said, as she always did. "But best of all, you've brought yourself back—I never saw anything like it, you really ought to give your wife a scolding! What are we to do with her? She's like a madwoman when you're away. Doesn't see anything, doesn't remember anything," she went on, repeating her usual phrases. "Look, Anna Timofeyevna," she added, turning to her companion, "see what a card box my son has brought us!"
Belova admired the presents and was delighted with her dress material.

Though Pierre, Natasha, Nicholas, Countess Mary, and Denisov had a great deal to talk over that they could not discuss in front of the old countess—not that anything was hidden from her, but because she had fallen so far behind in so many things that if they had started talking in her presence, they would have had to answer questions that made no sense anymore, and repeat things they had already told her many times over: that so-and-so was dead, that so-and-so had married, all of which she would once again be unable to remember—still, out of habit, they all sat down to tea around the samovar in the drawing room, and Pierre answered the countess's questions about whether Prince Vasili had aged, and whether Countess Mary Alexeyevna sent her greetings and still thought of them, and other matters that interested no one, including the countess herself.

This kind of conversation, interesting to no one and yet unavoidable, went on all through teatime. All the grown members of the family had gathered around the round tea table, where Sonya presided over the samovar. The children, with their tutors and governesses, had already had their tea, and their voices could be heard from the next room. At tea, everyone sat in their accustomed places: Nicholas by the stove, at a small table where his tea was brought to him; Milka, the old gray borzoi bitch, daughter of the first Milka, her face now quite gray and her large black eyes seeming more prominent than ever, lay in the armchair beside him; Denisov, his curly hair, mustache, and whiskers now half gray, sat beside Countess Mary, his general's tunic unbuttoned; Pierre sat between his wife and the old countess. He talked about the things he knew would interest the old lady and that she could follow. He told her of goings-on in society, and about the people who had once made up the circle of her contemporaries, a real, living, distinct group, but who were now for the most part scattered about the world, and, like herself, were gathering in the last ears of the harvests they had sown in earlier years. But to the old countess, those contemporaries of hers still seemed the only serious, real society there was. Natasha could tell, from how animated Pierre was, that his visit had been eventful and that he had a great deal to tell them, but did not dare say it in front of the old countess. Denisov, not being a member of the family, did not grasp Pierre's caution, and, being a malcontent deeply interested in what was going on in Petersburg, kept pressing Pierre to tell them what was happening in the Semyonovsky regiment, then about Arakcheev, then about the Bible Society. Once or twice Pierre got carried away and began speaking of these things, but Nicholas and Natasha always steered him back to the health of Prince Ivan and Countess Mary Alexeyevna.
"Well, and all this idiocy—Gossner and Tatáwinova? Is that weally still going on?" Denisov asked.
"Going on?" Pierre exclaimed. "Why, more than ever! The Bible Society is running the whole government now!"

"What's that, mon cher ami?" asked the countess, who had finished her tea and plainly needed a pretext for being angry now that her meal was done. "What's this about the government? I don't understand."

"Well, you know, Maman," Nicholas put in, knowing just how to translate things into his mother's language, "Prince Alexander Golitsyn has founded a society, and as a result he has great influence, they say."
"Arakcheev and Golitsyn," Pierre put in, without thinking, "are the whole government now! And what a government! They see treason everywhere and are afraid of everything."

"Well, and how is Prince Alexander to blame? He's a most estimable man. I used to meet him at Mary Antonovna's," the countess said, in an offended tone; and, still more offended that everyone had fallen silent, she went on: "These days everyone finds fault with everything. A Gospel Society! Well, and what's the harm in that?" and she rose—everyone else got up too—and, with a stern expression, sailed back to her table in the sitting room.
The melancholy silence that followed was broken by the sound of the children's voices and laughter from the next room. Some jolly commotion was plainly going on there.
"Finished, finished!" little Natasha's gleeful shriek rose above the rest.
Pierre exchanged glances with Countess Mary and Nicholas—he never once lost sight of Natasha—and smiled happily.

"Oh, I'll go and see," said Pierre, jumping up. "You know," he added, stopping at the door, "why I'm especially fond of that music? It's always the first thing that tells me all is well. When I was driving here today, the closer I got to the house, the more anxious I grew. As soon as I stepped into the anteroom, I heard Andrusha's peals of laughter, and I knew right then that everything was fine."
"I know! I know that feeling," said Nicholas. "But I mustn't go in there—those stockings are supposed to be a surprise for me."
Pierre went off to the children, and the shouting and laughter grew louder still.

"Come, Anna Makarovna," Pierre's voice could be heard saying, "come here, into the middle of the room, and at the word of command, 'One, two'—and when I say 'three'... You stand here, and you in my arms—now then! One, two!..." said Pierre, and a silence fell: "three!"—and a rapturous, breathless shout of children's voices filled the room. "Two, two!" they shouted.

This meant two stockings, which, by some secret method known only to herself, Anna Makarovna would knit at the same time on the same needles, and which, once they were finished, she would always draw out triumphantly, one from inside the other, right in front of the children.

Soon after this the children came in to say good night. They kissed everyone, the tutors and governesses made their bows, and they went out. Only young Nicholas and his tutor stayed behind. Dessalles whispered to the boy to come downstairs.
"No, Monsieur Dessalles, I'll ask my aunt to let me stay," answered Nicholas Bolkonski, also in a whisper.
"Ma tante, please let me stay," he said, going up to his aunt.
His face was full of entreaty, agitation, and ecstasy. Countess Mary glanced at him and turned to Pierre.
"When you're here, he can't tear himself away," she said.

"I'll bring him to you directly, Monsieur Dessalles. Good night!" said Pierre, offering his hand to the Swiss tutor, and then he turned to young Nicholas with a smile. "You and I haven't seen anything of one another yet.... How like he is growing, Mary!" he added, turning to Countess Mary.
"Like my father?" the boy asked, flushing crimson, looking up at Pierre with bright, rapturous eyes.

Pierre nodded, and went on with what he had been saying before the children interrupted. Countess Mary sat down to her woolwork; Natasha never took her eyes off her husband. Nicholas and Denisov got up, asked for their pipes, smoked, went to fetch more tea from Sonya, who sat weary but resolute at the samovar, and put questions to Pierre. The curly-headed, delicate boy sat unnoticed in a corner, his eyes shining, starting every now and then and muttering something under his breath, clearly caught up in some new and powerful feeling as he kept turning his curly head, with its thin neck bared by his turned-down collar, toward the place where Pierre sat.

The conversation turned to the current gossip about those in power—the subject most people find of greatest interest in domestic politics. Denisov, dissatisfied with the government on account of his own disappointments in the service, listened with pleasure to the things being done in Petersburg, things that struck him as foolish, and made sharp, forceful remarks on everything Pierre told them.

"One used to have to be German—now one has to dance with Tatáwinova and Madame Kwüdener, and wead Ecka'tshausen and the bwethwen. Oh, they should let that fine fellow Bonaparte loose—he'd knock all this nonsense out of them! Fancy giving command of the Semenov wegiment to a fellow like that Schwa'tz!" he cried.

Nicholas, though he lacked Denisov's readiness to find fault with everything, also thought that discussing the government was a very serious, weighty matter, and it seemed to him a matter of real importance that A had been appointed Minister of This, and B Governor General of That, and that the Emperor had said such and such, and this minister had said such and such. And so he thought it necessary to take an interest in these things, and questioned Pierre. The questions the two of them put kept the conversation from straying beyond its ordinary character—gossip about the upper reaches of government.

But Natasha, who knew all her husband's ways and ideas, could see that he had long been wanting, without managing it, to steer the conversation onto another track and give voice to the idea he felt so deeply, the very idea for whose sake he had gone to Petersburg to consult with his new friend Prince Theodore, and she came to his aid by asking how things had gone with Prince Theodore.

"Always the same thing," said Pierre, glancing around at his listeners. "Everyone can see things have gotten so bad that they can't go on this way any longer, and that it's the duty of every decent man to work against it as far as he can."
"What can decent men do?" Nicholas asked, frowning slightly. "What is there to be done?"
"Well, this..."

Natasha, who had long expected to be sent for to nurse her baby, now heard the nurse calling her and went off to the nursery. Countess Mary followed her. The men went into the study, and little Nicholas Bolkonski, unnoticed by his uncle, followed them in and sat down at the writing table, in a shadowy corner by the window.
"Always some fantastic scheme or other," said Nicholas.

"Why this," Pierre began, not sitting down but pacing the room, sometimes stopping short, gesturing, and lisping: "the situation in Petersburg is this. The Emperor pays no attention to anything anymore. He's given himself over entirely to this mysticism"—Pierre could no longer stand mysticism in anyone—"he only wants peace, and only these people, sans foi ni loi—without faith or law—can give it to him—people who go around recklessly hacking and strangling everything: Magnitsky, Arakcheev, and tutti quanti—and all the rest.... You'll agree that if you didn't oversee your own estates yourself, and only wanted a quiet life, the harsher your steward was, the more easily your object would be achieved," he said to Nicholas.
"Well, and where does that lead?" said Nicholas.

"Well, everything is going to ruin! Robbery in the law courts, nothing in the army but flogging, drilling, and Military Settlements; the people are being tormented, enlightenment is being crushed. Everything young and honest is being ground down! Everyone can see this can't go on. Everything is stretched so tight that it's bound to snap," said Pierre—much as everyone who has ever examined the actions of any government has said, since governments began. "I told them just one thing, in Petersburg."

"Well, you know whom," said Pierre, with a meaningful glance from under his brows. "Prince Theodore and the rest of them. Encouraging culture and philanthropy is all very well, of course. The aim is excellent—but under the present circumstances, something else is needed."
At that moment Nicholas noticed his nephew was in the room. His face darkened, and he went up to the boy.
"Why are you in here?"

"Why? Let him be," said Pierre, taking Nicholas by the arm and going on. "That's not enough, I told them. Something else is needed. When you're standing there expecting the overstretched string to snap at any moment, when everyone is expecting the inevitable catastrophe, then as many people as possible need to join hands, as tightly as they can, to stand against the general calamity. Everything young and strong is being lured away and corrupted. One man is drawn off by women, another by honors, a third by ambition or money, and off they go, over to that camp. There are no independent men left—men like you or me. What I'm saying is: widen the scope of our society, let the watchword be not virtue alone, but independence and action as well!"
Nicholas, who had left his nephew, irritably pulled up an armchair, sat down in it, and listened to Pierre, coughing with displeasure and frowning more and more.
"But action toward what end?" he burst out. "And what position would you take toward the government?"

"Why, the position of helpers. The society needn't be secret at all, if the government allows it. It's not just not hostile to the government—it's a society of true conservatives, a society of gentlemen in the fullest sense of the word. Its whole purpose is to stop some Pugachev or other from murdering my children and yours, and to stop Arakcheev from sending me off to some Military Settlement. We join hands only for the public good and the general safety."
"Yes, but it's a secret society, and so a hostile one, a harmful one, one that can only do harm."

"Why? Did the Tugendbund, which saved Europe" (they did not yet dare suggest that it was Russia that had saved Europe) "do any harm? The Tugendbund is an alliance of virtue: it's love, mutual aid... it's what Christ preached on the Cross."

Natasha, who had come in during the conversation, looked happily at her husband. It was not what he was saying that pleased her—that did not even interest her, since to her it all seemed extremely simple, and she felt she had known it for a long time, because she knew it sprang from Pierre's whole soul—but it was his animated, enthusiastic look that made her glad.

The boy with the thin neck rising from his turned-down collar—whom everyone had forgotten about—watched Pierre with even greater and more rapturous delight. Every word Pierre spoke burned itself into his heart, and, with a nervous movement of his fingers, he found himself unconsciously breaking the sealing wax and the quill pens that came to hand on his uncle's table.
"It isn't at all what you think; but that's what the German Tugendbund was, and it's what I'm proposing."

"No, my fwiend! The Tugendbund's all vewy well for sausage eaters, but I don't understand it and can't even pwonounce it," Denisov broke in, loudly and firmly. "I agwee that evewything here is wotten and howwible, but the Tugendbund I don't understand. If we're not satisfied, let's have a wevolt of our own. That's all wight. Je suis vot'e homme—I'm your man!"

Pierre smiled, Natasha burst out laughing, but Nicholas only knitted his brows further, and set about proving to Pierre that there was no real prospect of any great change, and that all the danger Pierre spoke of existed only in his own imagination. Pierre argued the opposite, and, since his mental powers were greater and more resourceful, Nicholas found himself cornered. This only made him angrier still, since he was fully convinced—not by reasoning, but by something inside him stronger than reason—of the rightness of his own view.

"I'll tell you this," he said, standing up and trying, with nervously twitching fingers, to prop his pipe up in a corner, then finally giving up the attempt. "I can't prove it to you. You say everything here is rotten, and that an overthrow is coming: I don't see it. But you also say our oath of allegiance is a conditional matter, and to that I reply: 'You are my best friend, as you well know, but if you formed a secret society and started working against the government—whatever government it may be—I know it's my duty to obey the government. And if Arakcheev ordered me to lead a squadron against you and cut you down, I wouldn't hesitate an instant, and I'd do it.' Argue about that all you like!"

An awkward silence followed these words. Natasha was the first to speak, defending her husband and attacking her brother. Her defense was weak and clumsy, but it did what she wanted. The conversation started up again, no longer in the unpleasantly hostile tone of Nicholas's last words.
When they all got up to go in to supper, little Nicholas Bolkonski went up to Pierre, pale, his eyes shining and radiant.

And Pierre suddenly grasped what a special, independent, complicated, and powerful process of thought and feeling must have been going on in this boy throughout the whole conversation, and, remembering everything he had said, he wished the lad had not heard him. Still, he had to give him some answer.
"Yes, I think so," he said, reluctantly, and left the study.
The boy looked down and seemed only now to notice what he had done to the things on the table. He flushed and went up to Nicholas.
"Uncle, forgive me, I did that... without meaning to," he said, pointing to the broken sealing wax and pens.
"All right, all right," he said, throwing the bits under the table.
And, plainly holding back his irritation with some effort, he turned away from the boy.
"You shouldn't have been in here at all," he said.

The talk at supper was not about politics or secret societies, but turned to the subject Nicholas liked best of all—memories of 1812. Denisov set it going, and Pierre was particularly agreeable and amusing on the subject. The family parted for the night on the friendliest terms.

After supper Nicholas, having undressed in his study and given his instructions to the steward, who had been waiting for him, went to the bedroom in his dressing gown, where he found his wife still at her table, writing.
Countess Mary blushed. She was afraid that what she was writing would not be understood or approved of by her husband.
She had wanted to keep what she was writing hidden from him, but at the same time she was glad he had caught her at it, glad that she would now have to tell him.
"A diary, Nicholas," she answered, handing him a blue exercise book filled with her firm, bold handwriting.
"A diary?" Nicholas repeated, with a touch of irony, and picked up the book.
It was written in French.

December 4. Today when Andrusha (her eldest boy) woke up, he did not want to dress, and Mademoiselle Louise sent for me. He was naughty and stubborn. I tried threats, but that only made him angrier. So I took the matter in hand: I left him alone and, with nurse's help, began getting the other children up, telling him I did not love him. For a long time he was silent, as if astonished, then he jumped out of bed, ran to me in his shirt, and sobbed so hard that I could not calm him for a long time. It was plain that what troubled him most was that he had grieved me. Later, in the evening, when I gave him his ticket, he again began to cry piteously and kiss me. One can get him to do anything through tenderness.
"What's a 'ticket'?" Nicholas asked.
"I've started giving the older ones marks every evening, showing how they've behaved."

Nicholas looked into the radiant eyes gazing up at him, and went on turning the pages and reading. In the diary, everything in the children's lives that had struck their mother as worth noting, whether as a sign of their character or as the basis for some general reflection on methods of upbringing, had been set down. Most of it was insignificant trifles, but they did not seem so either to the mother or, now, reading this diary about his own children for the first time, to the father.
Under the date "5" was entered:

Mitya was naughty at table. Papa said he was to have no pudding. He had none, but he looked so unhappily and greedily at the others while they were eating! I think that punishing children by depriving them of sweets only makes them greedier. Must tell Nicholas this.

Nicholas set the book down and looked at his wife. The radiant eyes gazed back at him questioningly: would he approve of her diary, or disapprove? There could be no doubt of his approval—or of his admiration for his wife.

Perhaps it needn't be done quite so pedantically, Nicholas thought, or even be done at all, but this tireless, unceasing spiritual effort, whose only aim was the children's moral welfare, delighted him. Had Nicholas been able to put his feelings into words, he would have found that his steady, tender, proud love for his wife rested on his sense of wonder at her spiritual depth, and at the lofty moral world, almost beyond his own reach, in which she had her being.

He was proud of her intelligence and her goodness, recognized his own insignificance beside her in that spiritual world, and rejoiced all the more that a soul like hers not only belonged to him, but was part of himself.

"I quite, quite approve, my dearest!" he said, with a meaningful look, and, after a short pause, added: "And I behaved badly today. You weren't in the study. We got into an argument—Pierre and I—and I lost my temper. But he's impossible: such a child! I don't know what would become of him if Natasha didn't keep him in hand.... Do you have any idea why he went to Petersburg? They've formed..."

"Well then, you know," Nicholas went on, growing hot all over again just remembering their discussion, "he wanted to convince me it's every honest man's duty to go against the government, and that the oath of allegiance and one's duty... I'm sorry you weren't there. They all fell on me—Denisov and Natasha... Natasha is absurd. The way she rules over him! And yet the moment there's an actual argument, she has no words of her own, only repeats his," added Nicholas, giving in to that irresistible urge that tempts us to sit in judgment over the people closest and dearest to us. He forgot that what he was saying about Natasha could be applied, word for word, to himself, in relation to his own wife.
"When I told him that duty and the oath stand above everything, he set about proving I don't know what! A pity you weren't there—what would you have said?"

"As I see it, you were quite right, and I told Natasha so. Pierre says everyone is suffering, being tormented and corrupted, and that it's our duty to help our neighbor. Of course he's right about that," said Countess Mary, "but he forgets that we have other duties closer to home, duties God Himself has laid on us, and that though we might risk ourselves, we mustn't risk our children."

"Yes, that's it exactly! That's just what I told him," put in Nicholas, who fancied he really had said it. "But they kept insisting on their own view—love of one's neighbor and Christianity—and all this in front of young Nicholas, who had come into my study and broken every single thing there."

"Ah, Nicholas, do you know, I'm often troubled about little Nicholas," said Countess Mary. "He's such an unusual boy. I'm afraid I neglect him for the sake of my own children: we all have children, relations, while he has no one at all. He's always alone with his own thoughts."

"Well, I don't think you have anything to reproach yourself for on his account. Everything the fondest mother could do for her son, you have done and are doing for him, and of course I'm glad of it. He's a fine boy, a fine boy! This evening he listened to Pierre as if in a trance, and just imagine—as we were going in to supper, I looked, and he'd broken everything on my table to bits, and he told me about it himself, right away! I've never known him to tell a lie. A fine boy, a fine boy!" Nicholas repeated, though at heart he was not particularly fond of Nicholas Bolkonski, but was always eager to acknowledge that he was a fine boy.

"Still, I'm not the same as his own mother would be," said Countess Mary. "I feel that I'm not, and it troubles me. A wonderful boy, but I'm dreadfully afraid for him. It would do him good to have some companions."

"Well, it won't be for long. Next summer I'll take him to Petersburg," said Nicholas. "Yes, Pierre always was a dreamer, and always will be," he went on, returning to the talk in the study, which had plainly unsettled him. "Well, what business is it of mine what goes on there—whether Arakcheev is bad, or any of that? What business was it of mine when I got married and was so deep in debt I was threatened with prison, and had a mother who couldn't see or understand any of it? And then there's you, and the children, and our own affairs. Do you think it's for my own pleasure that I'm out at the farm, or in the office, from morning till night? No, but I know I have to work, to comfort my mother, to repay you, and not to leave the children beggars the way I was."

Countess Mary wanted to tell him that man does not live by bread alone, and that he attached too much importance to these matters. But she knew she must not say this, and that it would be no use saying it. She only took his hand and kissed it. He took this as a sign of approval, a confirmation of his own thinking, and after a few minutes' reflection went on thinking aloud.
"You know, Mary, today Elias Mitrofanych"—this was his steward—"came back from the Tambov estate and told me they're already offering eighty thousand rubles for the forest."
And, his face eager, Nicholas began talking about the possibility of buying back Otradnoe before long, and added: "Another ten years of life, and I'll leave the children... in an excellent position."

Countess Mary listened to her husband and took in everything he told her. She knew that when he thought aloud like this, he would sometimes ask her what he had just been saying, and be annoyed if he noticed she had been thinking about something else. But she had to force herself to pay attention, because what he was saying did not interest her in the least. She looked at him, and instead of thinking, she felt something different. She felt a submissive, tender love for this man, who would never understand everything she understood, and this seemed to make her love for him even stronger, adding to it a touch of passionate tenderness. Besides this feeling, which absorbed her wholly and kept her from following the details of her husband's plans, thoughts unconnected with anything he was saying drifted through her mind. She thought of her nephew. Her husband's account of how agitated the boy had been while Pierre was speaking struck her forcibly, and various traits of his gentle, sensitive character came back to her; and thinking of her nephew, she found herself thinking of her own children too. She did not compare them with him, but compared her feeling for them with her feeling for him, and felt, with some regret, that something was lacking in her feeling for young Nicholas.

Sometimes it seemed to her that this difference came simply from the difference in their ages, but she felt herself at fault toward him, and promised herself, in her heart, to do better, to achieve the impossible—to love, in this life, her husband, her children, little Nicholas, and all her neighbors, as Christ loved mankind. Countess Mary's soul always strove toward the infinite, the eternal, the absolute, and so could never be at peace. A stern expression, marking the lofty, secret suffering of a soul weighed down by the body, showed on her face. Nicholas looked at her. "O God! What will become of us if she dies, as I always fear when her face looks like that?" he thought, and, placing himself before the icon, he began to say his evening prayers.

Natasha and Pierre, alone together, began to talk the way only a husband and wife can: with remarkable clarity and speed, each understanding and finishing the other's thoughts in ways that violated every rule of logic — no premises, no chain of reasoning, no conclusions, and in a quite peculiar way. Natasha was so used to talking this way with her husband that for her the surest sign something was wrong between them was if Pierre started reasoning logically. When he began proving a point, arguing something out calmly, and she, following his lead, did the same, she knew they were on the edge of a quarrel.

From the moment they were alone, and Natasha came to him with her eyes wide open and happy, quickly grabbing his head and pressing it to her chest, saying, "Now you're all mine, mine! You won't get away!" — from that moment this conversation began, defying every law of logic, and defying it precisely because entirely different subjects were being discussed at the very same time. This simultaneous discussion of many topics didn't get in the way of clear understanding — on the contrary, it was the surest sign that they understood each other completely.

Just as in a dream everything is uncertain, unreasoning, and contradictory except for the feeling that steers the dream, so in this exchange — which broke every law of reason — the words themselves were not consecutive or clear, only the feeling behind them was.

Natasha talked to Pierre about her brother's life and doings, about how she'd suffered and lacked life during his absence, about how she'd grown fonder than ever of Mary, and how Mary was better than her in every way. In saying this Natasha was sincere in acknowledging Mary's superiority, but at the same time, by saying it, she was making a demand on Pierre: that he should still, after all, prefer her to Mary and to every other woman, and that now, especially after seeing so many women in Petersburg, he should say so again.
Pierre, responding to Natasha's words, told her how unbearable he'd found it to meet ladies at dinners and balls in Petersburg.
"I've completely lost the knack of talking to ladies," he said. "It was simply dull. Besides, I was very busy."
Natasha looked at him intently and went on.
"Mary is wonderful," she said. "The way she understands children! It's as if she sees straight into their souls. Yesterday, for instance, Mitya was being naughty..."
"How like his father," Pierre put in.

Natasha knew exactly why he'd brought up Mitya's resemblance to Nicholas: the memory of his argument with his brother-in-law was unpleasant to him, and he wanted to know what Natasha thought about it.
"Nicholas has this weakness — he can never agree with anything that isn't generally accepted. But I understand you value what breaks new ground," she said, repeating words Pierre had once used.

"No, the main thing is that for Nicholas, ideas and arguments are a kind of amusement — almost a pastime," said Pierre. "For instance, he's building a library, and he's made it a rule never to buy a new book until he's read what he'd already bought — Sismondi and Rousseau and Montesquieu," he added with a smile. "You know how much I..." he began to soften what he'd said, but Natasha cut him off to show it wasn't necessary.
"So you're saying ideas are just an amusement to him..."
"Yes, and for me nothing else is serious. The whole time I was in Petersburg I saw everyone as if in a dream. When I'm gripped by a thought, everything else is mere amusement."
"Oh, I'm so sorry I wasn't there when you met the children," said Natasha. "Which one was most excited? Lisa, I'm sure."

"Yes," Pierre replied, and went on with what was on his mind. "Nicholas says we ought not to think. But I can't help it. Besides, when I was in Petersburg I felt — I can say this to you — that the whole undertaking would fall apart without me, that everyone was pulling in his own direction. But I managed to bring them all together, and my idea is so clear and so simple. You see, I'm not saying we should oppose this or that. We could be wrong. What I say is: 'Join hands, all of you who love what is right, and let there be a single banner — that of active virtue.' Prince Sergey is a fine man, and clever."

Natasha would have had no doubt at all about the greatness of Pierre's idea, except that one thing unsettled her. "Can a man so important, so necessary to society, also be my husband? How did that happen?" She wanted to put this doubt to him. "Now who could really say whether he was cleverer than everyone else?" she asked herself, and ran through everyone Pierre most respected. Judging by what he'd said, there was no one he respected as highly as Platon Karataev.
"Do you know what I'm thinking about?" she asked. "About Platon Karataev. Would he approve of you now, do you think?"
Pierre wasn't at all surprised by the question. He understood the way his wife's mind worked.
"Platon Karataev?" he repeated, and thought about it, evidently sincerely trying to imagine what Karataev's opinion would be. "He wouldn't have understood... and yet maybe he would."
"I love you awfully!" Natasha suddenly said. "Awfully, awfully!"

"No, he wouldn't have approved," Pierre said after reflection. "What he would have approved of is our family life. He was always so eager to find seemliness, happiness, and peace in everything, and I would have been proud to have him see us. You know, you talk about my being away, but you wouldn't believe what a special feeling I have for you after a separation..."
"Yes, I imagine..." Natasha began.
"No, it's not that. I never stop loving you. And one couldn't love more — but this is something special... Yes, of course—" he didn't finish, because their eyes meeting said the rest.

"What nonsense it is," Natasha suddenly burst out, "all that talk about honeymoons, and how the greatest happiness comes at the very beginning! It's the opposite — now is the best of all. If only you didn't have to go away! Do you remember how we used to quarrel? And it was always my fault. Always mine. And what did we even quarrel about — I don't even remember!"
"Always about the same thing," said Pierre with a smile. "Jealo—"
"Don't say it! I can't bear it!" Natasha cried, and her eyes glittered coldly and vindictively. "Did you see her?" she added after a pause.
"No, and if I had, I wouldn't have recognized her."

"Oh, do you know? While you were talking in the study I was watching you," Natasha began, clearly wanting to clear away the cloud that had settled over them. "You're as alike as two peas — like the boy." (She meant her little son.) "Oh, it's time to go to him... the milk's come... but I hate to leave you."

They were both silent for a few seconds. Then suddenly, at the same moment, they both started to speak. Pierre began with self-satisfaction and enthusiasm, Natasha with a quiet, happy smile. Having interrupted each other, they both stopped to let the other go on.
"No. What were you saying? Go on, go on."
"No, you go on, I was just talking nonsense," said Natasha.

Pierre finished what he'd started to say. It was the continuation of his self-satisfied reflections on his success in Petersburg. At that moment it seemed to him that he'd been chosen to give a new direction to the whole of Russian society, and to the whole world.

"I only wanted to say that ideas with great consequences are always simple ones. My whole idea is this: if wicked people band together and become a power, then honest people must do the same. It's really as simple as that."
"Me? Just nonsense."
"But still?"

"Oh, it's nothing, just a trifle," said Natasha, smiling more brightly still. "I only wanted to tell you about Petya: today nurse came to take him from me, and he laughed, shut his eyes, and clung to me. I'm sure he thought he was hiding. Awfully sweet! There, now he's crying. Well, goodbye!" — and she left the room.

Meanwhile downstairs, in little Nicholas Bolkonski's bedroom, a small lamp burned as it always did. (The boy was afraid of the dark, and they hadn't been able to cure him of it.) Dessalles slept propped up on four pillows, his Roman nose giving off a steady, rhythmic snore. Little Nicholas, who had just woken up in a cold sweat, sat up in bed and stared ahead with wide-open eyes. He'd woken from a terrible dream. He'd dreamed that he and Uncle Pierre, wearing helmets like the ones pictured in his Plutarch, were leading a huge army. The army was made up of white slanting lines that filled the air like the strands of cobweb that drift about in autumn — the ones Dessalles called les fils de la Vierge, the Virgin's threads. Out in front was Glory, which looked like those threads, only thicker. He and Pierre were being carried forward, light and joyful, closer and closer to their goal. Then suddenly the threads carrying them began to go slack and tangle, and it grew hard to move. And Uncle Nicholas stood before them, stern and threatening.

"Did you do this?" he said, pointing to some broken sealing wax and pens. "I loved you, but I have orders from Arakcheev, and I will kill the first one of you who moves forward." Little Nicholas turned to look at Pierre, but Pierre was no longer there. In his place stood his father — Prince Andrew — and his father had neither shape nor form, and yet he existed, and when little Nicholas made him out he went faint with love: he felt himself powerless, limp, formless. His father caressed him and pitied him. But Uncle Nicholas kept coming nearer and nearer to them. Terror seized young Nicholas, and he woke up.

"My father!" he thought. (Though there were two good portraits of Prince Andrew in the house, Nicholas never pictured him in human shape.) "My father was here with me, and he caressed me. He approved of me, and of Uncle Pierre. Whatever he tells me to do, I will do. The Roman Mucius Scaevola burned his hand. Why shouldn't something like that happen to me too? I know they want me to keep studying. And I will study. But someday I'll be finished, and then I'll do something. I only pray to God that something happens to me like what happened to Plutarch's men, and I'll act as they did. I'll do even better. Everyone will know me, love me, be delighted with me!" And suddenly his chest heaved with sobs and he began to cry.
"Are you ill?" he heard Dessalles' voice ask.

"He's good and kind, and I'm fond of him!" he thought of Dessalles. "But Uncle Pierre! Oh, what an extraordinary man he is! And my father? Oh, Father, Father! Yes, I will do something that even he would be satisfied with..."
History is the life of nations and of humanity. To grasp it and put it into words — to describe directly the life of humanity, or even of a single nation — seems impossible.

The ancient historians all used one and the same method to describe and capture what seems so elusive: the life of a people. They described the actions of the individuals who ruled the people, and treated the actions of those men as standing for the actions of the whole nation.

The question — how did individual men make nations act as they wished, and what in turn guided the will of those individuals themselves? — the ancients answered by pointing to a divinity that subjected nations to the will of a chosen man, and that guided that chosen man's will toward ends already fixed in advance.
For the ancients, these questions were settled by a belief in the direct participation of God in human affairs.

It might seem that having rejected the ancients' belief in mankind's subjection to God, and in a predetermined goal toward which nations are led, modern history ought to study not the outward signs of power but the causes that produce it. But modern history has not done this. Having rejected the ancients' view in theory, it still follows it in practice.

Instead of men endowed with divine authority and directed straight by the will of God, modern history has given us either heroes endowed with extraordinary, superhuman gifts, or simply men of every possible kind, from monarchs down to journalists, who lead the masses. Instead of the old divinely appointed goals of the Jewish, Greek, or Roman peoples, which ancient historians took to represent the progress of humanity, modern history has set up goals of its own — the welfare of the French, the Germans, or the English, or, in its most abstract form, the welfare and civilization of humanity in general, by which is usually meant the peoples occupying a small northwestern corner of one large continent.

Modern history has rejected the beliefs of the ancients without putting a new conception in their place, and the logic of the situation has forced historians, having apparently thrown out the divine authority of kings and the "fate" of the ancients, to arrive at the very same conclusion by a different road — that is, to accept (1) that nations are guided by individual men, and (2) that there exists a known goal toward which these nations, and humanity as a whole, are moving.

At the root of the work of every modern historian from Gibbon to Buckle, despite their apparent disagreements and the seeming novelty of their outlooks, lie those same two old, unavoidable assumptions.

In the first place, the historian describes the actions of the individuals who, in his view, have directed humanity (one historian counts only monarchs, generals, and ministers as such men, while another adds orators, scholars, reformers, philosophers, and poets). Secondly, it is assumed that the goal toward which humanity is being led is known to the historians: to one of them this goal is the greatness of the Roman, Spanish, or French state; to another it is liberty, equality, and a certain kind of civilization belonging to a small corner of the world called Europe.

In 1789 a ferment breaks out in Paris; it grows, spreads, and expresses itself as a movement of peoples from west to east. Several times it surges eastward and collides with a countermovement coming from the east. In 1812 it reaches its farthest point, Moscow, and then, with remarkable symmetry, a countermovement runs from east to west, drawing in, as the first movement had, the nations of central Europe. This countermovement reaches the starting point of the first movement, in the west — Paris — and subsides.

During that twenty-year span, an immense number of fields lay untilled, houses burned down, trade shifted direction, millions of people migrated, were reduced to poverty or grew rich, and millions of Christians, who professed a law of love for their fellow men, killed one another.

What does all this mean? Why did it happen? What made these people burn houses and kill their fellow men? What were the causes of these events? What force made people act this way? These are the plain, instinctive, and entirely legitimate questions that humanity asks itself whenever it comes across the monuments and traditions of that period.
For an answer to these questions, the common sense of mankind turns to the science of history, whose purpose is to let nations and humanity come to know themselves.

If history had kept the conception held by the ancients, it would say that God, to reward or punish his people, gave Napoleon power and directed his will toward fulfilling divine ends, and that answer would be clear and complete. One might believe or disbelieve in Napoleon's divine significance, but for anyone who did believe it, nothing in the history of that period would remain unintelligible, and there would be no contradictions.
But modern history cannot give that answer. Science does not accept the ancients' notion of the direct participation of God in human affairs, and so history has to come up with other answers.
Modern history, answering these questions, says: you want to know what this movement means, what caused it, what force produced these events? Then listen:

"Louis XIV was a very proud, self-assured man; he had this mistress and that, this minister and that, and he governed France badly. His descendants were weak men, and they too governed France badly. And they had their own favorites and their own mistresses. Meanwhile certain men were writing certain books. By the end of the eighteenth century there were a couple dozen men in Paris who started talking about how all men are free and equal. This set off a wave across France in which people slashed and drowned one another. They killed the king, and a great many other people besides. At that time France had a man of genius — Napoleon. He conquered everyone everywhere, meaning he killed a great many people, because he was a great genius. And for some reason he went off to kill Africans, and killed them so thoroughly, and was so clever and cunning, that when he came home to France he ordered everyone to obey him, and everyone obeyed him. Once he had made himself Emperor, he went out again to kill people in Italy, Austria, and Prussia. And there too he killed a great many. In Russia there was an Emperor, Alexander, who decided to restore order in Europe, and so he fought against Napoleon. In 1807 the two of them suddenly became friends, but in 1811 they quarreled again and once more began killing large numbers of people. Napoleon led six hundred thousand men into Russia and captured Moscow; then he suddenly fled Moscow, and the Emperor Alexander, guided by the advice of Stein and others, united Europe to arm itself against the man who had disturbed its peace. All of Napoleon's former allies suddenly turned into his enemies, and their armies advanced against the fresh forces he had raised. The Allies defeated Napoleon, entered Paris, forced him to abdicate, and sent him to the island of Elba — without stripping him of the title of Emperor, and treating him with every mark of respect — even though five years earlier, and again a year later, they all considered him an outlaw and a brigand. Then Louis XVIII, who up to that point had been a laughingstock to both the French and the Allies, began his reign. And Napoleon, weeping in front of his Old Guard, gave up the throne and went into exile. Then the skillful statesmen and diplomats — Talleyrand above all, who managed to sit down in a particular chair before anyone else, and by doing so extended the borders of France — talked things over in Vienna, and by these conversations made whole nations happy or unhappy. Suddenly the diplomats and monarchs nearly fell out and were on the point of once again ordering their armies to kill one another, but just then Napoleon landed in France with a single battalion, and the French, who had been hating him, immediately submitted to him again, every one of them. But this enraged the Allied monarchs, and they went to fight the French once more. And they defeated the genius Napoleon and, suddenly declaring him a brigand after all, sent him off to the island of St. Helena. And the exile, cut off from the beloved France so dear to his heart, died a slow death on that rock, and left his great deeds to posterity. But in Europe a reaction set in, and the sovereigns all went back to oppressing their subjects."

It would be a mistake to think this is meant ironically — a caricature of historical writing. On the contrary, it is a fairly mild version of the contradictory answers, none of which actually meet the questions asked, given by all the historians, from the compilers of memoirs and the histories of individual states to the writers of general histories and the newest histories of the culture of that period.
The strangeness and absurdity of these answers comes from the fact that modern history, like a deaf man, answers questions nobody asked.

If the purpose of history is to describe the movement of humanity and of peoples, the first question — without an answer to which everything else remains incomprehensible — is: what is the force that moves peoples? To this, modern history laboriously answers either that Napoleon was a great genius, or that Louis XIV was very proud, or that certain writers wrote certain books.

All of that may well be true, and mankind is ready to agree with it, but it is not what was asked. All of it would be interesting if we accepted a divine power, grounded in itself, consistently steering its nations through the likes of Napoleons, Louis-es, and writers; but we do not accept such a power, and therefore, before talking about Napoleons, Louis-es, and authors, we need to be shown the connection between these men and the movement of the nations.
If some other force has taken the place of divine power, it needs to be explained what this new force actually consists of, because the whole interest of history lies precisely there.

History seems to take it for granted that this force is self-evident and known to everyone. But however much one might wish to treat it as known, anyone who reads a good number of historical works cannot help wondering whether this new force — understood so differently by the historians themselves — is really well understood by anybody at all.
What force moves the nations?

Historians who write biographies, or histories of a single nation, understand this force as a power built into heroes and rulers. In their telling, events happen purely by the will of a Napoleon, an Alexander, or whichever figure they are writing about. The answers this kind of historian gives to the question of what force makes events happen are satisfying only so long as a single historian is covering a single event. As soon as historians of different nationalities and different leanings start describing the same event, their answers immediately lose all meaning, because this force is understood by each of them not just differently, but often in quite contradictory ways. One historian says an event was produced by Napoleon's power, another that it was produced by Alexander's, a third that it came from the power of some other person. What's more, historians of this kind contradict one another even on the question of what a given person's authority was based on. The historian Thiers, a Bonapartist, says Napoleon's power rested on his virtue and his genius. The historian Lanfrey, a Republican, says it rested on his trickery and his deception of the people. So historians of this class, by tearing down each other's positions, tear down any understanding of the force that produces events, and give no answer to history's essential question.

Writers of universal history, who deal with all nations, seem to recognize how mistaken the specialist historians' view of the force producing events is. They do not treat it as a power built into heroes and rulers, but as the resultant of many differently directed forces. In describing a war, or the subjugation of a people, a general historian looks for the cause of the event not in the power of one man, but in the interaction of the many people connected to that event.

On this view, the power of historical figures—presented as the product of many forces—can no longer, it would seem, be treated as a force that itself produces events. And yet in most cases the universal historians still use the idea of power as a force that produces events in its own right, and treat it as a cause. In their accounts, a historical figure is first the product of his era, his power merely the resultant of various forces—and then his power is itself a force producing events. The historians Gervinus, Schlosser, and others, for instance, at one point prove that Napoleon was a product of the Revolution, of the ideas of 1789 and so on. At another point they plainly state that the campaign of 1812, and other things they disapprove of, were simply the product of Napoleon's misguided will, and that the very ideas of 1789 were stopped in their development by Napoleon's whim. The ideas of the Revolution and the general temper of the age produced Napoleon's power. But Napoleon's power suppressed the ideas of the Revolution and the general temper of the age.

This curious contradiction is not an accident. Not only does it turn up at every step, but the universal historians' accounts are made up, from end to end, of a chain of such contradictions. It happens because once the universal historians enter the field of analysis, they stop halfway.

To find component forces equal to a composite or resultant force (as in mechanics), the sum of the components must equal the resultant. The universal historians never observe this condition, and so, to explain the resultant forces, they are forced to bring in—alongside their insufficient components—some other, unexplained force acting on the outcome.

Specialist historians describing the campaign of 1813, or the restoration of the Bourbons, state plainly that these events were produced by Alexander's will. But the universal historian Gervinus, refuting this view of the specialist historians, tries to show that the campaign of 1813 and the restoration of the Bourbons came about because of other things besides Alexander's will—the activity of the statesmen and writers Stein, Metternich, Madame de Staël, Talleyrand, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others. The historian, in effect, breaks Alexander's power down into its components: Talleyrand, Chateaubriand, and the rest. But the sum of those components—that is, the interactions among Chateaubriand, Talleyrand, Madame de Staël, and the others—plainly does not add up to the resultant: the fact of millions of Frenchmen submitting to the Bourbons. The fact that Chateaubriand, Madame de Staël, and the others said certain things to one another only affected their own mutual relations, but does not account for the submission of millions. And so, to explain how the submission of millions of people resulted from these relations of theirs—that is, how component forces adding up to some quantity A produced a resultant a thousand times greater than A—the historian is again forced to fall back on power. This is the force he had denied, and he now treats it as the resultant of the forces, which means admitting an unexplained force acting on the outcome. And that is exactly what the universal historians do, and as a result they contradict not only the specialist historians but themselves.

Peasants, who have no clear idea of what causes rain, say, depending on whether they want rain or fine weather: "The wind has blown the clouds away," or, "The wind has brought up the clouds." In the same way, the universal historians sometimes, when it suits them and fits their theory, say that power is the result of events, and sometimes, when they want to prove something else, say that power produces events.

A third class of historians—the so-called historians of culture—following the path laid down by the universal historians, who sometimes treat writers and society ladies as forces producing events, take that force to be something else again. They find it in what is called culture, in intellectual activity.

The historians of culture are quite consistent with their forerunners, the writers of universal history: if historical events can be explained by the fact that certain people treated one another in such and such ways, why not explain them by the fact that certain people wrote certain books? Out of the immense number of signs that accompany every living phenomenon, these historians pick out the sign of intellectual activity and declare that this sign is the cause. But despite all their efforts to prove that the cause of events lies in intellectual activity, one can admit any connection between intellectual activity and the movement of peoples only with a considerable stretch. And one can never admit that intellectual activity controls people's actions. This view is not confirmed by facts such as the extremely cruel murders of the French Revolution, which grew out of the doctrine of the equality of man, or the extremely cruel wars and executions that grew out of the preaching of love.

But even granting as valid every one of the cleverly constructed arguments these histories are full of—even granting that nations are governed by some undefined force called an idea—history's essential question still goes unanswered. To the old power of monarchs, and to the influence of advisers and other people brought in by the universal historians, a newer force is now added—the idea—whose connection to the masses still needs explaining. One can understand that Napoleon had power, and so events occurred. With some effort, one can even accept that Napoleon, together with other influences, was the cause of an event. But how a book, Rousseau's Le Contrat Social (The Social Contract), had the effect of making Frenchmen start drowning one another cannot be understood without an explanation of the causal chain linking this new force to the event.

Undoubtedly some relation exists among everyone who lives at the same time, and so it's possible to find some connection between men's intellectual activity and their historical movements, just as a connection can be found between the movements of humanity and commerce, handicraft, gardening, or anything else you like. But why intellectual activity should be treated by the historians of culture as the cause, or as the expression, of the whole historical movement is hard to understand. Only the following considerations can have led historians to such a conclusion. (1) History is written by learned men, and so it is natural and gratifying for them to think that the activity of their own class provides the basis for the movement of all humanity—just as the same belief comes naturally and agreeably to merchants, farmers, and soldiers. (If they do not say so, it is simply because merchants and soldiers do not write history.) (2) Spiritual activity, enlightenment, civilization, culture, ideas—these are all vague, indefinite notions, under whose banner it is very easy to use words with an even less definite meaning, and which can therefore be worked into any theory.

But setting aside the intrinsic worth of histories of this kind (which may perhaps even be useful to someone, for something), the histories of culture—which all general histories are increasingly coming to resemble—are revealing in this respect. After seriously and painstakingly examining various religious, philosophical, and political doctrines as the causes of events, the moment they have to describe an actual historical event, such as the campaign of 1812, they involuntarily describe it as the outcome of an exercise of power. They say plainly that it was the result of Napoleon's will. In saying this, the historians of culture unwittingly contradict themselves, and show that the new force they have invented does not account for what happens in history, and that history can only be explained by bringing in a power they apparently do not recognize.

A locomotive is moving. Someone asks, "What's making it move?" A peasant says the devil is moving it. Another man says the locomotive moves because its wheels go round. A third insists the cause of its movement lies in the smoke the wind is carrying off.

The peasant cannot be refuted. He has a complete explanation. To refute him, someone would have to prove to him that there is no devil, or another peasant would have to explain that it isn't the devil but a German who's moving the locomotive. Only then, through the contradiction between them, would they see that both are wrong. But the man who says the movement of the wheels is the cause refutes himself, because once he's begun to analyze, he ought to keep going and explain why the wheels turn — and until he has traced things back to the ultimate cause, the pressure of steam in the boiler, he has no right to stop looking. The man who explains the movement of the locomotive by the smoke being carried backward has noticed that the wheels don't really explain anything, and has simply grabbed the first sign that occurred to him and offered that instead.
The only idea that can explain the movement of the locomotive is that of a force commensurate with the movement we observe.
The only idea that can explain the movement of peoples is that of some force commensurate with the whole movement of the peoples.

Yet to supply this idea, various historians reach for forces of entirely different kinds, none of which is commensurate with the movement observed. Some see it as a force built directly into heroes, the way the peasant sees the devil in the locomotive; others see it as a force resulting from the interplay of several other forces, like the movement of the wheels; others again see it as an intellectual influence, like the smoke that is blown away.

So long as histories are written about individuals — whether Caesars, Alexanders, Luthers, or Voltaires — rather than histories of everyone, absolutely everyone, who took part in an event, it is simply impossible to describe the movement of humanity without the idea of a force compelling people to direct their activity toward some given end. And the only such idea known to historians is power.

This idea is the one handle by which the material of history, as it is presented today, can be picked up and handled at all, and anyone who breaks that handle off, as Buckle did, without finding some other way of dealing with the material, simply deprives himself of the one available way of handling it. The necessity of the idea of power for explaining historical events is best demonstrated by the universal historians and the historians of culture themselves, who profess to reject that idea and yet inevitably fall back on it at every step.

In dealing with humanity's great question, the science of history so far is like money in circulation — paper money and coin. Biographies and the histories of individual nations are like paper money. They can be used, they can circulate, and they can serve their purpose without doing anyone any harm, and even to real advantage, as long as no one asks what actually backs them. You only have to forget to ask how the will of heroes produces events, and histories like Thiers' will be interesting, instructive, and may even carry a certain poetry. But just as doubts about the real value of paper money arise either because it is easy to print and too much of it gets printed, or because people try to exchange it for gold, so too doubts about the real value of such histories arise either because too many of them get written, or because someone, in simple honesty, asks: by what force did Napoleon actually do this? — that is, wants to exchange the current paper money for the real gold of genuine understanding.

Writers of universal history and of the history of culture are like people who, recognizing the flaws of paper money, decide to replace it with coin made of some metal that doesn't have the specific weight of gold. It may make a nice jingling sound, but that's all it will do. Paper money can fool the ignorant, but nobody is fooled by tokens of base metal that have no real value beyond their jingle. Just as gold is gold only if it can be put to use and not merely exchanged, universal historians will only be worth something once they can answer history's essential question: what is power? The universal historians give contradictory answers to that question, while the historians of culture dodge it and answer something else entirely. And just as tokens of imitation gold can only be used among people who have agreed to accept them as gold, or among those who don't know what real gold is, so the universal historians and historians of culture, without answering humanity's essential question, serve as currency for purposes of their own — only in universities, and among the mass of readers with a taste for what they call "serious reading."

History has given up the ancients' idea that a nation's will is divinely subordinated to some chosen man, and that this man's will in turn is subordinated to God. Without that idea, history cannot take a single step without contradicting itself, until it chooses one of two things: either return to the old belief in the direct intervention of God in human affairs, or arrive at a definite explanation of what is meant by that force which produces historical events and which we call "power."
A return to the first is impossible; the belief has been destroyed. And so it becomes essential to explain what power means.

Napoleon ordered an army raised and sent to war. We are so used to this idea, so accustomed to it, that the question of why six hundred thousand men went off to fight when Napoleon spoke certain words strikes us as senseless. He had the power, and so what he ordered was done.

This answer is entirely satisfactory if we believe the power was given to him by God. But the moment we stop believing that, it becomes essential to determine just what this power of one man over others actually is.

It cannot be the direct physical power of a strong man over a weak one—a domination based on applying or threatening physical force, like the strength of Hercules; nor can it rest on moral force, as some historians naively suppose when they say that the great figures of history are heroes, meaning men gifted with a special strength of soul and mind called genius. This power cannot rest on a predominance of moral strength, because—setting aside heroes like Napoleon, whose moral qualities are a matter of sharp disagreement—history shows us that neither a Louis XI, the French king, nor a Metternich, the Austrian statesman—both of whom ruled over millions of people—possessed any particular moral qualities; but, on the contrary, they were generally morally weaker than any of the millions they ruled.

If the source of power lies neither in the physical nor in the moral qualities of the one who holds it, then it must evidently be sought elsewhere—in the relation between the man who wields power and the people over whom he wields it.
And that is exactly how power is understood by the science of jurisprudence—that exchange bank of history, offering to trade history's understanding of power for real gold.
Power is the collective will of the people, transferred, through expressed or tacit consent, to their chosen rulers.

In the domain of jurisprudence, which consists of discussions about how a state and its power might be arranged if such an arrangement were possible at all, everything here is perfectly clear. But applied to history, this definition of power needs explaining.

The science of jurisprudence treats the state and power the way the ancients treated fire—as something that simply exists, absolutely. But for history, the state and power are merely phenomena, just as for modern physics fire is not an element but a phenomenon.

This basic difference between how history views the matter and how jurisprudence views it has a consequence. Jurisprudence can tell us, in detail, how power ought—in its opinion—to be constituted, and what power is when treated as something fixed outside of time. But to history's questions about how power actually changes over time, jurisprudence can give no answer at all.

If power is the collective will of the people transferred to their ruler, was Pugachev—the Cossack who led a peasant uprising—a representative of the people's will? If not, why was Napoleon I? Why was Napoleon III a criminal when he was captured at Boulogne, and why, later, were the people he himself arrested the criminals?

Do palace revolutions—in which sometimes only two or three people take part—transfer the people's will to a new ruler? In international relations, is the people's will also transferred to a conqueror? Was the will of the Confederation of the Rhine, the alliance of German states under Napoleon, transferred to Napoleon in 1806? Was the will of the Russian people transferred to Napoleon in 1809, when our army, allied with the French, went to fight the Austrians?
To these questions three answers are possible:

Three assumptions are possible. (1) We may assume that the will of the people is always transferred unconditionally to the ruler or rulers it has chosen, so that every emergence of a new power, every struggle against a power already appointed, must be regarded as a violation of the real power. (2) We may assume that the will of the people is transferred to rulers conditionally, under definite and known conditions, and show that every limitation on power, every conflict, even every destruction of power, results from the rulers' failure to observe the conditions under which their power was entrusted to them. (3) We may assume that the will of the people is delegated to rulers conditionally, but that the conditions are unknown and undefined, and that the rise of rival authorities, their struggles, and their falls, result simply from how well or badly the rulers fulfilled these unknown conditions under which the people's will passes from one person to another.
And these are the three ways historians actually do explain the relation between a people and its rulers.

Some historians—the biographical and specialist historians already mentioned—fail, in their simplicity, to grasp the real question of what power means. They seem to consider that the collective will of the people is transferred unconditionally to historical figures. So, in describing any single state, they treat that state's particular power as the one absolute, real power, and treat any force opposing it not as a power at all but as a violation of power—sheer violence.

Their theory, well suited to primitive and peaceful periods of history, runs into trouble when applied to complex and turbulent periods in the life of nations, during which several powers arise at once and struggle against one another. A Legitimist historian—a supporter of the old monarchy—will prove that the National Convention and the Directory, the revolutionary governments that followed, and Bonaparte too, were nothing but usurpers of the true power. A Republican historian will prove that the Convention was the real power, and a Bonapartist—a supporter of Napoleon—that the Empire was, and that all the rest were violations of power. Since these explanations plainly contradict one another, they can satisfy no one but young children.

Recognizing the falseness of this view of history, another group of historians say that power rests on a conditional delegation of the people's will to its rulers, and that historical leaders hold power only on condition of carrying out the program that the people's will has, by tacit agreement, prescribed for them. But what this program actually consists of, these historians do not say—or if they do, they keep contradicting one another.

Each historian, depending on his own view of what constitutes a nation's progress, looks for these conditions in the greatness, wealth, freedom, or enlightenment of the citizens of France or some other country. But setting aside the historians' disagreements over the nature of this program—even granting that some single, general program of these conditions exists—the facts of history almost always contradict the theory. If the conditions under which power is entrusted consist in the wealth, freedom, and enlightenment of the people, how is it that Louis XIV and Ivan the Terrible end their reigns peacefully, while Louis XVI and Charles I are executed by their own people? To this, historians answer that Louis XIV's conduct, though it went against the program, reacted on Louis XVI. But why did it not react on Louis XIV himself, or on Louis XV—why did it have to react precisely on Louis XVI? And what is the time limit on such reactions? These questions have no answer, and can have none. Just as little does this view explain why, for several centuries, the collective will is never withdrawn from a given line of rulers and their heirs, and then, suddenly, over the course of fifty years, passes to the Convention, to the Directory, to Napoleon, to Alexander, to Louis XVIII, to Napoleon again, to Charles X, to Louis Philippe, to a Republican government, and to Napoleon III. Trying to explain these rapid transfers of the people's will from one person to another—especially once international relations, conquests, and alliances are factored in—historians are forced to admit that some of these transfers are not normal delegations of the people's will, but accidents resulting from cunning, from mistakes, from craft, or from the weakness of some diplomat, ruler, or party leader. So that the greater part of the events of history—civil wars, revolutions, conquests—end up being presented by these historians not as the outcome of free transfers of the people's will, but as the outcome of the misdirected will of one or a few individuals—that is, once again, as usurpations of power. And so these historians too end up seeing, and admitting, historical events that are exceptions to their own theory.

These historians resemble a botanist who, having noticed that some plants grow from seeds that produce two seed-leaves, insists that everything that grows must sprout in exactly that way, and that the palm, the mushroom, and even the oak—which grow into full maturity looking nothing like two leaves—are deviations from the theory.

Historians of the third class assume that the will of the people is transferred to historical figures conditionally, but that the conditions themselves are unknown to us. They say that historical figures hold power only because they carry out the will of the people that has been delegated to them.
But in that case, if the force that moves nations lies not in the historical leaders but in the nations themselves, what significance do those leaders have at all?

But then the question arises whether the entire activity of the leaders serves as an expression of the people's will, or only some part of it. If the whole of a leader's activity counts as an expression of the people's will, as some historians suppose, then every detail of court scandal found in the biographies of a Napoleon or a Catherine must also express the life of the nation. That is obvious nonsense. But if only some particular side of a historical leader's activity expresses the people's life, as other, so-called "philosophical" historians believe, then, to know which side of a leader's activity expresses the nation's life, we would first have to know what the nation's life actually consists of.

Faced with this difficulty, historians of this class devise some highly obscure, intangible, and general abstraction, broad enough to cover any conceivable occurrence, and declare this abstraction to be the goal of humanity's movement. The most common generalizations adopted by nearly all historians are: freedom, equality, enlightenment, progress, civilization, culture. Having set up some such generalization as the goal of humanity's movement, historians go on to study the men who left behind the greatest number of monuments—kings, ministers, generals, authors, reformers, popes, journalists—according to how far, in the historian's opinion, these people advanced or hindered that abstraction. But it is nowhere proven that the goal of humanity actually consists in freedom, equality, enlightenment, or civilization. And the connection between the people and the rulers and enlighteners of humanity rests only on the arbitrary assumption that the collective will of the people is always transferred to the men we have noticed. So the activity of the millions who migrate, burn houses, abandon their fields, and destroy one another is never actually captured in the account of the activity of a dozen or so people who did none of that burning, farming, or killing.

History bears this out at every turn. Is the ferment among the peoples of the West at the end of the eighteenth century, and their surge eastward, explained by the activity of Louis XIV, XV, and XVI, their mistresses and their ministers, and by the lives of Napoleon, Rousseau, the philosopher Diderot, the playwright Beaumarchais, and the rest?
Is the movement of the Russian people eastward, toward Kazan and Siberia, captured in the details of Ivan the Terrible's disturbed character, or in his correspondence with the nobleman Kurbsky?

Is the movement of the peoples at the time of the Crusades explained by the lives and activities of the Godfreys—men like the Crusader Godfrey—and the Louis-es, the various kings named Louis, and their ladies? For us, that movement of peoples from west to east, leaderless, made up of a crowd of wanderers, and with Peter the Hermit, a preacher, among them, remains incomprehensible.
