And still more incomprehensible is the way that movement stopped once a rational and sacred goal for the Crusade—the liberation of Jerusalem—had been clearly spelled out by the historical leaders. Popes, kings, and knights urged the peoples on to free the Holy Land; but the people did not go, because the unknown cause that had earlier driven them to go no longer existed. The history of the Godfreys and the Minnesingers, the medieval poet-singers, plainly cannot cover the life of the peoples. And the history of the Godfreys and the Minnesingers has remained just that—the history of the Godfreys and the Minnesingers—while the history of the life of the peoples and their impulses has remained unknown.
Still less does the history of authors and reformers explain the life of the peoples to us.

The history of culture explains to us the impulses and living conditions and thoughts of a writer or a reformer. We learn that Luther had a hot temper and said such and such things; we learn that Rousseau was suspicious and wrote such and such books; but we do not learn why, after the Reformation, whole peoples massacred one another, or why, during the French Revolution, they guillotined one another.
If we combine both these kinds of history, as the newest historians do, we end up with a history of monarchs and writers—but not a history of the life of the peoples.

The life of nations is not contained in the lives of a handful of men, because the connection between those men and the nations has not been found. The theory that this connection rests on the transfer of the people's collective will to certain historical figures is a hypothesis unsupported by the experience of history.

The theory of the transfer of the people's collective will to historical figures may perhaps explain a great deal within the domain of jurisprudence, and be essential for its purposes; but applied to history, the moment revolutions, conquests, or civil wars occur—that is, the moment history actually begins—that theory explains nothing.
The theory looks irrefutable precisely because the act of transferring the people's will cannot be verified, since it never took place.
Whatever happens, and whoever may stand at the head of affairs, the theory can always claim that this person took the lead because the collective will was transferred to him.

The answers this theory gives to historical questions resemble the answers of a man who, watching a herd of cattle move, pays no attention to the varying quality of pasture in different parts of the field, or to the herdsman driving them, and instead credits the direction the herd takes to whichever animal happens to be walking in front.

"The herd is heading that way because the animal in front is leading it, and the collective will of all the other animals has been vested in that leader." This is what historians of the first class say—those who assume the people's will is transferred unconditionally.

"If the animals leading the herd keep changing, that's because the collective will of all the animals is transferred from one leader to another, depending on whether the animal is or isn't leading them in the direction the whole herd has chosen." That is the answer given by historians who assume that the collective will of the people is delegated to rulers under conditions they take to be known. (With this method of observation, it often happens that the observer, influenced by whichever direction he himself prefers, regards those as leaders who, owing to the people's change of direction, are no longer in front—they may be off to one side, or even at the back.)

"If the animals in front keep changing and the whole herd's direction keeps shifting, that's because, in order to follow a given direction, the animals transfer their will to whichever animals have caught our attention, and so to study the movements of the herd we have to watch the movements of all the prominent animals on every side of it." So say the third class of historians, who treat every historical figure, from monarchs to journalists, as the expression of their age.
The theory of the transfer of the people's will to historical figures is nothing but a paraphrase—a restatement of the question in different words.

What causes historical events? Power. What is power? Power is the collective will of the people transferred to one person. Under what condition is the people's will delegated to one person? On condition that this person expresses the will of the whole people. That is: power is power—in other words, power is a word whose meaning we do not understand.

If the realm of human knowledge were limited to abstract reasoning, then, having subjected to criticism the explanation of "power" that juridical science gives us, mankind would conclude that power is merely a word with no real existence behind it. But to understand phenomena, man has, besides abstract reasoning, experience, by which he tests his reasoning. And experience tells us that power is not merely a word, but a phenomenon that actually exists.

Not to speak of the fact that no description of the collective activity of men can do without the idea of power, the existence of power is proven both by history and by observing events happening around us now.

Whenever an event occurs, a man appears, or several men appear, by whose will the event seems to have taken place. Napoleon III issues a decree, and the French go to Mexico. The King of Prussia and the Prussian statesman Bismarck issue decrees, and an army enters Bohemia. Napoleon I issues a decree, and an army enters Russia. Alexander I gives a command, and the French submit to the Bourbons, France's former ruling dynasty. Experience shows us that, whatever the event, it is always tied to the will of one or several men who decreed it.

Historians, following the old habit of acknowledging divine intervention in human affairs, want to see the cause of events in the expressed will of someone who holds power—but that assumption is confirmed neither by reason nor by experience.

On one hand, reflection shows that the expression of a man's will—his words—is only part of the general activity expressed in an event, as in a war or a revolution, and so, without assuming some incomprehensible, supernatural force—a miracle—one cannot accept that words could be the immediate cause of the movements of millions of men. On the other hand, even granting that words could be the cause of events, history shows that the expressed will of historical figures does not, in most cases, produce any effect. Their commands are often not carried out, and sometimes the exact opposite of what they order happens instead.
Without admitting divine intervention in human affairs, we cannot treat "power" as the cause of events.
Power, seen from the standpoint of experience, is simply the relationship that exists between the expression of someone's will and the carrying out of that will by others.
To explain the conditions of that relationship, we must first establish a conception of the expression of will as it applies to man, not to God.

If God issues a command, expresses His will, as ancient history tells us, then the expression of that will is independent of time and caused by nothing, since the Divine is not subject to events. But when we speak of commands that express the will of men acting in time and in relation to one another, to explain the connection between commands and events we must restore two things: (1) the condition underlying everything that happens—the continuity of movement in time, both of the events themselves and of the person giving the command; and (2) the inevitability of the connection between the person giving the command and those who carry it out.

Only the expression of God's will, independent of time, can apply to a whole chain of events unfolding over years or centuries, and only God, independent of everything, can by His will alone determine the direction of humanity's movement; but man acts in time, and takes part himself in what happens.

Restoring the first condition we left out — that of time — we see that no command can be carried out without some earlier order having already been given that makes carrying out the later command possible.

No command ever appears out of nowhere, and no single command covers a whole chain of events on its own; each command follows from another, and never refers to a whole series of events, only to one moment of an event.

When, for instance, we say Napoleon ordered his armies to go to war, we are compressing into one simultaneous statement a whole series of consecutive commands, each dependent on the last. Napoleon could not have ordered, and never did order, an invasion of Russia as a single act. Today he ordered such and such dispatches written to Vienna, to Berlin, to Petersburg; tomorrow such and such decrees and orders to the army, the navy, the commissariat, and so on and so on — millions of commands, forming a whole series that corresponded to the series of events which brought the French armies into Russia.

If, throughout his reign, Napoleon issued commands about invading England, and spent more time and effort on that scheme than on anything else, and yet, across his entire reign, never once actually attempted to carry it out, while he did undertake an expedition into Russia, a country with which he repeatedly said he thought it desirable to remain allied — that happened because his commands did not correspond to the actual course of events in the first case, but did correspond to it in the second.

For an order to be reliably carried out, it is necessary that a man order something that can actually be carried out. But knowing in advance what can and cannot be carried out is impossible — not just in a case like Napoleon's invasion of Russia, in which millions of people took part, but even in the simplest event, since in either case a million obstacles can arise to prevent it. Every order that is carried out is always just one out of an immense number that go uncarried out. All the impossible orders, the ones inconsistent with the course of events, simply go uncarried out. Only the possible ones link up with a consecutive series of commands matching a series of events, and get carried out.

Our mistaken idea that an event is caused by the command that precedes it comes from the fact that once the event has happened, out of thousands of commands only the handful consistent with that event were actually carried out, and we forget all about the rest, which went uncarried out simply because they couldn't be. Beyond that, the main source of our error here is that in historical accounts, a whole series of countless, varied, petty events — like all the ones that led the French armies into Russia — gets generalized into a single event, matching the result that series of events produced, and to match this generalization, the whole series of commands also gets generalized into a single expression of will.

We say that Napoleon wanted to invade Russia, and invaded it. In reality, nowhere in the whole of Napoleon's activity do we find anything resembling a single expression of that wish; instead we find a long series of orders, or expressions of his will, pointed in all sorts of different and indefinite directions. Out of a long series of Napoleon's orders that were never carried out, one series — the one for the campaign of 1812 — was carried out, not because those particular orders were any different from the rest that went uncarried out, but because they happened to coincide with the actual course of events that led the French army into Russia. It is exactly as in stencil work: this or that figure comes out not because the paint was applied from this side or that, but because it was applied everywhere, all over the figure cut into the stencil.
So when we examine the relation in time between commands and events, we find that a command can never be the cause of an event, but that a definite kind of dependence does exist between the two.

To understand what this dependence consists of, we need to restore another condition we left out — one that applies to every command that comes not from God but from a man: namely, that the man giving the command himself takes part in the event.
This relation between the one who commands and those he commands is exactly what we call power. This relation consists of the following.

For joint action, people always come together in certain arrangements in which, whatever differences there may be in the goals set for the joint action, the relation among the people taking part is always the same.

When people come together in these arrangements, they always settle into relations such that the larger number take the more direct part, and the smaller number the less direct part, in the collective action they have joined together to perform.
Of all the arrangements in which people join together for collective action, one of the most striking and clear-cut examples is an army.

Every army is made up of the lowest ranks — the rank and file — of whom there are always the greatest number; then the next rank up — corporals and noncommissioned officers — of whom there are fewer; then still-higher officers, of whom there are fewer still; and so on, up to the highest military command, which is concentrated in a single person.

A military organization can quite accurately be compared to a cone, whose base, with the widest diameter, consists of the rank and file; the next, smaller section of the cone consists of the next grades up in the army; and so on up to the apex, whose point represents the commander in chief.

The soldiers, of whom there are the most, make up the lower section of the cone, its base. The soldier himself does the stabbing, the hacking, the burning, the pillaging, and always receives his orders for these actions from men above him; he himself never gives an order. The noncommissioned officers, of whom there are fewer, carry out the action itself less often than the soldiers do, but they already give commands. An officer acts directly even less often, but commands still more. A general does nothing but command the troops, point out the objective, and almost never uses a weapon himself. The commander in chief never takes any direct part in the action itself, but only issues general orders about the movement of the whole mass of troops. The same kind of relation among people shows up in every combination of men formed for a common activity — in farming, in trade, in every kind of administration.

And so, without going through every adjoining layer of the cone, every rank in the army, or every position in any administrative or public undertaking from the lowest to the highest, we can see a law: that people, in order to act together, combine in relations such that the more directly they take part in carrying out the action, the less they command and the more numerous they are, while the less direct their part in the action itself, the more they command and the fewer of them there are — rising this way from the lowest ranks up to the man at the very top, who takes the least direct part in the action and directs his activity almost entirely to commanding.
This relation between those who command and those who are commanded is what makes up the essence of the idea we call power.

Having restored the condition of time under which all events occur, we find that a command is carried out only when it corresponds to a matching series of events. Having restored the essential condition of the relation between those who command and those who carry out, we find that, by the very nature of things, those who command take the smallest part in the action itself, and that their activity is directed almost entirely to commanding.

When an event is taking place, people voice their opinions and wishes about it, and since the event results from the collective activity of many people, one of the opinions or wishes expressed is bound to come true, at least approximately. When one of these expressed opinions comes true, it gets linked to the event as a command that preceded it.

Some men are hauling a log. Each of them says how and where he thinks it should be hauled. They haul the log away, and it turns out to have been done the way one of them said. He gave the order. There we have command and power in their most basic form. The man who did the most physical work could hardly think much about what he was doing, or reflect on or command what the joint effort would produce; while the man who did more commanding would obviously work less with his hands, given how much more talking he was doing.

When a larger group of people direct their activity toward a shared goal, there is a still sharper division of those who, because their activity goes toward directing and commanding, take less part in the direct work.

When a man works alone, he always has a certain set of reflections which, as it seems to him, guided his past activity, justify his present activity, and steer his plans for the future. A group of people does exactly the same thing, letting those who don't take a direct part in the activity work out considerations, justifications, and guesses about their collective activity.

For reasons known or unknown to us, the French began drowning and killing one another. And to match the event, its justification appeared: the belief that this was necessary for the welfare of France, for liberty, for equality. People stopped killing one another, and this event too came with its justification: the necessity of centralizing power, of resisting Europe, and so on. Men marched from west to east killing their fellow men, and the event was accompanied by phrases about the glory of France, the baseness of England, and so on. History shows us that these justifications make no sense at all and contradict one another—as when killing a man is the result of recognizing his rights, and the killing of millions in Russia is justified by the need to humiliate England. But in their own day, these justifications carry a very necessary meaning.

These justifications free the people who produce events from moral responsibility. These temporary goals are like the broom fixed to the front of a locomotive to clear snow off the rails ahead: they clear men's moral responsibility out of their path.

Without such justification, there would be no answer to the simplest question that comes up when examining any historical event: how is it that millions of men commit collective crimes—wage war, commit murder, and so on?

Given the complicated forms of political and social life in Europe today, can any event be imagined that is not prescribed, decreed, or ordered by monarchs, ministers, parliaments, or newspapers? Is there any collective action that cannot find its justification in political unity, in patriotism, in the balance of power, or in civilization? So that every event that occurs inevitably coincides with some expressed wish, and, once it has found its justification, presents itself as the result of the will of one man, or of several men.

Whichever direction a ship is moving, the flow of the water it cuts will always be visible just ahead of it. To the people on board, the movement of that flow will seem like the only perceptible motion there is.

Only by watching closely, moment by moment, the movement of that flow, and comparing it with the movement of the ship, do we convince ourselves that every bit of it is caused by the ship moving forward, and that we were misled because we ourselves were moving without noticing it.

We see the same thing if we watch, moment by moment, the movement of historical figures—that is, if we restore the necessary condition of everything that happens, the continuity of movement in time—and if we never lose sight of the essential connection between historical figures and the masses.

When the ship moves in one direction, there is one and the same wave ahead of it; when it turns often, the wave ahead of it turns often too. But wherever it turns, there will always be a wave anticipating its movement.

Whatever happens, it always looks as though that very event had been foreseen and decreed. Wherever the ship goes, the rush of water ahead of it—which neither steers it nor speeds it up—foams out in front, and from a distance seems to us not merely to move on its own but to govern the ship's movement too.

By examining only those expressions of the will of historical figures which, as commands, were related to events, historians have assumed that events depended on those commands. But by examining the events themselves, and the connection historical figures actually had to the people, we have found that they, and their orders, were dependent on events. The undeniable proof of this conclusion is that, no matter how many commands are issued, the event does not happen unless other causes exist for it. But as soon as an event does happen, whatever it may be, some will always be found, out of all the continually expressed wishes of different people, which, by their meaning and their timing, are related as commands to the events.
Arriving at this conclusion, we can now answer directly and positively history's two essential questions:
(2) What force produces the movement of the nations?

(1) Power is the relation of a given person to other individuals, in which the more this person expresses opinions, predictions, and justifications for the collective action being carried out, the less he actually takes part in that action.

(2) The movement of nations is caused not by power, nor by intellectual activity, nor even by some combination of the two, as historians have supposed, but by the activity of all the people who take part in the events, and who always combine in such a way that those who take the largest direct share in an event bear the least responsibility for it, and vice versa.

Morally, it looks as though the person wielding power causes the event; physically, it is those who submit to that power who cause it. But since moral activity is inconceivable apart from physical activity, the cause of the event lies neither in the one nor the other, but in the union of the two.
Or, put another way, the very idea of a "cause" does not apply to the phenomena we are examining here.

In the last analysis, we arrive at the circle of infinity—the final boundary that human reason, in every field of thought, reaches whenever it is not merely toying with its subject. Electricity produces heat; heat produces electricity. Atoms attract one another; atoms repel one another.

Speaking of the interaction between heat and electricity, or between atoms, we cannot say why it happens; we simply say that it is so, because it is inconceivable otherwise, because it has to be so, and call it a law. The same applies to historical events. Why wars and revolutions happen, we do not know. We only know that to produce one action or the other, people combine into a certain formation in which they all take part, and we say this is so because it cannot be thought of otherwise—in other words, that it is a law.

If history dealt only with external phenomena, establishing this simple, obvious law would be enough, and we could consider the argument finished. But the law of history concerns man. A particle of matter cannot tell us that it doesn't feel the law of attraction or repulsion and that the law is false — but man, who is the subject of history, says plainly: I am free, and therefore not subject to the law.
The problem of man's free will, even when it goes unspoken, makes itself felt at every step of history.

Every historian who has thought seriously about the subject has run up against this question, whether he wanted to or not. All the contradictions and obscurities in history, and the false path historical science has followed, come down to nothing but the failure to solve that question.
If every man's will were free — if each man could act however he pleased — then all of history would be nothing but a series of disconnected incidents.

If, over the course of a thousand years, even one man in a million could act freely, that is, exactly as he chose, then it is obvious that a single free act by that one man, in violation of the laws governing human action, would destroy the very possibility of there being any laws at all for the whole of humanity.
If there is even one law governing the actions of men, free will cannot exist, because then a man's will is subject to that law.

In this contradiction lies the problem of free will, which since the most ancient times has occupied the best human minds, and since the most ancient times has been presented in its whole tremendous significance.

The problem is this: if we consider man as a subject of observation, from whatever standpoint — theological, historical, ethical, or philosophical — we find a general law of necessity to which he, like everything that exists, is subject. But if we look at him from within, as something we are directly conscious of, we feel ourselves to be free.
This consciousness is a source of self-knowledge entirely separate from, and independent of, reason. Through reason, man observes himself; but only through consciousness does he know himself.
Apart from consciousness of self, no observation and no use of reason is even conceivable.

To understand, to observe, to draw conclusions, a man must first of all be conscious of himself as a living being. A man is only conscious of himself as living through the fact that he wills — that is, that he is conscious of his own volition. But his will, which forms the very essence of his life, he can only recognize, and cannot help recognizing, as free.

If, watching himself, a man sees that his will is always steered by one and the same law — whether he is observing his need to eat, or to use his mind, or anything else — he can only recognize this unvarying direction of his will as a limitation on it. If it weren't free, it couldn't be limited. A man's will seems limited to him only because he is never conscious of it except as free.
You say: I am not free. But I have lifted my hand and let it fall. Everyone understands that this illogical answer is an irrefutable demonstration of freedom.
That answer expresses a consciousness that is not subject to reason.

If the consciousness of freedom were not a separate and independent source of self-consciousness, it would be subject to reasoning and to experience — but in fact no such subjection exists, and none is even conceivable.

A whole series of experiments and arguments proves to every man that, as an object of observation, he is subject to certain laws, and man submits to them, and never resists the laws of gravity or impermeability once he has learned them. But that same series of experiments and arguments proves to him that the complete freedom he is conscious of in himself is impossible, that his every action depends on his makeup, his character, and the motives acting on him — and yet man never submits to the conclusions of these experiments and arguments. Having learned from experiment and argument that a stone falls downward, a man believes this without question, and always expects the law he has learned to hold.
But learning, with equal certainty, that his will is subject to laws, he does not, and cannot, believe it.

However often experiment and reasoning may show a man that he will do the same thing as before, under the same conditions and with the same character, yet when he approaches, under those same conditions and with that same character, an action that always ends the same way — even for the thousandth time — he feels just as certain as he did before the experiment that he can act however he pleases. Every man, savage or sage, however irrefutably reason and experiment may prove to him that it is impossible to imagine two different courses of action under exactly the same conditions, feels that without this irrational notion — which is the very essence of freedom — he cannot imagine life. He feels that however impossible it may be, it is so, because without this idea of freedom he would not only be unable to understand life, he would be unable to live for even a single moment.

He could not live, because every one of man's efforts, every impulse toward life, is nothing but an effort to increase freedom. Wealth and poverty, fame and obscurity, power and subordination, strength and weakness, health and sickness, culture and ignorance, work and leisure, having enough and going hungry, virtue and vice — these are all just greater or lesser degrees of freedom.
A man with no freedom at all cannot be conceived of except as a man deprived of life.

If the idea of freedom looks, to reason, like a senseless contradiction — like the possibility of performing two actions at the very same instant, or an effect without a cause — that only proves that consciousness is not subject to reason.

This consciousness of freedom is unshakeable and irrefutable. No experiment or argument can touch it. Every thinker has recognized it, and every person without exception has felt it. Without it, no conception of man is even possible. It makes up the other side of the question.
Man is the creation of an all-powerful, all-good, all-seeing God. What is sin — the idea that arises from man's consciousness of his own freedom? That is a question for theology.

The actions of men are subject to general, unchanging laws expressed in statistics. What is man's responsibility to society — the idea that follows from the idea of freedom? That is a question for jurisprudence.

A man's actions arise from his innate character and the motives acting on him. What is conscience, and the perception of right and wrong in actions, which follows from the consciousness of freedom? That is a question for ethics.

Man, seen in connection with the general life of humanity, appears subject to the laws that determine that life. But the same man, apart from that connection, appears to be free. How should the past life of nations, and of humanity, be regarded — as the result of man's free activity, or as the result of his constrained activity? That is a question for history.

Only in our own self-confident age of popularized knowledge — thanks to that most powerful engine of ignorance, the diffusion of printed matter — has the question of free will been put on a level on which the question itself cannot exist. In our time, the majority of so-called advanced people — that is, the crowd of ignoramuses — have taken the work of naturalists, who deal with only one side of the question, for a solution to the whole problem.

They say, and write, and print, that the soul and free will do not exist, because man's life is expressed in muscular movements, and muscular movements are conditioned by the activity of the nerves. And they say the soul and free will do not exist because, at some unknown point in time, we descended from apes. They say this without the least suspicion that thousands of years ago this same law of necessity, which they are now trying so eagerly to prove through physiology and comparative zoology, was not merely acknowledged by every religion and every thinker, but has never been denied. They fail to see that the role of the natural sciences here is simply to serve as an instrument for illuminating one side of the question. The fact that, from the standpoint of observation, reason and will are merely secretions of the brain, and that man, following the general law, may have developed from lower animals at some unknown point in time — this only restates, from a new angle, a truth admitted thousands of years ago by every religious and philosophical system: that from the standpoint of reason, man is subject to the law of necessity. But it does not advance the solution of the question by a hair's breadth; the question has another side, the opposite side, grounded in the consciousness of freedom.

If men descended from apes at some unknown point in time, that is just as comprehensible as their having been made from a handful of earth at some fixed point in time. In the first case the unknown quantity is the time; in the second it is the origin. And the question of how man's consciousness of freedom can be reconciled with the law of necessity to which he is subject cannot be solved by comparative physiology and zoology. In a frog, a rabbit, or an ape we can observe only muscular and nervous activity; but in man we observe consciousness as well as muscular and nervous activity.

The naturalists, and their followers, who think they can settle this question, are like plasterers assigned to plaster one side of a church wall who, taking advantage of the head foreman's absence, get carried away and plaster right over the windows, the icons, the woodwork, and the walls that still have no buttresses — and are delighted that, from a plasterer's point of view, everything now looks so smooth and even.

In solving the question of free will versus inevitability, history has one advantage over the other branches of knowledge that deal with the question: for history, the question does not concern the essence of man's free will as such, but only its manifestation in the past, under specific conditions.
With respect to this question, history stands to the other sciences the way experimental science stands to abstract science.

And so for history, the insoluble mystery presented by the incompatibility of free will and inevitability, which exists for theology, ethics, and philosophy, does not exist in the same way. History looks at a picture of man's life in which the union of these two contradictions has already taken place.

In actual life, every historical event, every human action, is understood very clearly and definitely, without any sense of contradiction, even though every event presents itself as partly free and partly compelled.

To resolve the question of how freedom and necessity combine, and what constitutes the essence of these two ideas, the philosophy of history can and should take the opposite path from the other sciences. Instead of first defining the ideas of freedom and inevitability on their own, and then sorting the phenomena of life under those definitions, history should derive its definition of freedom and inevitability from the immense quantity of phenomena it has before it — phenomena that always appear to depend on these two elements.
Whatever picture we consider of the activity of many men, or of a single individual, we always take it to be the result partly of man's free will and partly of the law of inevitability.

Whether we're talking about the migrations of peoples and the incursions of barbarians, or the decrees of Napoleon III, or someone's choice, an hour ago, of one direction over several possible ones for a walk, we are not conscious of any contradiction. The degree of freedom and the degree of inevitability governing these people's actions seem clearly defined to us.

Our sense of how much freedom is involved often shifts depending on the point of view from which we look at the event, but every human action appears to us as some combination of freedom and inevitability. In every action we examine, we see a certain measure of freedom and a certain measure of inevitability. And always, the more freedom we see in an action, the less inevitability we perceive, and the more inevitability, the less freedom.
The proportion of freedom to inevitability shrinks and grows depending on the point of view from which we regard the action, but the relation between them is always an inverse one.

A drowning man who grabs onto someone else and pulls him under; a hungry mother, worn out from feeding her baby, who steals food; a soldier trained to obey discipline who, on duty, kills a defenseless man at the word of command — all of these seem less guilty, that is, less free and more subject to the law of necessity, to someone who knows the circumstances these people were in, and more free to someone who does not know that the man was himself drowning, that the mother was starving, that the soldier was standing in the ranks under orders, and so on. In the same way, a man who committed a murder twenty years ago and has since lived peacefully and harmlessly in society seems less guilty, and his action more the product of the law of inevitability, to someone considering it twenty years later than to someone who examined it the day after it happened. And in just the same way, every action of an insane man, a drunk man, or a man in a state of high excitement seems less free and more inevitable to someone who knows the mental state of the person who did it, and seems more free and less inevitable to someone who doesn't know it. In every one of these cases, our sense of freedom grows or shrinks, and our sense of compulsion shrinks or grows correspondingly, depending on the point of view from which we look at the action. So that the greater our sense of necessity, the smaller our sense of freedom, and the other way around.
Religion, the common sense of mankind, the science of jurisprudence, and history itself all understand this relation between necessity and freedom in the same way.
Every single case in which our sense of freedom and necessity increases or decreases depends on three considerations:
(1) The relation of the man who commits the act to the external world.
(2) His relation to time.
(3) His relation to the causes that led to the action.

The first consideration is how clearly we perceive the man's relation to the external world, and how clearly we understand the particular position he occupies among everything that coexists with him. This is what makes it obvious that a drowning man is less free and more subject to necessity than a man standing on dry land, and why the actions of a man tightly bound up with others in a densely populated area, or bound by family, professional, or business obligations, seem clearly less free and more subject to necessity than the actions of a man living alone, in isolation.

If we consider a man in isolation, apart from his relation to everything around him, every one of his actions seems free to us. But the moment we see his relation to anything around him — his connection to anything at all, a person speaking to him, a book he is reading, the work he is engaged in, even the air he breathes or the light falling on the things around him — we see that each of these circumstances influences him and controls at least some part of his activity. And the more of these influences we perceive, the more our sense of his freedom shrinks, and the more our sense of the necessity weighing on him grows.

The second consideration is how clear or unclear the man's relation to time is, and how clearly we perceive the place his action occupies in time. This is the reason the fall of the first man, which resulted in the whole human race, seems clearly less free than a man's marrying today. It's the reason the life and activity of people who lived centuries ago, connected to me only through time, cannot seem to me as free as the life of a contemporary, whose consequences are still unknown to me.
The degree of our sense of freedom or inevitability depends, in this respect, on how much or how little time has passed between the performance of the action and our judgment of it.

If I examine an act I performed a moment ago, in roughly the same circumstances I am in now, the action seems to me undoubtedly free. But if I examine an act performed a month ago, now that I am in different circumstances, I cannot help recognizing that if that act had not been committed, much that came from it — good, pleasant, even essential — would not have happened. If I think back on an action still further in the past, ten years ago or more, the consequences of my action become even plainer to me, and I find it hard to imagine what would have happened had I not performed it. The further back I go in memory — or, which comes to the same thing, the further forward I go in judgment — the more doubtful my belief in the freedom of my own action becomes.

In history we find a very similar progression of conviction concerning the part free will plays in the general affairs of humanity. A contemporary event seems to us, without question, the doing of everyone known to be involved in it; but with a more distant event, we already see its inevitable results, results that rule out any possibility of things having gone otherwise. And the further back we go in examining events, the less arbitrary they appear.

The Austro-Prussian war seems to us, without doubt, the result of Bismarck's cunning maneuvering, and so on. The Napoleonic wars still seem to us, though already less certainly, the result of their heroes' will. But in the Crusades, we already see an event occupying a definite place in history, one without which we cannot imagine the subsequent history of Europe, even though to the chroniclers of the Crusades that event appeared to be simply the result of certain people's will. As for the migration of the peoples, it does not occur to anyone today to suppose that the remaking of the European world depended on Attila's whim. The further back in history the object of our observation lies, the more doubtful the free will of those involved in the event becomes, and the more evident the law of inevitability.

The third consideration is the degree to which we grasp that endless chain of causation, which reason inevitably demands, in which every phenomenon we understand — and therefore every one of man's actions — must have its own definite place, as the result of what came before and the cause of what will follow.

The better we know the physiological, psychological, and historical laws that observation has established, laws by which man is governed, and the more accurately we perceive the physiological, psychological, and historical causes of an action, and the simpler the action we are observing, and the less complex the character and mind of the person involved, the more subject to inevitability, and the less free, our own actions and those of others appear to us.

When we don't understand the cause of an action at all — whether it's a crime, a good deed, or even something simply neither one nor the other — we credit it with a greater degree of freedom. In the case of a crime, we demand punishment for it most urgently of all; in the case of a virtuous act, we rate its merit most highly. In a neutral case, we see in it more individuality, more originality, more independence. But if even one of the countless causes of the act becomes known to us, we recognize a certain element of necessity in it, and we grow less insistent on punishing the crime, or praising the virtuous act, or crediting the seemingly original action with real freedom. That a criminal was raised among criminals lessens his guilt in our eyes. The self-sacrifice of a father or a mother, or self-sacrifice that comes with some hope of reward, is easier to understand than self-sacrifice with no reward at all, and so it strikes us as less deserving of sympathy and less the result of free will. The founder of a sect, or of a political party, or an inventor, impresses us less once we know how, or by what means, the ground was prepared for his work. If we have a large stock of examples before us, if our attention is constantly bent on tracing the connection between cause and effect in people's actions, then the more correctly we trace effects back to their causes, the more compelled and the less free their actions appear to us. If we examined simple actions, and had a vast number of such actions under observation, our sense of their inevitability would be even greater still. The dishonest conduct of the son of a dishonest father, the misbehavior of a woman who has fallen in with bad company, a drunkard's relapse into drinking, and so on, are all actions that seem less free to us the better we understand their cause. If the man whose actions we are considering stands on a very low level of mental development — a child, a madman, a simpleton — then, knowing the causes of the act and the simplicity of the character and intelligence involved, we see so large an element of necessity, and so little free will, that as soon as we know the cause behind the action, we can predict the result.

These three considerations alone are the basis for the idea of diminished responsibility for crimes, and for the extenuating circumstances recognized by every legal code. Responsibility appears greater or smaller depending on how much or how little we know about the circumstances the person being judged was placed in, on how much or how little time has passed between the act and its investigation, and on how much or how little we understand the causes that led to the action.

In this way, our conception of free will and inevitability gradually shrinks or grows according to how closely or loosely a man is connected to the external world, how remote or recent the time is, and how dependent his life is on the causes in relation to which we consider it.

So that if we examine a man whose connection to the external world is well known, where a great deal of time separates the action from our examination of it, and where the causes of the action are most accessible to us, we arrive at the conception of a maximum of inevitability and a minimum of free will. If we examine a man who depends little on external conditions, whose action took place very recently, and the causes of whose action lie beyond our knowledge, we arrive at the conception of a minimum of inevitability and a maximum of freedom.

In neither case can we ever arrive at a conception of either complete freedom or complete necessity — no matter how much we shift our point of view: however clearly or however obscurely we make out the connection between the man and the external world, however long or short the interval of time, however comprehensible or incomprehensible the causes of the action.

(1) No matter to what degree we imagine a man exempt from the influence of the external world, we never arrive at a conception of freedom in space. Every human action is inevitably conditioned by what surrounds him and by his own body. I raise my arm and let it fall. My action seems free to me; but when I ask myself whether I could have raised it in every possible direction, I see that I raised it in the direction where there was the least obstruction to the action, either from the things around me or from the way my own body is built. Out of every possible direction, I chose the one with the fewest obstacles. For my action to be free, it would have had to meet no obstacle at all. To imagine a man as free, we would have to imagine him outside of space — which is plainly impossible.

(2) No matter how closely we bring the moment of judgment up against the moment of the deed, we never arrive at a conception of freedom in time. If I examine an action carried out a second ago, I still have to recognize it as unfree, because it is irrevocably tied to the instant at which it was performed. Can I lift my arm? I lift it — but then I ask myself: could I have refrained from lifting it at that moment, the one that has already passed? To convince myself, I don't lift it the next moment. But I am not now refraining from doing so at that first moment when I asked the question. Time has gone by, time I could not hold back; the arm I lifted then is not the same arm I am now refraining from lifting, nor is the air I lifted it in the same air that surrounds me now. The moment in which that first movement happened is irrevocable, and in that moment I could make only one movement, and whatever movement I made would be the only one. That I did not lift my arm a moment later does not prove that I could have refrained from lifting it then. And since at that single moment of time I could make only one movement, it could not have been any other. To imagine it as free, we would have to imagine it in the present, on the border between past and future — that is, outside of time, which is impossible.

(3) No matter how much harder we make it to trace the causes, we never arrive at a conception of complete freedom, that is, of an absence of cause. However inaccessible to us the cause of any expression of will may be, whether our own or someone else's, the first demand of reason is to assume a cause and go looking for it, because no phenomenon is conceivable without one. I raise my arm to perform an action independent of any cause — but my very wish to perform an action without a cause is itself the cause of my action.

But even granting that we could reduce this remaining element of inevitability to something infinitely small, equal to zero — by imagining a man wholly exempt from every influence, considering only his momentary action in the present, unprompted by any cause — we still would not have arrived at a conception of complete freedom in man, because a being uninfluenced by the external world, standing outside time and independent of cause, is no longer a man at all.
In the same way, we can never imagine the action of a man entirely without freedom and wholly subject to the law of inevitability.

(1) However much we increase our knowledge of the spatial conditions in which a man is situated, that knowledge can never be complete, because the number of those conditions is as infinite as space itself. And so, as long as not every condition influencing a man has been identified, there is no complete inevitability, but a certain measure of freedom remains.

(2) However much we lengthen the period of time between the action we are examining and our judgment of it, that period will be finite, while time itself is infinite, and so here too there can never be absolute inevitability.
(3) However accessible the chain of causation behind any action may be, we will never know the whole of it, since it has no end — and so again we never arrive at absolute inevitability.

But beyond this: even granting that the remaining minimum of freedom equals zero, suppose we assumed a complete absence of freedom in some particular case — say, that of a dying man, an unborn child, or an idiot. Doing so would destroy the very conception of man in the case we are examining, because the moment there is no freedom, there is also no man. And so the conception of a man's action subject solely to the law of inevitability, with no element of freedom at all, is just as impossible as the conception of a man's completely free action.

And so, to imagine the action of a man entirely subject to the law of inevitability, without any freedom, we would have to assume knowledge of an infinite number of spatial relations, an infinitely long period of time, and an infinite chain of causes.
To imagine a man perfectly free, not subject to the law of inevitability at all, we would have to imagine him utterly alone, beyond space, beyond time, and free of any dependence on cause.

In the first case, if inevitability were possible without freedom, we would have arrived at a definition of inevitability purely by the laws of inevitability itself — that is, a mere form without content.

In the second case, if freedom were possible without inevitability, we would have arrived at an unconditioned freedom beyond space, time, and cause, which, precisely because it was unconditioned and unlimited, would amount to nothing — mere content without form.
We would, in fact, have arrived at the two fundamentals out of which man's whole view of the universe is built: the incomprehensible essence of life, and the laws that define that essence.

Reason says: (1) space, along with every form of matter that makes it visible, is infinite, and cannot be imagined otherwise. (2) Time is infinite motion, without a single moment of rest, and cannot be thought of otherwise. (3) The connection between cause and effect has no beginning and can have no end.

Consciousness says: (1) I alone exist, and everything that exists is nothing but me; therefore I contain space within myself. (2) I measure the flow of time by the fixed moment of the present, the only moment in which I am conscious of myself as alive; therefore I stand outside time. (3) I am beyond cause, because I feel myself to be the cause of every manifestation of my own life.
Reason gives voice to the laws of inevitability. Consciousness gives voice to the essence of freedom.
Freedom limited by nothing is the essence of life, in man's consciousness. Inevitability without content is man's reason, in its three forms.
Freedom is the thing examined. Inevitability is what does the examining. Freedom is the content. Inevitability is the form.

Only by separating these two sources of knowledge, related to one another as form is related to content, do we arrive at the mutually exclusive, separately incomprehensible conceptions of freedom and inevitability.
Only by uniting them do we get a clear conception of man's life.
Apart from these two concepts, which in their union define one another as form and content, no conception of life is possible at all.
Everything we know about the life of man is nothing but a certain relation between free will and inevitability — that is, between consciousness and the laws of reason.
Everything we know about the external world of nature is likewise nothing but a certain relation between the forces of nature and inevitability, or between the essence of life and the laws of reason.

The great forces of nature lie outside us, and we are not conscious of them; we call those forces gravitation, inertia, electricity, animal force, and so on. But we are conscious of the force of life within man, and we call that freedom.

But just as the force of gravitation, incomprehensible in itself yet felt by every man, is only intelligible to us to the extent that we know the laws of inevitability it is subject to — from the first realization that all bodies have weight, up to Newton's law — so too the force of free will, incomprehensible in itself yet something everyone is conscious of, is only intelligible to us to the extent that we know the laws of inevitability it is subject to — from the fact that every man dies, all the way up to knowledge of the most complex economic and historical laws.
All knowledge is simply a matter of bringing this essence of life under the laws of reason.

Man's free will differs from every other force in that man is directly conscious of it, but to reason, it is no different from any other force at all. The forces of gravitation, electricity, or chemical affinity are only distinguished from one another by how reason defines them. In just the same way, the force of man's free will is distinguished by reason from the other forces of nature only by the definition reason gives it. Freedom, apart from necessity, that is, apart from the laws of reason that define it, is in no way different from gravitation, or heat, or the force that makes things grow — to reason, it is nothing but a momentary, undefinable sensation of life.

The undefinable essence of the force moving the heavenly bodies, the undefinable essence of the forces of heat and electricity, or of chemical affinity, or of the vital force — these form the content of astronomy, physics, chemistry, botany, zoology, and so on. In exactly the same way, the force of free will forms the content of history. But just as the subject of every science is the manifestation of this unknown essence of life, while that essence itself can only be the subject of metaphysics — so too the manifestation of the force of free will in human beings, in space, in time, and in dependence on cause, forms the subject of history, while free will itself is the subject of metaphysics.

In the experimental sciences, what we know we call the laws of inevitability; what we don't know we call vital force. Vital force is merely an expression for the unknown remainder left over, beyond what we know, of the essence of life.

So too in history: what is known to us we call the laws of inevitability; what is unknown we call free will. Free will, for history, is merely an expression for the unknown remainder of what we know about the laws of human life.

History examines the manifestations of man's free will in connection with the external world, in time, and in dependence on cause — that is, it defines this freedom by the laws of reason, and so history is a science only to the extent that this free will is defined by those laws.

Treating man's free will as something capable of influencing historical events — that is, as a force not subject to law — would be the same for history as the recognition of a free force moving the heavenly bodies would be for astronomy.

That assumption would destroy the very possibility of there being laws at all — of there being any science whatsoever. If even a single body moves freely, the laws of Kepler and Newton are overturned, and no conception of the movement of the heavenly bodies survives. If a single action is due to free will, then not one historical law can exist, and no conception of historical events either.

For history, there exist lines along which human wills move, lines whose one end is lost in the unknown, but at whose other end a man's conscious will, in the present, moves through space, time, and dependence on cause.
The more this field of motion opens up before our eyes, the more evident the laws governing that movement become. Discovering and defining those laws is the task of history.

From the standpoint history now occupies, on the path it currently follows — looking for the causes of events in man's free will — a scientific statement of those laws is impossible, because however restricted man's free will may be, the moment we treat it as a force not subject to law, the existence of any law becomes impossible.

Only by shrinking this element of free will down to the infinitesimal — that is, by treating it as an infinitely small quantity — can we convince ourselves of the absolute inaccessibility of the causes, and only then, instead of searching for causes, will history be able to take the discovery of laws as its task.

The search for these laws has long since begun, and the new ways of thinking that history must adopt are being worked out at the very same time as the old method of history — endlessly dissecting and re-dissecting the causes of phenomena — moves toward its own self-destruction.

Every human science has traveled this same road. On reaching the infinitesimal, mathematics, the most exact of sciences, abandons the process of analysis and takes up a new process, the integration of unknown, infinitely small quantities. Setting aside the conception of cause, mathematics looks instead for law — that is, for the property common to all these unknown, infinitely small elements.

The other sciences have proceeded, in a different form, along that same path of reasoning. When Newton stated the law of gravity, he did not say that the sun or the earth possessed a property of attraction; he said that all bodies, from the largest to the smallest, have the property of attracting one another — that is, setting aside the question of what causes the bodies to move, he expressed the property common to all of them, from the infinitely large to the infinitely small. The natural sciences do the same: setting the question of cause aside, they search for laws. History stands on that same path. And if history's real object is to study the movement of nations and of humanity, and not simply to narrate episodes from the lives of individuals, then it too, setting aside the conception of cause, should search for the laws common to all the inseparably interconnected, infinitesimal elements of free will.

From the moment Copernicus's law was discovered and proved, the simple recognition that it was not the sun but the earth that moved was enough to destroy the ancients' entire picture of the cosmos. By disproving that law, it might have been possible to hold onto the old conception of how the heavenly bodies moved; but without disproving it, it would seem impossible to keep studying the Ptolemaic universe. And yet, even after Copernicus's law was discovered, the Ptolemaic universe went on being studied for a long time.

From the moment the first person stated and proved that the number of births, or of crimes, is governed by mathematical laws, that a given form of government is determined by certain geographic and economic conditions, and that certain relations between population and land produce the migrations of peoples, the foundations on which history had been built were, in essence, destroyed.

By refuting these new laws, the old view of history might have been preserved; but without refuting them, it would seem impossible to go on studying historical events as the results of man's free will. Because if a given form of government was established, or a given migration of peoples took place, as a consequence of such and such geographic, ethnographic, or economic conditions, then the free will of the individuals who appear to us to have established that form of government, or brought about the migration, can no longer be regarded as the cause.

And yet the old kind of history continues to be studied side by side with the laws of statistics, geography, political economy, comparative philology, and geology — laws that directly contradict its own assumptions.

The struggle between the old views and the new was long and stubbornly fought out in the philosophy of the physical world. Theology stood guard over the old views and accused the new ones of violating revelation. But once the truth had won out, theology settled itself just as firmly onto the new foundation.

Just as long and just as stubborn is the struggle now underway between the old and the new conception of history, and theology, in the same way, stands guard over the old view and accuses the new one of undermining revelation.

In both cases, on both sides, the struggle stirs up passion and smothers the truth. On one side there is fear, and regret at the thought of losing the whole edifice built up over centuries; on the other, a passion for tearing it down.

To the men who fought against the emerging truths of physical philosophy, it seemed that admitting that truth would destroy faith in God, in the creation of the firmament, and in the miracle of Joshua the son of Nun. To the defenders of the laws of Copernicus and Newton — to Voltaire, for example — it seemed that the laws of astronomy destroyed religion, and he used the law of gravitation as a weapon against it.

Just so, it now seems as though the moment we admit the law of inevitability, we destroy the conception of the soul, of good and evil, and every institution of church and state built upon those conceptions.

And just so, uninvited defenders of the law of inevitability today, like Voltaire in his own time, use that law as a weapon against religion — even though the law of inevitability in history, like the law of Copernicus in astronomy, far from destroying the foundation on which the institutions of church and state are built, actually strengthens it.

Just as in the question of astronomy then, so in the question of history now, the whole disagreement rests on whether or not we accept something absolute as the measure of visible phenomena. In astronomy it was the fixity of the earth; in history it is the independence of the individual personality — free will.

Just as in astronomy the difficulty of accepting the earth's motion lay in giving up the immediate sensation of the earth's fixity and of the planets' motion, so in history the difficulty of accepting that personality is subject to the laws of space, time, and cause lies in giving up the direct feeling of one's own independence. But just as in astronomy the new view said, "It's true that we don't feel the earth moving, but by assuming it stands still we arrive at absurdity, while by assuming it moves, though we don't feel it, we arrive at laws," so too in history the new view says, "It's true that we aren't conscious of our own dependence, but by assuming we have free will we arrive at absurdity, while by assuming our dependence on the external world, on time, and on cause, we arrive at laws."

In the first case, it was necessary to give up the consciousness of an unreal fixity in space, and to accept a motion we could not feel; in the present case, it is just as necessary to give up a freedom that does not exist, and to accept a dependence we are not conscious of.
